shlokas.artha: King Daśaratha, a friend of gods and subduer of foes, was known for his scriptural knowledge. Seeing his virtues, the Eternal Lord himself chose to become his son under the guise of aiding the world.
He studied the Vedas, performed sacrifices for the gods, honored his ancestors and kinsmen, mastered his senses, delighted in political ethics, and completely destroyed his enemies.
He distributed wealth as a cloud sheds water, shared a seat with Indra, worshipped none other than Śiva, and surpassed the fame of all great archers.
Virtuous and surrounded by a multitude of great Brahmins, that excellent king, who satisfied the denizens of heaven, shone for the stability of the world like the consecrated fire at a sacrifice.
That famous king, equal to Indra, resided in Ayodhyā, a city that rivaled heaven in prosperity, was pleasant in all seasons, and was inhabited by enlightened Brahmins.
The city of Ayodhyā stood as the ultimate limit of Brahmā's creative skill, seemingly mocking Indra's celestial city with the upward-leaping rays of its brilliant jewels.

In that city, the houses containing excellent gems, pearls, and diamonds, decorated with various minerals and gardens, and filled with beautiful women, resembled the peaks of Mount Meru inhabited by Apsarases.
The brilliant rays of jewels from within the houses, emerging through the lattice windows, appeared like the falls of the Gaṅgā's waters from the cliffs of the Himālayas.

The wise king took delight in his three excellent wives—who were virtuous and brought desire, wealth, and fame—just as a scholar delights in the three branches of knowledge acquired at the proper time.
Desiring sons, the king had the wise and high-minded Sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a master of rituals with mature spiritual insight, brought to his city by beautiful women.

The self-controlled king desired the lord of sages to perform a sacrifice for obtaining sons; subsequently, that diligent sage, a repository of knowledge, performed the ritual for the birth of progeny.
The sage drove away demons from the altar, performed the main and ancillary rites, offered oblations, and sought a boon for the king's attainment of sons.
When the meticulously performed and flawless sacrifice was completed, the three noble queens consumed the remains of the oblation to give birth to four capable sons.
Kausalyā easily gave birth to Rāma, Kaikeyī followed with Bharata, and Sumitrā gave birth to the noble-acting Śatrughna along with Lakṣmaṇa.
The wise Vasiṣṭha, foremost of self-controlled ascetics and knower of supreme truth, honored the twice-born, warded off terrifying spirits, and performed the initiation ceremony for the princes.
They studied the entire Veda with its limbs and mastered victorious weapons. Being virtuous, they simultaneously occupied the minds of the people despite their diverse dispositions.
Then Viśvāmitra, whose sacrifices were hindered by demons, approached the king to request Rāma for protection. The king welcomed him with the traditional madhuparka offering.
The king asked the sage if his meditation was auspicious—the meditation through which he sought to conquer rebirth, withdrew from sensory perceptions, and realized the ultimate truths.
The sage declared the well-being of his meditation but noted that demons were obstructing forest sacrifices. He requested that Rāma, with Lakṣmaṇa, destroy those enemies and their power.
Hearing those words, the king fainted, unable to bear separation from his son. Then the prosperous monarch was addressed by the eminent and powerful ascetic.

You have found protection in me during times of fear, and we too have attained protection through you for the enhancement of Dharma. The warrior class and the priestly class exist for mutual benefit; therefore, do not harbor doubt and send your son.

By him, the great enemy who stands at the forefront of the battle shall be slain. O great-souled King, do not disregard me; a person like me does not entrust a heavy responsibility to one who is unworthy.

Reflecting that the fire of a Brahmana's anger would consume his family and that his departing son would cause him grief-stricken pain, the King first deliberated in this manner and then permitted his son's departure.
Honoring the King with blessings, the gratified sage set out again for his hermitage. The humble Prince, bearing a bow glowing with deadly arrows, followed behind him as a vanguard.
As the victorious Rāma, with a radiant countenance, set out for the sacred forest, the bold Lakṣmaṇa—son of the three mothers, master of all weapons, and devoted to virtue—accompanied him.

As the lion of the Raghu dynasty departed, armed with arrows and intent on slaying the demons, while gripping his bow firmly with colorful finger-guards, the auspicious young women of the city somehow restrained their tears despite their heavy grief.

Then the Brahmanas loudly offered blessings to him, while others sounded trumpets with a tumultuous and sweet noise. His arm throbbed auspiciously, signaling the desired outcome, and favorable birds chirped loudly in the trees.
Having departed from that city, he beheld the autumn season before him, spreading its splendor all around over the trees, lakes, rivers, and the bright, lustrous quarters of the sky.
The red lotuses, with petals trembling from the touch of waves, appeared like the brilliance of a blazing fire with smoke due to the swarming bees, shining with extraordinary fiery beauty.

Seeing their own richness stolen by the waters through the reflections of the riverside forests, the banks, as if in indignation, displayed the beauty of lotuses through the blossoming of land-lotuses.
At daybreak, the tree on the bank, with clear dewdrops trickling from the tips of its leaves like tears and birds chirping, seemed to weep for the closing night-lotus.
The forests and waters, with flowers and lotuses containing hidden bees resembling eyes, seemed to gaze at each other's beauty with wonder and respect.

The day-lotus, its form trembling from the morning breeze, discarded the bee whose body was yellowed by the pollen of the night-lotus, acting like an angry, proud woman who cannot tolerate her lover's union with another.

The hunter, wishing to kill a deer that stood still while captivated by the song of honey-licking bees, failed to concentrate on his target as he himself became distracted by the melodious cries of eager swans.
A cloud on the mountain slope, scattered by the wind, white like snow with little water remaining, and enhancing the mouths of rivers, imitated the majesty of the lord of mountains.
A lion, roaring in a mountain bower near water, heard his own echoes and, mistaking them for the roars of another lion, prepared in anger to pounce.
He saw waters filled with fresh lotuses, heard the humming of bees, and smelled the fragrant breeze blowing, which was infused with the scent of lotuses.
Kākutstha plucked flowers by bending the creepers, touched the waters by descending to the river, and sat upon a beautiful stone out of curiosity with a gentle smile.
In the morning, he saw the eastern waters nearby, shimmering with the rays of the sun, looking like the gathered brilliance of the sun melted on the earth by streams of light.
He was delighted to see long, straight rows of excellent crops spreading across the directions, alluring to the eyes, clean, appearing to ooze sap, and free of weeds in between.
He observed cow-pens crowded with honest men, untouched by the sorrow of separation, who paid the prescribed royal taxes on time and were devoid of artificial finery.
He rejoiced upon seeing the cowherd women’s modest behavior—the true ornament of women—their lovely, straightforward glances, and their simple, trustworthy natures.
The dance of the cowherd women, characterized by turning sides, graceful limb movements, and beautiful swaying hips, accompanied by the deep rhythmic sound of churning, delighted him.
Nearby, a herd of swift-footed, timid deer, leaping high and appearing beautiful in the forest at the end of the rainy season, increased his curiosity.
Flocks of swans, white as Kunda flowers, hidden among clusters of white lotuses and on sandy banks covered with foam, were recognized only by their melodious cries, pleasing to the ear.
There was no water without beautiful lotuses, no lotus without a bee clinging to it, no bee that did not hum sweetly, and no humming that did not captivate the heart.

Constant performers of sacrifices, emaciated by penance, wandering ascetics holding jars of consecrated water, and other sages worshipped him—the adorable one, worthy of the world’s worship—with flowers and fruits.

Then, the son of Gādhi, of unblemished soul, intending to have the demons slain in battle, taught the prince the sciences known as Vijayā and Jayā in the prescribed manner to repel the hosts of Rākṣasas.

Ever vigilant for the welfare of others, the sage gave Rāma a collection of unerring missiles that would remain steady in combat, for the sake of the imminent great battle and the destruction of the night-stalkers.

In the forest, a demoness named Tāḍakā, intent on killing and seeking an opportunity to strike, approached him who appeared like a Brāhmaṇa but held brilliant weapons. Rāma slew her as she sought to destroy the sacrifice.

Then he beheld the penance grove, its lush branches glistening with the soot from the flames of sacrificial fires, and where the sweet chirping of birds was drowned out by the rising sounds of Vedic chanting.
There, lions did not devour the small deer, and birds felt completely secure. The swaying creepers shone, bending down as if out of a desire to offer their fruits.
The chief forest-dwellers, experts in hospitality, honored them with seats, water for the feet, and garlands. The two princes accepted the seats and other offerings mixed with madhuparka.
"You have borne the burden of the world submerged and oppressed by demons with your arms. Now, protect the sacrificial offerings as well," thus the ascetics addressed the two princes.
Rāma replied to them, "Let the proposed righteous work proceed as desired. May the fire of our arrows be fanned by the winds of your penance against the fuel-like enemies."
Then they duly commenced the ritual with the prepared sacrificial materials. The ritual, performed by skilled priests and directed toward the south, was noticed by the encroaching demons.
Then the sky was pervaded by night-stalkers, like monsoon clouds, with reddish-brown, coarse, upright hair, veiny legs, tall as mountain peaks, and large tawny eyes.
With his bow strung, his arm and fist steady, his eyes raised, his right thigh bent, and his left leg lowered, Lakṣmaṇa, drawing the bow vigorously, struck them with pure arrows.

To Mārīca, pointed out by Viśvāmitra, who was screaming harshly and was famous for his illusions, Rāma, an expert in missiles, spoke these profound words loudly with a smiling face as he stood firm in battle.
"You, who only fill your own belly, kill those who gather fruits from the trees for the sake of human flesh. Why do you not show mercy to those whose wealth does not last until tomorrow?"

The demon replied, "O son of Daśaratha, we eat Brāhmaṇas and kill those who perform sacrifices. We turn cities into abodes of the dead. This is our innate nature; we have never been ordained for Vedic conduct."

Rāma said, "O Rākṣasa, it is true that this is your nature. But my duty is different and opposed to yours. Following the conduct of a Kṣatriya, wielding the bow and arrow, I shall destroy you, the haters of Brahman."

Thus, speaking to each other, Rāma and the night-stalker began their combat. Then the scion of Raghu, regarding the demon as insignificant as a blade of grass, threw him far from the battlefield with an arrow.
The minds of the Brāhmaṇas became tranquil. The sky rained down showers of flowers. The sacrifice proceeded without hindrance. The sage then addressed more words to the prince.

"This earth, possessing heroes and being greatly honored by you—the conqueror of the devourers—at this sacrifice for the gods, does not feel inferior even to heaven, which is adorned by the wielder of the thunderbolt."
By whom Bali was bound, the ocean churned, nectar taken, the demon host conquered, and the earth supported during its distress at the end of an aeon—to him, this current burden is not at all heavy.
Speaking such sweet and beneficial words, the pleased sage, wishing Rāma to seize the fame of kings, led him to the sacrificial ground of the King of Mithilā at the conclusion of the sacrifice.

Are these two Mitra and Varuṇa? Or are they the two Aśvins eager to drink the Soma juice? Those two lions among men amazed and surpassed everyone present in the hermitage of Janaka with their extraordinary beauty.

Wishing to test the strength of Rāma's arms, Janaka had him hold that bow with which the wielder of Pināka (Śiva) had destroyed the city of the demons. The scion of the Raghu dynasty (Rāma), smiling, broke it easily.

Then, desiring to give away his daughter, Janaka, the chief of Mithilā, dispatched messengers—skilled in crossing rivers, knowledgeable about mountains, and experienced travelers—on swift horses to Ayodhyā, the city of King Daśaratha.

Thereafter, though he was very old, King Daśaratha, having heard of his son's deeds from the messengers, traveled on swift horses. Without any fatigue in his journey, he reached Mithilā quickly, just like a young man.

Janaka honored King Daśaratha, who was the most eminent among kings, most beloved, as venerable as a teacher, great in character, an abode of virtuous deeds, possessed of vast fame, and superior in glory.

Janaka addressed King Daśaratha, saying that Indra, by sharing his throne with him (who is well-versed in the three goals of life), had proven his wisdom among the gods. Then the King of Mithilā spoke these words.

His daughter, the Princess of Mithilā (Sītā), who appeared like a moving golden creeper, like a stationary flash of lightning fallen from heaven, or like the presiding deity of the moon's beauty, was given in marriage to Rāma.
Then Rāma, whose conduct was beneficial to the whole world, married Sītā. She was suitable for him and enhanced the glory of the Raghu dynasty, appearing as radiant as fine gems, pearls, and gold.
At a suspicious dawn, filled with joy and praised by panegyrists, the army, well-traveled and abundant in cavalry, kings, and elephants, set out toward Ayodhyā along with the King.

On the way, the formidable Paraśurāma, son of Jamadagni, appeared before them. He was broad-chested, held an arrow in hand, was as tall as two palm trees, carried a bow, and had arms reaching down to his knees.
Paraśurāma loudly challenged Rāma: "String this bow with an arrow; do not pass by!" King Daśaratha, knowing the prowess of the sage and loving his children, humbly spoke, seeking to appease him.

"O Paraśurāma, you have conquered the assembly of kings many times and satisfied your ancestors with the blood of kings. Restraining your anger against those who are not your enemies, why do you pay heed to this child Rāma?"
When Paraśurāma, out of pride, did not heed Daśaratha's words, the young Prince Rāma then strung the bow with a heavy arrow and cut off the heavenly worlds conquered by the sage.
With Paraśurāma defeated, the armies, becoming cheerful and making loud sounds, fearlessly and swiftly marched along various paths with the permission of the elderly King Daśaratha.
Due to its great speed, the army brought near the distant regions and quickly left behind the places it had just reached. Without fatigue, the radiant army arrived swiftly at Ayodhyā.
Through the slaughter of the demons in battle and the defeat of Paraśurāma, the exterminator of the Kṣatriyas, Prince Rāma became enriched with glory. There was no one to whom he did not become dear.
Then, proclaiming loudly, "I shall consecrate my son to the kingdom," King Daśaratha, having gladdened the hearts of his citizens and servants, made the entire world extremely happy once again.
He ordered for him a throne with a footstool, resembling a blazing fire, made of refined gold and beautiful diamonds, with highly precious gems arranged in distinct sections.
He quickly dispatched strong-bodied, well-fed men in groups, carrying golden jars, to fetch sacred water from all directions on foot with great effort.
Skilled men appointed by the King to various tasks sprinkled the city's streets, hoisted flags, released incense into the air, and scattered various flowers in all directions.
At that time, unable to endure the situation and without consulting Bharata, who had gone to his maternal grandfather's house, Kaikeyī—driven by delusion—chose Rāma's exile to the forest.
Incited with greed for the kingdom by backbiters and transformed by feminine frailty, she did not consider the fault in Rāma's exile, public infamy, or the impending death of the King.
Even as the King promised wealth and lands to turn Rāma back, he was disregarded by her. The demand for Bharata's consecration was driven into his mind like a stake of sorrow.
Then, wishing to send the Prince into exile, the grieving King ordered his departure to the forest in a chariot driven by Sumantra, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā.
Some blamed the restless King, while others wept loudly with tears. Some spoke of Bharata's deceit, and another exclaimed, "Fie upon Kaikeyī!"
Thinking "Tomorrow Rāma will be gone to the forest," the people suffered intensely from grief. However, other steady-minded individuals, having abandoned their anger, resolved to follow the Prince.

As the two were about to depart, they said to the lamenting people who approached them: "Alas, why do you grieve for us in this moment of prosperity, when we have fulfilled our purpose by obeying our father's command?"
Can the great debt to him—who created us, protected us from fears, and always nourished us well—be repaid by this trivial act of going to the forest?
Better for one to perish instantly like a flash of lightning or wither away like parched grass than to fail to abide by the command of elders, whether for a difficult goal or even exile.
"O citizens, return!" he said. "Be the removers of father's grief, and do not regard Bharata as different from me." Then he told the charioteer, "Drive the chariot onward."
Perceiving the people's intention to follow by their gestures, Rāma spent one night with them. Then, protecting them from the hardships of forest life, he departed stealthily by a ruse at dawn.
They shed tears and wailed piteously, sighing warmly again and again. Crying out, "O Rāma! Alas, what misery!" they returned with their hearts still dwelling on him.
The charioteer too, filled with great sorrow, purified himself and the horses with the waters of the Gaṅgā. Thinking of the two descendants of Raghu and Sītā, and sighing warmly, he entered the city.
Upon returning, the people saw the city like a sky deprived of the sun and the moon. Though filled with the stars of kings, all its activities were paralyzed by the darkness of grief.
Seeing Sumantra without Rāma, the King lost all hope and fell from his fortitude. He desired no wine, did not anoint himself with perfumes, and took no interest in beautiful garments.

Consumed by the fire of grief, King Daśaratha could not find rest anywhere. Despite being anointed with cooling sandalwood paste, uśīra, and lotus stalks to soothe his body, he succumbed to the agony of separation from his sons and ascended to the heavenly abode.

The queens of the king wailed loudly, tore their hair, and beat their bodies in despair. They cast off their ornaments, fell upon the ground, and shattered their bangles in intense mourning for their departed lord.

While the relatives comforted the queens, they preserved the king's body in oil, awaiting Bharata's return. Following the advice of the ministers, they dispatched young messengers to bring the prince back quickly from his maternal home.

Residing at his maternal home, Bharata perceived an ill omen concerning the king. He described a dream to his friends in which he saw the sun falling from the sky and flickering on the earth below, indicating a great calamity.

When the messengers arrived and urged him to depart, informing him of the urgent situation, Bharata was filled with longing for his elders. Desirous of reaching home quickly, he set out with great haste.

Driven by affection and mental agitation, Bharata feared that some misfortune had befallen his kinsmen. Ominous signs appeared as packs of jackals and deer made terrifying sounds and did not move in auspicious directions.

Returning from his journey and preparing to enter the city, Bharata noticed an eerie silence. He did not hear the usual roar of the crowds, the chanting of the Vedas, or the busy sounds of merchants trading in the marketplace.

His mothers, their eyes brimming with tears, approached and wailed loudly for the deceased king. The warriors, led by the priests and ministers, were also overcome with intense grief and lamentation as they met Bharata.

Looking around for Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa and failing to find them, Bharata began to weep uncontrollably. He questioned those present, who then related the tragic events exactly as they had transpired.
With a fierce frown and eyes reddened and swollen with rage and tears, Bharata severely rebuked Kaikeyī. He repeatedly plunged into an ocean of ceaseless sorrow, unable to contain his grief.

Bharata lamented that the princes and Sītā were suffering in the forest, the king was dead, the queens were widowed, and the land was left without a ruler. He cursed the great misfortune and ignominy initiated by Kaikeyī.
Declaring that this was not his will, Bharata swore thousands of oaths to prove his innocence. Overwhelmed by grief for his father and the exiled Rāma, he rolled on the ground, weeping piteously.

Consoling the prince, the ministers bore the king's body to the cremation ground. Accompanied by priests, they arranged the sacrificial vessels, preparing to perform the final oblations and funeral rites for the monarch.
They raised banners of silk and fine cloth, and played flutes, drums, and cymbals. Loud conches were blown in every direction, and saffron and sandalwood were brought to honor the departed king.

Placing gold pieces on the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth, they laid the body on an antelope skin with the head pointing east. After arranging the vessels according to tradition, the priest offered the body to the blazing funeral pyre.

After the offerings of water and funeral cakes were completed, Bharata rejected the coronation offered by the subjects. Wishing to humbly bring Rāma back, he set out for the forest accompanied by the citizens of Ayodhyā.

The earth shone with the multitude of people, mighty elephants, chariots, and horses moving swiftly in all directions, even through pathless terrain. Though the people were without ornaments due to grief, the massive procession appeared magnificent.

They gathered fruits and flowers from the forests, bathed in the rivers, and offered libations to their ancestors. They wandered freely on the sandy banks and rested under the cool shade of trees along their journey.

Reaching the banks of the Tamasā river, which is purified by its connection with the Gaṅgā, they proceeded to bathe in the holy waters of the Yamunā, their weariness dispelled by the sacred atmosphere.

They reached the hermitage of the sage Bharadvāja, where Rāma had previously rested. The sage, who had conquered hunger through his spiritual power, quenched their thirst with cool water and offered them the abundance of forest fruits.

The travelers, proceeding on foot, bowed with humility to Sage Bharadvāja and his disciples, who were then instructing those observing silence, sleeping on the ground, constantly practicing yoga, and seeking liberation.
To offer hospitality to the guests, the wish-fulfilling trees (Kalpavṛkṣas) bore fruit through yogic power. They also produced garments that were soft, long, and full of splendor.
In that place, celestial women led by Tilottamā, eager to follow commands, stood with humility. They sang passionately, danced with graceful gestures, bowed elegantly, and spoke noble words.
The affectionate Sage, having prepared various garments, food, drinks, and beds in a pleasant space, then said to them: 'Enter, sit down, drink, eat, and sleep.'
Having eaten happily, worn fine clothes, and stayed the night, they reached the beautiful forests of the Mandākinī river at dawn, traveling quickly with chariots, horses, and elephants.
After hearing news of Rāma from the Vaikhānasa ascetics, they climbed towards Mount Citrakūṭa, where chirping birds gathered and whose peaks touched the clouds, blocking the sun’s path.
Seeing the army covering the directions, Lakṣmaṇa (Saumitri), having strung his bow and donned armor, stood ready to fight with sharp arrows, his eyebrows raised in agitation.

Rāma (Dāśarathi) recognized those approaching slowly on foot as his own kinsmen; they wore white upper garments, carried no weapons, were filled with sorrow, lacked hostile thoughts, and desired to salute him.

Driven by intense grief, they reached Rāma’s presence, crying and expressing their sorrow completely. They loudly announced that the King (Daśaratha) had died due to the grief of separation from Rāma.
Having wept piteously for a long time and recited the lineage names, they reached the river. Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa then offered two handfuls of water as a libation while standing in the water.

Rāma spoke to his younger brother: 'Father assigned me to the easy task of forest exile, but alas, he assigned you to the difficult task of ruling the kingdom. O hero! Do not grieve; bear this burden.'
If you, who are wise and learned in the wisdom of elders, do not fulfill our father's word, how could any man ever desire a son even if his lineage were perishing?
If you value our word, and if you rule while I am away, and if you feel ashamed for not abiding by our father's command, then abandon your doubt, go, and rule the earth.
Bharata righteously replied to Rāma: 'How can I, being younger, venture to bear the burden of the kingdom meant for the eldest? Do not involve me in the destruction of our family's fame.'
This powerful force of elephants and horses, these royal jewels, and this assembly of kings—that I should be the lord of the earth while you are present is unthinkable; let that thought be stilled.
To him who spoke thus, Rāghava said: 'Go, Bharata, taking my sandals. Casting aside all doubt and being honored by the people, govern the kingdom of the entire world according to our resolve.'
After Bharata returned, the wise Rāma, honored by the sage Atri, entered the penance-forest and proceeded toward the Daṇḍaka forest.
While wandering through the great forest with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he was forcibly seized and carried away by a terrifying, hungry demon who had lifted him up.
Breaking the arms of the demon named Virādha, who was difficult even for Yama to subdue, the two brothers buried him head-downwards and feet-upwards in the earth.
Then, those two tigers among the Raghus went to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga, which was graced with divine splendor and was a refuge for those seeking protection.
Śarabhaṅga, after pointing out the nearby dwelling of the sage Sutīkṣṇa, offered his body into the fire in the presence of Rāma.
"We remained in this forest because we knew you would come. Now that you have been seen, may you be well; we are departing for the state won by our own merits."
After Śarabhaṅga had been consumed by fire, Rāma lived in a leaf-hut near the sage Sutīkṣṇa, constantly visiting various hermitages.
Living in forests suitable for habitation and sleeping on beds of leaves, the hospitable Rāma roamed about, piercing deer with his arrows immediately after rising from bed.
Honoring those who studied the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda, the golden-complexioned Rāma ate the best roasted meat after first offering it to the gods.
Wearing tree-bark garments as fine as newly woven cloth that covered his whole body, Rāma, equipped with arrows, a sword, a bow, and armor, wandered while protecting the Brāhmaṇas.
Rāma, the enemy of serpents and fearless as a cloud, roamed through forests where satiety was achieved through fruits alone, abandoning pastures fit for cattle.
His bright weapons ready for bands of wicked beings, Rāma wandered through the nearby hermitages, honoring those who performed sacrifices and were surrounded by assemblies of great sages.
Thinking about the prosperity and adversity of the great sages today, yesterday, tomorrow, and on other days, he became dear to them.
Reciting prayers during the evening twilight when the cows return, and waking up earlier than the birds to bow to the sun in the morning, he remained steadfast.
Then, he was seen at his leaf-hut by a lustful demoness. She, disregarding him because he was married, directed her attention toward the son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa).
She possessed a waist with three folds and eyes reaching the roots of her ears; with her exquisite skin and speech, she was like a crescent moon at the beginning of a fortnight.
She had beautiful feet, thighs like an elephant's trunk, and soft palms and fingers; she was endowed with broad and firm hips.
Carrying a face with a prominent nose, pure teeth, and dangling earrings, the garlanded woman with a smiling countenance brought happiness to those who beheld her.
Moving repeatedly after approaching the best of the Raghus (Rāma) and desiring him as her husband, the lustful and sweet-speaking woman requested him to make her his beloved.
"O son of Sumitrā! Being desirous, marry me, who am lovely and submissive, to be your companion for the enjoyment of a full human lifespan without any hesitation."
He (Lakṣmaṇa) said to her: "In this forest, once a cow-pen but now terrifying to both men and women, why do you, whose beauty is unseen even by the sun, wander about so fearlessly?"
Desiring mortal men, you who are radiant and possess divine attributes, moving like an apsaras, how do you roam here so independently?
In this forest crowded with those who look fiercely, why are you, devoid of modesty and skilled in soliciting lovers, not accompanied by a husband?
Desire the descendant of Raghu (Rāma) as your husband in the leaf-hut; he is my master, possesses a beautiful wife, and has eyes extending to his ears.
His body is anointed with sandalwood paste, his face is adorned with ear-rings, and his hands, efficient in all deeds in battle, reach down to his knees.
He has tied a sword near his waist for the protection of the weak and wields a bow as hard as stone, along with arrows, which is unbearable for others to carry.

He is the conqueror of those who obstruct sacrifices in battle, the progenitor of the continuity of dharma in the forest, and provides constant fearlessness to the sages along with their wives and cattle.
Then, repeatedly turning back and saying respectful words like "O Rāma, marry me!", she entered the hut of Rāma.
Rāma said: "That one (Lakṣmaṇa) is without a wife, while I have one; he will cherish you better as a husband. Go to him alone, do not let him go."
Her mind tormented by the falling of Cupid's weapons, she, lusting like a cow for a great bull, went back to Lakṣmaṇa.
While she was repeatedly approaching, the best of the Raghus (Lakṣmaṇa), being prone to cutting, raised his sword and made her face noseless.
She said: "I am Śūrpaṇakhā by name; surely I was not recognized by you, since this punishment fit for a territory has been inflicted upon me."
Desirous of destroying them, she stood in the sky, showed her terrifying form, cursed them, and repeatedly boasted about the prowess of her kinsmen.
Wishing to incite them against Rāma, she lamented before her brothers Khara and Dūṣaṇa, who were residents of the Daṇḍaka forest.
"See the actions of those two sons of an unfortunate mother, who were exiled by their father for the sake of Bharata, the son of the favored wife!"
"This humiliation of mine—your sister, whose protector is Rāvaṇa—has come from a wretched ascetic; forgive it if it seems appropriate to you."
"Even though they wear unrefined clothes, eat uncultivated fruits, and have no paid attendants, they have nevertheless insulted me."
She was answered by her brothers: "You will attain ultimate welfare. We live for the sake of your honor; go, take heart, and do not weep."
"O timid one, we devour men day and night even when they are faultless; why then would we tolerate those who have actually caused us harm?"
Then those two (Khara and Dūṣaṇa), leading a force of fourteen thousand, set out accompanied by soldiers armed with axes, bows, spears, and darts.
Then, in the battle, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa struck down the terrifying demons with many heads, two heads, and three heads as they were rushing forward, using their sharp arrows.
The earth was covered with those demons who were cut, shattered, bent, crushed, split, destroyed, drowned, distressed, ashamed, and miserable.
Some demons experienced trembling, others intense burning pain, and some vomited blood; none amongst them possessed any brilliance or splendor anymore.

Then Tri-mūrdha approached the son of Raghu (Rāma) like a deer approaching a hunter, like a thirsty person in a desert heading toward the scorching southern direction, or like a snake approaching the fierce-faced king of birds, Garuḍa.

With all his heads severed by sharp arrows, appearing like a mountain whose peaks are shattered by an earthquake, he (Tri-mūrdha) became a portentous sign of the impending destruction of the entire demon race, instilling terror in them.
Khara and Dūṣaṇa, eager to repel others, stayed in the battle, grew in strength, leaped forth, and endured the fight as they moved about.
Holding swords, clubs, spears, discuses, arrows, and maces in their hands, the two created a shadow of weapons in the battle obscured by thick dust.
Then, the two best of the Raghu lineage, remaining undeluded, repeatedly pierced the enemies in their vital spots with sharp iron arrows and sent them to the abode of Yama.
Having lost her kinsmen, Śūrpaṇakhā then went from the forest to her lord Rāvaṇa, who was residing in Laṅkā across the ocean.
Reaching the assembly of demons, overwhelmed with rage, she cried out and wept for her two brothers, mentioning their names and villages in the presence of Rāvaṇa.
O Hero! The two excellent demons who inhabited the Daṇḍaka forest, along with their attendants, have been slain in battle by two men, merely increasing the bulk of the earth.
You are at war with Śakra, who has Bṛhaspati as his priest, and with Kumāra, the commander of the army. What kind of policy is it that you remain negligent?
O Lord! If I, noseless and with my kinsmen slain, had not come here, you, being negligent and weak in espionage, would not have known all this.
One should know what the enemies have done and what they intend to do. Even after an injury has been inflicted, are you ignorant or no longer desirous of victory?
Surrounded by fair-weather friends, lying on your couch, negligent, addicted to drink, and distracted, you will not lead your fortune to permanence.
Now Indra (Duścyavana) goes to the hermitages of those who have performed the Soma sacrifice in rituals involving the piling of the sacrificial fire to consume his portion.
The demons no longer even obstruct the curd and milk meant for āmikṣā, the herbs meant for the sacrificial cake, or the clarified butter made from yesterday's cow's milk.
Rāma, who has a young wife, stands on the ground with a bow in hand and, with arrows resembling death, kills the demons who range in the sky and harass the sacrifices.
The deities now eat the meat offerings that were previously snatched from their lips, because the demons, fearing Rāma, are fleeing in all directions.
Sharpen your intellect, abandon self-indulgence, and ensure that your hereditary fortune reaches your sons and grandsons.
Do not rest easy having grasped that fickle fortune which many powerful, diligent, and skillful rivals desire.
Fortune, desiring union with a man, like an unchaste woman out of curiosity, looks at another through some pretext even while standing near her lord.
His beloved wife Sītā is the most excellent among women, possessing a gait like a swan, dark-complexioned like a blade of dūrvā grass, and perfectly proportioned.
He who does not behold her face, nor her lips, nor hear her words, has in vain controlled his senses.
She is the essence of all objects of the senses; he who possesses her has true joy. I consider dallying on a couch with other women to be worthy of reproach.
I see no one whose mind she would not agitate. Having acquired her even at the cost of the three worlds, you, a fortunate one, should become successful.
Neither Indrāṇī, nor Rudrāṇī, nor any mortal woman, nor Rohiṇī, Varuṇānī, or Agnāyī is equal to that lady.
The lord of the Rākṣasas replied to her: "O talkative night-wanderer, take heart! Why do you fear? Abandon your agitation. For I am Rāvaṇa."
Desiring to see me, Hari (Indra), struck by the staff-bearers and eager to receive my commands, waited upon me from afar, viewed with a side-glance of indifference.
The powerful vajra, its sharp-edged tip shattered against my chest, considers itself strong only because it did not break into a hundred pieces.
Having used the trees of Laṅkā as tying posts, I released the elephant Airāvata, who was bowed down, like a blade of grass, because he was useless to be bound.
Behold my self-importance; in my city, where darkness is destroyed by the luster of excellent gems, the full moon is ever present.
Does not the mountain-shatterer Indra, deprived of his gems, fallen from effort, and paying tribute to the Rākṣasas, approach his wife Śacī with shame in heaven?
A conflict with Rāma, who possesses unequal luster, is indeed shameful for me; nevertheless, I shall strive to subdue him.
Springing into the sky, the ten-necked one Rāvaṇa, moving with the speed of thought and bearing sharp weapons, proceeded toward Mārīca, who resided near the ocean.
Reaching his abode, he related the news. Then, the ten-faced one was addressed by the terrified Mārīca, who had heard the matter.
O Lord of Rākṣasas, conceal yourself from that tiger among the Raghus, Rāma, who, holding a bow with a firm grip, is difficult to approach in battle.
That Rāma has conquered the world-renowned slayer of Kārtavīrya, who had once forced you into a disadvantageous peace.
Tāḍakā, who has seen the face of Death, knows his prowess. I too, thinking myself a hero, was cast out from the battlefield by him, who roars like a lion.
You have not experienced him, nor has he been experienced by you. But he has been experienced by me, and I have been experienced by him.
Rāma is the foremost among weapon-bearers; those like me are inferior when facing him. In Mithilā, at the sacrifice, he broke the bow that was the bride-price for the maiden.
Khara and Dūṣaṇa, his fellow combatants, know his power. So do the sacrificers along with those who press the Soma juice, whom he protected during the sacrifices.
Born to happiness, drinking wine, devouring men, and wearing garlands, you should sport with women in Laṅkā. Do not undertake a war with the strong.
Rebuking the terrified one, Rāvaṇa replied: "Even if that Rāma conquered one who was exhausted, what of it?"
He killed Tāḍakā, whose ornaments were shame and fear. If such an act against womankind is praiseworthy, then fie upon the small-minded world.
Rāvaṇa tells Mārīca that Rāma scaring a coward in his own home is no display of valor against a powerful king, addressing him as a wretched priest.
He dismisses Rāma's feat of breaking the bow, claiming there is no wonder in snapping an ancient, worm-eaten bow in the presence of insignificant kings.
Rāvaṇa argues it is no surprise that the two brave forest ascetics killed Khara and Dūṣaṇa, who were overconfident and lacked respect for their foes.
Rāvaṇa rebukes Mārīca as a coward and a fool who constantly seeks refuge, denies the virtues of his own side, and always praises their enemies.
He threatens to decapitate Mārīca or force him to aid in his plan to capture the two forest-dwellers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Fearing for his life as Rāvaṇa raised his sharp sword, Mārīca attempted to appease him, declaring that he would side with him against the enemy.
Mārīca agrees to transform into a deer to lure away Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, telling Rāvaṇa to proceed with his efforts against the enemy as he pleases.
Then, the deer made of gold and gems, appearing wondrous, leaped in front of Sītā, greatly enticing her with its beauty.
The deer-eyed Maithilī, wishing to wear the deer’s skin, urged the broad-chested Rāma to pursue the animal for sport.
After entrusting Lakṣmaṇa with the safety and care of Sītā, the elephant-striding Rāma followed the tracks of the deer.
Rāma was amazed by the deer’s strange behavior, as it alternately moved after stopping and stood still after running short distances.
After a long pursuit, Rāma, a marksman of vital spots, shot the demon who was leaping wildly, making a loud noise, and causing terror.
Hearing a cry like a thunderclap and believing Rāma to be in distress, the lamenting Sītā urged Lakṣmaṇa to go to his aid.
Sītā cried out, "This brother of yours is shouting like a monsoon cloud! O Lakṣmaṇa, fulfill your duty to your kin and save Rāghava from danger!"
Lakṣmaṇa replied to her, "This is not Rāma's cry, but that of a deceptive deer; it is merely a sound mimicking Rāma's voice."
Lakṣmaṇa asks, "O fearful one, who can withstand in battle the enraged Kākutstha, who has broad shoulders and neck and who covers the directions with arrows?"
The deer, wishing to consume its body in the fire of weapons and gambling with its life, approached Rāma, whose thumb was hardened by the bowstring, desiring death.
Lakṣmaṇa continues, "Who can astonish Rāma, who terrifies his enemies? Do not fear; you will see your husband today, having successfully achieved his objective."
Sītā spoke to him, "I wish for you to go, but you do not dare to leave; it seems you desire to possess me yourself."
To Sītā who spoke such false words, the self-controlled Raghūttama, who always spoke the truth, departed while cursing her, saying she would fall into the enemy's hands.
After Jatāyu departed, Rāvaṇa appeared disguised as an ascetic. Pure like fire, with clean teeth, a tuft of hair, and a rosary, he carried soft gourds and constantly chanted prayers.
With a clean-shaven head and carrying a beggar's bowl and a staff, he dressed in saffron garments and arranged his few belongings to complete his ascetic disguise.
Appearing to study the science of the Self and observing the vow of a wandering monk, he spoke while snapping his fingers and casting glances with expressive movements of his eyebrows.
Wishing to display a peaceful demeanor and conceal his demonic nature, the wanderer approached Sītā and addressed her, saying, 'May you be happy.'
Sītā, with a pure smile and eternal radiance that put to shame the evening moon and the daytime beauty of lotuses, looked upon him.
'O timid one, who are you alone in this forest devoid of kinsmen? How is it that hungry beasts have not devoured you, left as you are without a protector?'
'You, with a heart-stealing form, make even this terrifying forest appear charming. Tell me, for what reason have you come here?'
'You who perform pleasant acts, whose merit do you steal? Whom do you serve? Which virtuous person, flattering you, acts as your servant in pleasures?'
'Your beauty excels everything up to the heavenly world and is rare to find. Having seen this form of yours, our lives have become truly meaningful.'
'Like a lotus on a bright day, its honey sipped by bees and possessing excellent fragrance, I believe you are not without a husband.'
'Lakṣmī's fame is a myth; she only thinks herself the goddess of fortune. Viṣṇu's pride is also false. Seeing you, I believe you steal the very beauty of Lakṣmī herself.'
'If Smara had seen you, would he not have felt intense longing? Constantly playful, he would no longer even dwell with his consort, Rati.'
'Seeing you acting so gracefully, which woman here would not feel jealous? Who, even if as steady as a pillar, would not be attracted to your brilliance?'
'Every other man suffers; he alone is truly happy towards whom you, full of longing, do not act adversely while remaining near him.'
'Who is that person, acting like a wise man, who brought you here—you who are as precious as a prize—and lived in this empty forest while fearing enemies?'
Exerting herself, the daughter of Janaka offered guest-water to the ten-headed Rāvaṇa and, with respect, spoke these words in a voice trembling with emotion.
'My husband is the son of Daśaratha, born in the noble Ikṣvāku lineage; he does what is pleasing to his father and ensures the welfare of ascetics.'
'He is the slayer of those who create enmity, a great benefactor to the virtuous, and the one who neutralized the power of Paraśurāma in battle.'
'He is the protector of those performing sacrifices and always fulfills his duties; he abandoned kingship by his father's command and came to the forest.'
'In this fearsome forest, the demons who were food for jackals now lie in heaps, having been cut down by his powerful arrows.'
How do you not recognize Rāma, who sports with sharp arrows, hurls mighty maces, and slaughters his enemies?
Entrusting me to his brother, that expert hunter departed for the chase; now, his younger brother, sent by me to seek him, has also gone into the forest.
Then Daśānana, becoming agitated with reddened eyes and prominent drops of flowing sweat, revealed his inner intent and spoke to her.
Who would highly regard Rāghava, who resembles a naked, plundered beggar, having been exiled for the sake of the youngest wife’s son?
O frog in a well! If he defeated those demons, who are heroes only over sacrificial offerings, during the rituals of young boys, why are you so proud of such a feat?
My prowess has stripped him of his kingdom, enjoyments, and retinue. Is it even fitting for me to describe how even Hari (Indra) now lives like a pauper because of me?
Who does not know the reason why the Lord of Wealth, deprived of Laṅkā, his pride shattered, and his Puṣpaka chariot stolen, now dwells within the mountains?
Yama himself, fearing me like a man with a broken boat and brooding, remains inactive with a face darkened by gloom.
O Maithili, my city named Laṅkā is golden, situated in the valley of the ocean and on the mountain peaks; it is a supreme treasury of jewels.
Dwell there with me in an abode sprinkled and swept clean, where you shall be anointed with perfumes, scented, and adorned with long, fragrant garlands.
O beautiful girl, O youthful woman, unite with me, a manly youth! Rāghava is a wretched wanderer; abandon that destitute man.
Occupied with eating and drinking, devoted to the acts of love, and having brought Daśagrīva under your control, rejoice in this magnificent palace.
Do not be a fault-finder, O timid one! Be eager to depart. Becoming radiant, be the one who embraces my chest.
Perceiving her to be hostile, the night-stalker of terrifying form, desiring to seize her, embraced her by forcibly crushing her arms and soared into the sky.
As he carried her away trembling toward the abode of the night-stalkers, the deer and birds remained silent, paralyzed by fear.
Jaṭāyu, the lord of birds, reached that pitiable woman as she cried out loudly for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, addressing the harsh Rāvaṇa with stern words.
O enemy! You, a thief roaming the forest, have seized the best of forest-dwellers; being a leader of the base, do not think you can pass before me.
Fie on you, shameless one, who torments Rāma, whose conduct brings glory, who is renowned on earth for his compassion, and who fulfills his father's command.
O Rākṣasa, I am surely your destroyer, just as the sun is to darkness; I am not one to be led away like some mere servant of Rāma.
To kill the man-eater who causes pain to the virtuous and incites enmity, that bird, seeking a quarrel and crying out, swooped down from the sky.
Shaking the canopy of his wings that covered every direction in the sky, Jaṭāyu fought by delivering blows with his beak that exposed flesh and blood.
He neither feared, nor felt ashamed, nor grew weary, nor suffered pain; whether striking or being pierced, he did not retreat from the battlefield.
In battle, he smashed the terrifying chariot—which was drawn by demon-faced beasts, equipped with an umbrella and armor, and adorned with a banner—as if it were a worthless vehicle.
He terrified the enemy and delighted the watching gods; he compelled the twenty-armed foe to release Sītā.
Unperturbed by weapons yet losing his splendor, Rāvaṇa coughed in distress; meanwhile, the bird, whose weapons were his talons and beak, repeatedly wounded him.
Driven by anger, the two strove to kill each other; the bird did not flee, and the Rākṣasa showed no mercy.
Gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras gathered to watch the combat; then the flesh-eater Rāvaṇa deceitfully hacked off the wings of the bird.

Seeing the noble bird severed and rolling on the ground, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa rejoiced; seizing the beloved wife of Rāma, he ascended his excellent chariot drawn by terrifying beasts and departed for his own city.
The fire of lust scorched the ten-faced Rāvaṇa day and night. He also came to know that Vaidehī was disinterested in anyone other than Rāma.
Out of concern, he remained constantly awake, monitoring the enemy's activities. Apprehensive, he lived in fear of the descendant of Kakutstha, Rāma.
Though rebuked after entreating Sītā, he felt no shame. Being excessively attached to Vaidehī, he could no longer maintain his strength or vigor.
He commanded his own people to find out about Rāma's activities. Being diligent, he ordered the Rākṣasas to guard Sītā.
Rāma, having killed Mārīca, heard the harsh cries of cruel jackals howling inauspicious omens as he was returning.
Fearing that Vaidehī might have been eaten, struck down, or dead, he saw the brother of Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, approaching from a distance.
Realizing that Sītā was left alone, fearful, and abandoned by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma thought, 'Prosperity is rare when destruction is imminent.'
Praying to the gods for her welfare, he asked Lakṣmaṇa about Sītā. The distressed brother then told Rāma everything exactly as it had happened.
Seeing the cottage empty and begging the forest for his beloved, he felt as if his life-force was being drained away; he suppressed his grief within.
'She might have gone to gather flowers from the hermitage trees, or perhaps she is where Sutīkṣṇa instructs the ascetics in righteousness.'
He lamented greatly, saying, 'Alas! What misery! Oh, wonder! Fie on the deities! Oh Mother! Oh Father! Where are you, O fair-browed one?'
'She sat here, she slept here, she moved sportively from here.' Remembering her thus, the elder brother of Bharata grew faint for the sake of Maithilī.
'This flower-garland from last night and this one from today, hanging on the branch, seem to wither from grief in her absence.'
'We used to watch her repeatedly while she slept, fearing she might be dead. Alas, it is hard to die out of season, as we still live without her.'
'O Sītā, this jest is dangerous. Do not test me. Do not hide from me. Do not sport with our lives.'
'I have slain the terrible demon of cruel valor. O beloved, do not hide yourself from your husband; do not fail to embrace your dear one.'
'Do not see an imaginary fault in me. Do not torment me, your devotee. Has the beautiful lady taken refuge in the mountain or run towards the river?'
'O, speak! My courage has flowed away because of you. By disappearing, you have as if consumed my intellect and taken away my very life.'
'Because of you, my eyes have swollen from weeping and my face has become bloated. I am dying. If you have discarded me, do not fail to tell me your intention.'
'Lakṣmaṇa, tell me if she mentioned any cause for anger. How can a remedy be applied if the fault itself is unknown?'
Remembering her, Rāma lamented, "Here she applied perfumes, here she bathed and sprinkled herself with water, and here I called her to see her." Thus reminiscing, he fainted.
The blazing fire of grief consumed his heart like wood. Though the cool forest breeze touched him, it did not refresh him; it felt as if it merely smeared his body without providing any relief.
Weeping for his beloved, he bathed in the water. Overwhelmed by grief, he likewise offered libations of water to his ancestors, performing the sacred rites amidst his sorrow.
Even though he was deeply distressed, he never abandoned his religious duties at the proper time. Indeed, the obligatory duties of the great do not falter even during times of calamity.
He repeatedly challenged the brave and called out to the Rākṣasas, shouting, "Come forth, you enemies of Sītā! Confront Rāghava in battle!"
"O young birds and deer! Tell me where she has gone—she who nurtured you as her own and who shone with a beauty rivaling the moon."
Desiring to find the daughter of Janaka, Rāma wandered along the mountain. He pointed out to Lakṣmaṇa the signs indicating that a great battle had taken place there.
"O Saumitri! Surely two Rākṣasas fought here, wishing to kill Sītā. This fresh blood must have dripped during their violent encounter."
"This armor has fallen, and this chariot with its horses has been crushed. Come, let us quickly enter this mountain to search for her."
"I believe my wrath has been checked, and despair has paralyzed my effort. My wisdom seems to have decayed, and my strength has withered due to grief."
"Look, Lakṣmaṇa! The wings of this vulture have been lopped off. Surely, this destruction befell him from a night-stalker as he tried to rescue her from being devoured."
The tiger of the Raghu clan blazed with anger, his eyes turning red in an instant. Like the sun, he filled the space with his radiance, and the three worlds felt the agitation of his power.
His supreme courage expanded, and he felt replenished as if he had already achieved his goal. The great power of the enraged Rāma increased significantly.
His despair seemed to vanish, and his prowess, though previously restrained, was ready for action. He became the embodiment of anger and sighed deeply and repeatedly.
Then, grasping his bow, Rāma, possessing the strength of an elephant, roared: "I shall block the path of the sun and shatter the principal mountains!"
"I will empty the waters of the ocean and scatter the gods from heaven. I will crush the serpents in the underworld and annihilate the night-roaming Rākṣasas!"
"Inflaming my mastery of weapons, I shall yoke Yama with death itself. Unwearied by my own splendor, I shall grind the earth into dry powder!"
"I shall destroy the prosperity of the Yakṣas and strike down the prowess of Indra. I will break all bounds of nature and solidify the vast sky!"
"This world thinks I do not strike because I lack valor." Saying this, the son of Daśaratha joined a lethal arrow to his bow, ready for destruction.
Lakṣmaṇa restrained him as he was about to destroy the world. Then, near the hermitage, they both beheld a vulture as large as a mountain.
Thinking that he was the killer of Sītā, Rāma rushed to kill him. Jaṭāyu said, "Rāma, I have seen Sītā; do not kill me, for I am Jaṭāyu."
When Jaṭāyu spoke thus, Rāghava approached his father's friend and questioned the bird about the news of Jānakī and the battle.
Fainting from the pain of his wounds, the bird died in the mountain cave. After performing his cremation and water-libations, the two brothers set out again into the forest.
They were seized by a long-armed demon, who was terrible, hungry, and constantly devouring creatures by dragging them in with force.
The two best of the Raghu dynasty cut off his arms with their swords. With his arms severed, he fell down agitated, shaking the earth.
To the demon who asked what was to be asked, the best of the Raghu dynasty told what was to be told—about himself, his forest exile, and the enemy to be conquered.
Rāma asked, "How is Vaidehī to be found? How can the enemy be seen? And how can this separation be endured? Tell me this."
He said to him, "O Rāma, I am the son of Śrī. Wandering like one drunk on wine, I became a practitioner of evil deeds due to a sage's curse."
"Purified by your weapon and having reached a state of restraint, I tell you: Sītā has been abducted by the enemy of the gods, Rāvaṇa, and taken to Laṅkā."
On Mount Ṛṣyamūka dwells a faultless monkey named Sugrīva, whose brother's death is to be bargained for. He, of beautiful prowess, should be chosen by you.
"With him as your supporter, you will slay the master of the man-eaters, the cruel-acting demon, the enemy of Indra, who dwells far away."
"That monkey remains remembering his beloved who was abducted by Vālin, just like a bull struck by a cow-herd's staff in a pen longs for a cow ready for mating."
"O Rāma, quickly form an undecaying alliance with that noble one. Then, having reached Laṅkā, you will slay the sinful ten-necked one."
"There is no falsehood in this; I speak what is truth-worthy. Having attained friendship with him, you will accomplish the killing of your enemy."
"Respected by that chosen one, united with the agreeable one, praiseworthy, and to be approached like a teacher by a disciple, you will obtain the desired object."
"For him, who possesses good servants, even the vast ocean is not impossible to cross. You should dispel his anger, and he shall wipe away your sorrow."
That night-walker, shining like the sun like one who has performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, speaking words that were not false and looking radiant, ascended to heaven.
Then the two sons of Daśaratha, seeing creepers whose fruits ripen without cultivation, wandered about like those who had lost all memory of jewels, food, drink, and base metals.
Crossing rivers resembling those to be breached or dammed, the two unshakeable ones reached Śabarī in the forest, who was as famous as a star to be propitiated.
They reached Śabarī, who was wearing pure bark garments, with a girdle made of muñja grass, emaciated, resembling a lump of collyrium, holding a staff, and seated on a deerskin.

Rāma saw the virtuous Śabarī, whose speech was as clear as the Pragṛhya vowels and whose form was distinct and unchanging. Being devoid of worldly desires, she was ungraspable by the senses, devoted to the divine, and entirely beyond reproach.

Observing her constantly engaged in righteous duties and subsisting only on uncultivated fruits, Rāma felt his fatigue vanish, much like a beast of burden feels relieved upon reaching its destination.
He then addressed her: "I hope you perform the ancestral rites on the new moon day using delicious fruits that do not require cooking."
"Do you purify the sacrificial oblation intended for the gods that must be purified? Do you pay homage to the Soma juice that is extracted by the twice-born during sacrifices?"
"Is the ritual sipping of water at the two twilights never neglected by you, who are devoted to truth? Do you honor a guest arriving at the proper time just like the consecrated fire?"
"O exalted lady! I hope no wicked person, hateful of righteousness and unfit for guidance, occupies your dwelling to obstruct your divine duties."
"O auspicious one! Do you always delight in the stories of those who perform the Kuṇḍapāyya sacrifice, the piling of the fire altar, and the construction of the sacrificial pile?"
"O timid one! Is your penance flourishing? You have conquered the leaders of obstacles and triumphed over desire and delusion; indeed, you have attained perfection through your humility."
"You do not grow weary while performing penance. You have fully satisfied your preceptors. You did not shrink from the self-restraints and remained content with your own asceticism."
Then, having respectfully brought water for the feet and the Madhuparka offering, and having worshipped the worshipful brothers with fruits, she declared that all was well in every respect.
"The joy of the monkeys, Sugrīva, will become your ally. You shall soon see Maithilī." Having said this, she vanished from sight.
Thereafter, the two heroic descendants of Raghu reached the forests of Pampā, which were the delight of the great sages and the pleasance of the forest-dwellers.
"Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at Pampā, adorned with the humming of bee-swarms, cuckoos, and cranes, and embellished with bright things; it pierces our hearts."
"Behold the radiant water-born lotuses that surpass the stars and churn the mind; they torment a person who is separated from his beloved."
"It is quite clear that beauty everywhere is dependent on one's beloved; for, in the absence of my dear one, even the notes of the swans and cuckoos have become discordant."
"With birds chirping and trees scattering flowers, only one who is ignorant or has no beloved would not feel faint with desire like a youth."
"We are deeply distressed by these birds that emit songs, drink nectar, and scent the fragrance of flowers."
"Alas! We are struck again by the trees, which bear waves of flowers, are capable of tormenting people, and cause the heart to tremble."
"By these breezes that grant sorrow to people like me, carry excellent fragrance, and seem to smear the body, what sentient being would not be inflamed?"
"The trickling dewdrops gathered at the tips of quivering leaves, possessing the luster of beautiful pearls, cause the heart to melt away."
When shall I reach the end of this sorrow? Yama, the taker of life, does not make me happy by claiming my life.
I am scorched by the pleasant breezes like a mountain by fierce forest fires. What fortunate means exists here by which I might, alas, become free from this fever of grief?
Seeing the forest edges like the dwellings of Smara, my mind feels possessed as if by a planet or seized by a crocodile in the ocean.
The trees, with branches swaying in the wind like dancers and surrounded by humming bee-singers, are indeed unbearable.
The two best of Raghu's lineage, reapers of enemy power, moving with the gait of one-year-old elephants, reached Mount Ṛṣyamūka.
The monkey Sugrīva, thinking them to be spies of Vālin, worried: 'Being opposed by my brother, how can I remain alive?'
Mistaking the two descendants of Raghu for slayers of enemies, Sugrīva went with his retinue to Mount Malaya, which rose up as if measuring the sky.
In a difficult situation, the elephant-like monkey Sugrīva dispatched Māruti, the steady monkey messenger who bestows comfort and removes grief.
Wearing a garb that inspires confidence, knowledgeable of the path, and capable of gauging the minds of those seeking victory, Hanumān leapt into the sky.
He reached Ṛṣyamūka, where trees tossed by the wind like drunkards, and bees sang like chanters of the Sāmaveda.
Reaching that beautiful mountain, Hanumān, whose form was like a mendicant and who brings happiness, spoke to the two armored heroes.
Powerful like two elephants, why do you discuss between yourselves this lord of mountains, which is difficult to access even for Śaṅkara?
This place is filled with cruel flesh-eaters and night-prowlers dwelling in caves, covered with tall rocks and trees, and beyond the reach of humans.
Having the brilliance of infants, how have you come through paths full of lions that make creatures tremble, paths that are heart-piercing and filled with uneven rocks?
How did you cross the terrifying rivers that overflow their banks? Why were you not attacked by elephants that uproot the riverbanks? Please tell me.
Rāma said to Hanumān: O wise one, by our father's command, we are here on this cloud-touching mountain, protecting the sages who cook very little for themselves.
Know our father to be Daśaratha, famous on earth, a supreme lord who feeds countless people and is fit for all enjoyments.
Our beloved, whose form has never seen the sun, was abducted from the forest through deceit by a demon who pierces the vitals. We are searching for her.
Māruti replied to Rāma: There is a monkey named Vālin, who could subdue even the scorching sun in battle.
His brother Sugrīva has been cast out by that fierce-looking one. I have arrived as a submissive messenger for him, who desires your friendship.
O scorcher of foes! Although I speak kindly, I never speak falsely. With Sugrīva as your ally, you will slay the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, the tormentor of his enemies.
I restrain my speech regarding falsehoods. I tell you this truth. Come, make the patient and all-enduring Vānara, Sugrīva, your friend.
Taking with him Rāma, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree with branches of all-surpassing fame, the monkey Hanumān reached Mount Malaya, which scrapes the clouds and abounds in fruit.
Exhausted, Sugrīva saw Rāma approaching like the cloud-forming monsoon and no longer feared the formidable sun-like Vāli.
Doing what was pleasing to each other, they established friendship near the fire. Then, they deliberated on actions that would bring about their mutual well-being.
Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, greatly appreciated the monkeys' self-satisfied eating, shouting, jumping, lying down, and standing, all done according to their free will.
Then Sugrīva told Rāma, the lord of the world of monkeys who was like the subduer of Bali, Viṣṇu, about Vāli's prowess in battle.
On the entire earth, there is no one as strong as Vāli. I speak this movingly to you, not out of a sense of defeat.
With arrows that travel far and reach their end, you have attained the height of glory. If angered, you could overcome even Indra; what then of Vāli?
By the boon of a sage, Vāli became a killer of foes in battle. His onset is irresistible, like the rising sun at dawn that destroys darkness.
O Rāma! Because it is so desirable, my heart does not feel cowardice or doubt regarding the imminent death of Vāli, which will remove my suffering.
Seeing you arrived, the slayer of enemies, I consider Vāli’s fortune as possessing the ill-fated marks of a husband-killer.
He who kills elephants and hurls natural mountains that destroy enemies in battle, though resourceful and furious, can be conquered by you who are assisted by the skilled hands of monkeys.
With valor that made him powerful, Vāli performed the difficult task of killing the buffalo-demon Mahisa, an enemy of the gods, thereby pleasing Indra.
Having thrown the dead body of Dundubhi for a yojana, he became pleasing. Though capable of causing harm, by not troubling anyone, he became dear to heaven.
To convince the doubtful Sugrīva who wished to know the power of his weapons, Rāma pierced seven trees that reached up to the sky.
Then, with Vāli as the sacrificial animal and Rāma as the officiating priest, Sugrīva, having overcome his fear, boldly approached his brother's dwelling while shouting.
Vāli emerged from the cave like a lion attacking a deer. Filling the quarters with his roar in battle, he brought fear to all.
Confused in distinguishing between the two who looked identical while struggling, Rāma, the joy of the Ikṣvāku clan, held back his raised arrow.
Severely crushed by Vāli, breathing warmly and exhausted like a deer, the monkey Sugrīva quickly fled to Mount Ṛṣyamūka.
Rāma distinguished Sugrīva, the enemy of Vālin, with a garland and challenged the monkey-killing Vālin to battle again to strike down Aṅgada’s father.
During the fierce conflict between the two monkey chiefs, Rāma, positioned at a distance, released a lethal arrow that pierced Vālin’s body and took his life.
Seeing the destroyer of foes, Vālin, fallen, the masterless monkeys wailed for their kinsman and fled in all ten directions.
Sages in the forest condemned the son of Daśaratha, while the wailing wives of the monkeys approached the fallen Vālin in deep sorrow.
Though fainting with the pain of his wound, the proud lord of monkeys loudly rebuked Rāma, treating the seemingly noble prince as if he were ignoble.
Vālin called Rāghava a false sacrificer and a fraudulent ascetic, claiming that killing a distracted opponent makes him as sinful as a killer of Brāhmaṇas.
He questioned how Rāma, the son of a virtuous king, could justify his wicked conduct after murdering an innocent being like himself.
Vālin asked why Rāma disregarded the legacy of his father, a king who maintained sacred fires and performed grand rituals like the Soma sacrifice.
He compared Rāma’s act to the censured work of a meat-selling hunter, accusing him of fearlessly committing a vile sin by striking him down.
Vālin claimed Rāma's father surely never intended for such a rogue to be king, as he struck an innocent warrior who was engaged in battle with another.
Addressing the son of Kausalyā, Vālin noted that monkeys are not among the five types of five-nailed animals permitted as food for the twice-born.
He questioned how a man so corrupt in Dharma could protect subjects or avoid feeling shame before himself and his younger brother Saumitri.
Vālin accused the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa of being of ignoble birth and not a true Kṣatriya, acting merely as a tool for his younger brother Sugrīva.
Rāma replied to the lord of monkeys that his actions were consistent with the traditions established by ancient sacrificers and elders regarding the punishment of animals.
Rāma explained that elders sought the death of animals through snares and nets, particularly for those who cohabited with the wives of others.
Rāma declared he intervened because he heard Vālin had enjoyed his younger brother's wife, an act for which the forest-monkey was condemned by the learned.
Overcome with shame, Vālin accepted Rāghava’s words and carefully entrusted his beloved son Aṅgada to the protection of the scion of Kākutstha.
While dying, Vālin attained a state of goodwill and reminded Sugrīva that they were both born of the same mother and shared a common bond.
He urged Sugrīva to remember their life in the mountains and their shared moments, stating that this was the time for kinsmen to be united.
Vālin concluded that Fate surely did not ordain happiness for both brothers simultaneously, as it had always kept their relationship in a state of turmoil.
Afflicted by his wounds, he gave his beloved wife and the excellent golden garland to his brother. Having entrusted the kingdom and its enjoyments to him, he passed away.
Having performed the necessary funeral rites for him by the command of Rāghava, Sugrīva quickly set his mind on going to the cave of the Kiṣkindhā mountain.

Praised loudly by the monkeys calling his name and shining with devotion toward the two best of the Raghu line, the lord of monkeys entered the Kiṣkindhā mountain as the rainy season neared. The mountain peaks were covered in greenery, and bees hummed there, intoxicated by honey.
Then the storm-wind of the rainy season blew, causing the forests to tremble; and the clouds, the fillers of the sky, rose up.
The radiant clouds, accompanied by thunder, released pure water—the satisfaction of germinating crops—as if they were breaking apart.
The shining, lightning-streaked, and wandering clouds rose up, obscuring the sun, moving through the sky, and adorning the heavens.
Seeing them, the victorious Rāma, unable to endure the separation while residing on Mount Malyavat, lamented like one distracted and grew weary like a timid person.
The whirling wind, fragrant with kadamba flowers and cooled by the mist of clouds, causes great exhaustion even to those who are self-controlled.
In my feverish and weary mind, the darkness—pierced by the contact of fireflies that steal the sight—appears unbearable and hostile.
The flickering streaks of lightning, mixed with the screaming cātaka birds that strike from all sides, make me lament.
The cool spray of water feels like it is burning upon contact; the playing and noisy peacocks have become impossible to endure.
These falling showers, though following the gods' command, torment a passionate person who has done no harm, as if they were enemies.
This thundering season, with its scattered waters, could cause even a self-realized yogi, who has renounced pleasure and pain, to become deluded.
The boastful and restless cātaka bird repeatedly begs the cloud for the water already given, as if tearing at my heart.
'When will these wicked frogs—the tormentors and killers of those separated from their loved ones—cease their croaking?' Thus Rāma lamented.
Thinking of the day as night, Rāma—the descendant of Kakutstha—somehow passed the rainy season while grieving, blaming the night, and suffering distress.
Then, at the onset of autumn, he saw the white sky filled with flocks of krauñca birds, whose movements and cries increased his longing.
Looking at the shining moon, the grieving Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: 'Behold the swans wandering about, eager for the lotuses.'
That monkey (Sugrīva) is still wandering about and has not become desirous of action; the stars, the ornaments of the sky, provoke my anger.
Does the monkey not recognize the sun, who at the start of the day dispels the mass of darkness and nourishes and illuminates the lotuses?
Now that the rainy season has passed, the negligent Sugrīva, remaining at home, will surely go the way Vālin has gone.
'O Lakṣmaṇa! You, the swift and victorious one, must go and speak harsh words to him as he sits among talkative women.'
Speak what is just to that sinful and unperturbed monkey who rests on the mountain, showing disregard and acting with insolence.
Speak quickly to the monkey who is sleeping like a cruel person on the mountain filled with trees, who yearns for women, is faithful, and wandering like a bee.
Lakṣmaṇa, moving swiftly, possessed of a sharp intellect, wise, and victorious, took up his shining bow and reached the departing monkeys.
Māruti, alert in his duties and humble, ushered the unshakable and radiant Lakṣmaṇa, the enemy of serpents, into the cave.
Surrounded by lovely women, wishing for his own welfare and desiring favor, Sugrīva bowed and spoke to the prince Lakṣmaṇa.
"Master of my desires and recipient of your grace, I lived fearlessly along with brilliant women who were full of praise," said Sugrīva.
"Engrossed in the pleasures granted by Rāma, I did not notice the fading of the sun's brilliance or the shining moon's disappearance."
"O Lord! I am now dispatching the heroic monkeys, destroyers of grief, who can reach the very ends of the earth, mountains, and oceans."
Then, the best among monkeys, Sugrīva, performing Rāghava's task, ordered the immediate arrival of all the monkey armies.
Sugrīva said, "We are going this very day, filled with haste, to see Rāma and perform our friend's work for the recovery of Sītā."
Then, groups of monkeys, for the prosperity of Rāghava, arrived joyfully filling the ten directions and striking fear in enemies.
Declaring they would destroy the enemy, they approached Sugrīva as if they were about to suddenly rid the world of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa.
Realizing that he would accomplish the task with those who arrived, Sugrīva approached the cool shade of the tree-like Kākutstha.
Seeing the powerful gathering of monkeys and the impending task, Rāghava considered the destruction of the ten-headed Daśāsya as already accomplished.
Then Sugrīva, like a teacher, instructed the gathered monkey host, who were united in resolve, about the vast distances of the directions.
He spoke to Hanumān, who roared like a water-laden cloud and moved beautifully, along with Aṅgada, Jāmbavān, and Nīla.
"Go with proper policy to the southern direction protected by Yama, roaring and challenging the loud sound of the great ocean's waters."
"Possessing beautiful prowess, roam freely by the fast paths of mountains, reaching the heights, and surveying the forest clearings."
"Eating your fill of fruits that are always fragrant in smell, and showing no interest in seizing heaps of grain."
"Listening to the buzzing of bees lying on flower beds, which sounds like the collective chanting of Sāmaveda singers at a great sacrifice."
"Observing the vastness of the southern ocean's waters and tasting the juice of fruits squeezed by the handful."
Whatever is appropriate should be performed in sequence by those who act without mutual opposition. Resting at night and collecting fruits must be done collectively.
Sītā should be searched for among the groups of demons by assuming small forms and using deceit, without resorting to the open mockery of the enemy hosts.
No loud clamor should be made until a sighting is achieved. Once Vaidehī is found, your suppression of the enemy will be meaningful.
Maithilī should be sought after with efforts similar to using handles for vessels. She must be identified by her gestures as she meditates on the arrival of Rāghava.
She, who is purified by sacrificial Brāhmaṇas like an altar and previously wore irreproachable attire, must be found before the final day of the month.
Go quickly and see her, whose unwavering virtues surpass even those of sages who subsist on wild grains, fruits, and roots.
Rāma, towering and possessing a voice like a thunder-cloud and the gait of an elephant, spoke to the monkey Hanūmān, who possessed a cloud-like roar and could leap great distances.
"Just as farmers pray for rain during a drought, so must you seek Sītā. Depart now, following the command of Sugrīva."
"Just as a merchant with capital travels at the right time for success, you too should depart with the ring, mindful of the geography."
Taking the token of recognition, they leaped into the sky like horses released from their reins on the chariot of the Sun.
The king of monkeys, acting with haste, dispatched Śatavali to the north and Suṣeṇa with a crore of monkeys to the western direction.
The calm Vinata went toward the east with an equal number of monkeys, like the Sun moving with far-leaping horses that are without reins.
Led by Māruti, the monkeys went to the Vindhya mountain, which was covered by autumnal clouds as if by excellent garments, to search for Sītā.
Insulting the lions on the mountain peaks, they roamed the Vindhya, which was comparable in height to the path of the sun.
Desiring the destruction of the enemy and certainty regarding Sītā, they wandered over lofty mountains and crossed unfordable rivers.
Not eating together and filling all directions, they moved with care even in difficult terrains, causing distress to other carnivorous animals.
Some wandered laughing, some roamed silently, and others, possessing self-restraint like ascetics, uttered holy recitations.
Then, silent from exhaustion like men who have lost their stakes in gambling, all of them sat down without pride on a single slope of the mountain.
Then they saw joyful birds emerging from the mouth of a cave, like cattle coming out in a herd.
Seeing the exit of the birds and desiring water, those wise in battle entered the cave, concealing their movements from one another.
Desiring to quench their thirst and calling out to their companions, the monkeys quickly entered the cave's mouth, which appeared as dark as a thick cloud.
Inside the dense interior of that cave, in the courtyard of a palatial mansion, they saw a woman with a beautiful body and shoulders as strong and solid as iron.
She, whose footsteps crushed clumps of grass, possessed a brilliance like the cloudless moon and arms as large as iron bolts. Smiling, she welcomed the monkeys.
She gratified the distinguished monkeys, who had arrived together seeking shelter in the mountain cave, with various wonderful fruits of different flavors and sweet, cool water.
Satisfied by the easily obtained fruits in that place covered by trees of varying heights, the monkeys asked the radiant woman: "To whom does this city belong?"
