"O auspicious lady, tell us why you guard this place so diligently. To us, the sight of you appears like finding a treasure in a dream."
Then she replied to the monkeys, who were as profound as the ocean: "This is the city of the demon king Maya, a creation of Viśvakarman."
"That demon, who lived here and violated the natural order, was killed by Indra. I am the daughter of Merusāvarṇi, known by the name Svayaṃprabhā."
"If you wish to move quickly or protect your reputation, I shall lead you outside. Close your eyes with your hands."
Just as a long-studied science guides those who follow its practice, she led the monkeys—who had closed their eyes and were walking along—out of the cave at her will.
Having emerged from the netherworld through her skill, the monkeys felt ashamed. Realizing that the allotted month had already passed, they were overcome with distress.
Filled with worry and fearing the consequences of their failure, they conversed among themselves: "How can we receive honor from the King without having completed our task?"
Seeking peace through a fast unto death, Aṅgada, the son of Vālin, adopted a yogic posture on the mountain while expressing the agony of his heart.
Shaken with distress, Jāmbavān meditated and spoke: "Fie on these sensory objects, which are like mere statues and allure the mind through imaginary pleasures."
"I shall also perform the same act that this prince is undertaking." Having said this, he too sat down to begin the fast.
Māruti spoke to the elder Jāmbavān and the prince who had turned ascetic: "I too shall undertake this fast unto death, as it has now come to my turn."
"In your absence, life would be worse than death for whoever remains." Saying this, all the monkeys sat down, assuming yogic postures.
They recalled the painless death of Kabandha by sword and fire, and cursed their own miserable fate of dying like orphans, wasting away in distress.
Then a large, unsightly, and slow-moving bird arrived, looking at their fast unto death as if they were a meal for him to consume.
Seeing the bird of ill omen with a beak sharp enough to tear flesh, the monkeys repeatedly lamented for themselves, feeling they had fallen into a sinful state.
The virtuous bird Jaṭāyu, who roamed the Daṇḍaka forest, has ascended to heaven after being consecrated by fire, having performed Rāghava’s task.
This visible incarnation of hell has appeared before us. Because of our lack of effort or our injustice here, we are destined to be devoured by him.
Having encountered this creature, whose heart is like a sharp tool, who resembles the net of Kṛtānta, and whose beak-tip pierces through bodies, happiness is impossible to find.
Even if he provides some minor benefit, he performs no auspicious deeds for the life hereafter. Exhausted by hunger, he approaches from here to consume us.
Reaching the monkeys, the bird spoke sweet words: 'Who are you on this mountain peak, a place so difficult to access that even the mind struggles to reach it?'
You lament for yourselves while recounting the story of Rāma, and you praise my brother Jaṭāyu with great respect.
The monkeys replied to the bird, whose words fanned away their doubts: 'We are the messengers of King Rāma, whose arrows cut down his enemies like a sickle.'
We seek to recover the noble beloved wife of that high-born King, who was stolen by a wretch of base descent.
Knowing that the thirtieth day—the deadline for our return—has passed, we, having failed in our mission, are grieving and preparing for death.
O best of birds! Since we cannot find the young, reachable beloved of the son of Kauśalyā, we are choosing death and shall not return.
The bird said to the monkeys: 'Surely you have not remembered your duty. Why do you resolve to perish at a time like this?'
This is not the time for ones like you to shrink from your master's work, especially when Rāma is deeply distressed, his wife stolen and his kingdom lost.
Quickly exert your efforts towards the south. There you will see a golden city that seems to cover the very heavens.
You will see the city named Laṅkā on the mountain top, ruled by the king of the Rākṣasas, which the celestial women saw after being brought there following Śakra's defeat.
I suspect she was created as the only such city on earth, standing upon the great mountain as if she had trampled the realm of Indra and extracted the essence of all worlds.
Having distressed the thousand-eyed Indra and labored with his own skills, the Creator built that unique city after much effort and long deliberation.
Go to that Laṅkā, where the wicked enemy lived after robbing the giver of wealth (Kubera), and which Śakra abandoned as if in tears.
Knowing your own power, be determined to seize Rāvaṇa. I have spoken to you who wished to ask. Do not be those who wish to remain inactive or sleep.
Prosperity does not come to a man who lacks the desire to know or who only wishes to weep. Why do you go like thieves, without the desire to strike back at the enemy?
You who desire to know, find Sītā quickly. I tell you: do not regard my words as false. Perform what is beneficial for your master.
Assemble before the enemy and gladden the best of the Raghu dynasty. Do not experience fear; the ten-faced Rāvaṇa has not wedded Sītā.
Then all the monkeys quickly set out toward the lord of mountains, Mahendra, shouting with joy and assuming great courage.
Having stayed in its beautiful bower, they shouted loudly and looked upon the ocean, which was resting upon gems and jewels.
They saw the ocean, which seemed angry as it struck the coastal mountains with its watery waves, was completely illumined with splendor, and appeared as if rolling about in intoxication.
Purified by cool breezes, the ocean stood as if stringing together rays of light and repeatedly threw out waves from all sides as if weaving them.
Although it had far surpassed the sky, it remained within its own self, and appeared as if thirstily drinking the sweet water of the rivers incessantly.
Shining by the moon at night and increased by its rays, the ocean repeatedly desired to shine brightly as if to conquer the vastness of Mount Meru.

Beholding sky-scraping mountain-like waves in the sea and perceiving the water below terrifying with wandering crocodiles, the monkey leaders quickly dispatched Māruti, the best of monkeys, who possessed the heavy stride of a great elephant and was capable of going and returning.
Then, the giant-bodied Hanūmān ascended into the sky. Neither Garuḍa, the sun, nor the wind could surpass his incredible speed.
He shone like the sun on a clear autumn morning. As he strode forward, there was no part of the path ahead that remained unreached by him.
The monkey and the ocean extended their forms into the sky, mutually stretching. They both traversed the celestial path frequented by the sun, Indra, and the moon.
Even the ocean could not surpass his courage as he moved. Furthermore, even the fierce wind could not overtake the speed of his flight.
The son of the Wind killed the demoness who was striking back at him as he struck her; he entered her mouth, tore through her belly, and quickly emerged.
The ocean, tossed by the wind, and the dying demoness exchanged terrifying sounds, each drowning out the other's noise.
She alone, serving as a full meal for many crocodiles, sank into the ocean, which was crowded with huge aquatic predators.
He beheld Mount Maināka rising from the sea, seeking to repay the favor once done by Vāyu, who had protected it from Indra.
Rising high and appearing to conquer the sky, the mountain said to the son of the Wind: "Rest upon me and then conquer your enemy."
"Eat the various fruits, sport upon my peaks, and watch the flocks of birds playing delightfully following your lead."
"O auspicious one, stay for a moment and then you shall depart. The task undertaken by an expert like you will surely not remain unaccomplished."
"Our affection rests in you; we wait upon you. Who would not highly esteem you, who are exerting yourself for the sake of a friend?"
"The Brahmins who worship the sun with mantras thrice a day, though tormented by demons, are even now meditating on your success."
"O hero, rest here without anxiety. I am a friend of the Wind. The sun shines intensely; proceed after refreshing yourself on me."
"This heat, burning intensely, is unbearable; it is as if one is being struck repeatedly from all sides with blazing firebrands."
"Listen, O monkey! Enjoy my beautiful forests. Upon your arrival, my cherished desires have been fulfilled."
"Who does not know that Mount Maināka is the friend of the Wind? Recognizing this, I invite you with effort; please speak what you intend."
To that mountain, which seemed to weave the sky and was being extremely helpful, the monkey spoke, acting like a humble servant.
"O king of mountains, I am going in haste to see the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who has abducted a noble wife. Do not delay me for any reason."
"I shall today destroy the strength of him who stole Sītā from the forest and whom even Indra could not subdue, while I make fierce sounds."
Today I shall perform a deed in the city of that sinful enemy of the Raghus. I shall either sacrifice my dear life or attain glory.
Hanūmān, the son of the Wind, decides to vent his anger by entering the enemy assembly and swiftly leaps into the sky.
A terrifying demoness, appearing like an ominous comet in the sky, begins to test Hanūmān's prowess as he crosses the ocean.
Entering the hundred-yojana-wide mouth of the sea demoness, Hanūmān becomes minute and emerges unnoticed, continuing his journey.
Seeking Sītā, Hanūmān reaches the ocean shore, which is swarming with fierce and powerful demons wandering about.
The wise Hanūmān, shrinking to the size of a rabbit to remain unnoticed, spends the day waiting and resolves to search for Sītā at night.
Speaking softly and avoiding Rāvaṇa's alert followers, Hanūmān enters the formidable city of Laṅkā under the cover of night.
Hanūmān remains silent and avoids conflict, observing and listening to the residents of Laṅkā as they discuss the virtues of Rāvaṇa.
Filled with the sounds of music, dancing, and laughter, the vibrant city of Laṅkā appears to rival the splendor of Indra’s celestial city.
He observes the city inhabited by Brahma-rākṣasas engaged in intellectual disputes and Piśācas devouring flesh and blood.
In various gatherings, the inhabitants praise Rāvaṇa's qualities, while intoxicated groups of demons roam freely through the streets.
Some demons travel in grand chariots and on elephants, while others present beautiful flowers and fruits through their captives.
In feigned anger, some women refuse wine from their lovers, prompting the men to swear oaths to prove their devotion.
Distressed by the thought of the grieving Rāma, Hanūmān ignores the city's festive dancing and music to focus on his mission.
As if eager to see Laṅkā alongside the monkey hero, the moon rises in the eastern sky, dispersing the darkness with its rays.
Desiring news of Maithilī, Hanūmān moves fearlessly through the demonic mansions as the evening shadows provide cover.
Hanūmān witnesses a central guard of a hundred thousand demons, a force so terrifying that even Yama might fear them.
As the moon reaches the zenith of the sky, the city of Laṅkā glows brilliantly, illuminated by its magnificent white palaces.
The festive people, speaking sweet words, enjoyed the moon's reflection in their wine cups as if it were celestial nectar.
Under the moonlight, young demons abandon their pride and drink wine copiously, their longing intensified by the romantic atmosphere.
In the presence of his beloved, Rāvaṇa repeatedly made himself a source of confidence for sexual enjoyment and made her drink clear, lotus-scented honey.
Hanumān leapt from house to house without alerting those demons, experts in battle, who had once terrified Śakra.
Desiring to see Sītā, the concealed Hanumān did not provoke the demons and used his own powers to deceive the illusions of those enemies of men.
While avoiding detection by the enemies, he thought: "The lord of demons is making false proclamations through his spies."
Concealing his greatness and wandering through the halls of ministers, he reached the palace of Rāvaṇa, who was reviling humans.
He entered the palace crowded with excellent celestial women who illuminated all directions and possessed unsurpassed beauty.
The palace was filled with women constantly preparing for amorous enjoyment, who were well-versed in playful gestures and emotional expressions.
Through these women, who made intoxicated youths serve their desires, the shark-bannered god of love remained carefree while accomplishing his work.
Displaying their radiance and adorning their bodies, these women seemed to drink the hearts of onlookers with their eyes.
Passing them, Hanumān approached the Puṣpaka chariot, which rivaled the splendor of Mount Mandara.
In that chariot, he saw Rāvaṇa, who resembled Mount Kailāsa, with his heads as peaks and his arms as trees, surpassing the beauty of a mountain.
He saw Rāvaṇa emitting fragrance, sleeping with his retinue, rivaling Indra and excelling in amorous pursuits.
The son of the Wind paused for a moment upon seeing him, the one before whom the thousand-eyed Indra had ceased fighting out of fear.
Beholding him like the beautiful Mount Meru with its forests shaken by waves of breath, the monkey paused from his intended action.
Seeing the ten-faced Rāvaṇa alone with his beloved, the son of the Wind became dejected, concluding that Sītā was not there, and stopped.
Then, without waking the demons, he climbed the wall; though capable, he did not fight as he was eager to find Sītā.
He reflected: "How may I destroy the grief of Rāghava or bring supreme joy to Vaidehī?"
"After seeing the beloved of Rāghava, I shall put the demons to flight; for valor shown before finding her would ruin the objective."
Thus reflecting, he saw the nearby Aśoka grove, filled with flower clusters, whose tall trees seemed to reach the heavens.
The tiger among monkeys entered the grove slowly, without shaking the trees or disturbing the birds sleeping on the branches.
In that city, the wind blew gently as if making the creepers dance. The seasons, fearful of Rāvaṇa, did not cause any mutual distress despite their overlapping splendors.
In that place, by the command of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, the full moon constantly nourished the ponds filled with blooming lotuses with the nectar of its moonlight.
There, the captive women, surrounded by enchanting Rākṣasīs, were made to feel the torment of the flower-arrowed god of love, Kāma.
There, the enemy Rāvaṇa, driven by lust, merely kept Sītā in captivity; despite being clever and prosperous, he could not make himself pleasing to her.
With slow movements, the monkey Hanumān wandered everywhere amidst the trees that were turning green and rustling in the wind.
The moonstones began to ooze, the clusters of night-blooming lilies shone brightly, and heaps of fallen flowers were scattered and rolled about by the wind.
As Hanumān, whose success was imminent, desired to approach Sītā, auspicious birds warbling softly cheered him.
At that moment, Sītā perceived herself as if she were about to be in her husband's presence, guided by true and favorable omens.
Hanumān thought that if news of Sītā were not to be obtained, all their efforts would have surely turned out to be in vain.
Moving from tree to tree while remaining invisible, Hanumān saw the daughter of Janaka, Sītā, who was terrified of Rāvaṇa and saw no protection from her enemy.
He looked with affection upon Sītā, who needed protection from the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, yet was being overcome by distress, hiding from the Rākṣasīs, soiled, and with withered hair.
The noble monkey Hanumān, the son of Vāyu, who had learned the message from Rāma, saw Sītā, whose smile had vanished and who appeared as radiant as energy emerging from the Sun.
Then the King of Rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, arrived there, looking splendid; he was one who had bestowed wealth upon evil demons and who boasted before the wives of others.
Infatuated by love and concealing his true nature, Rāvaṇa made vows to Sītā; he approached her as if he were offering her immense riches.
Longing for her, he spoke many pleasant words. Showing conciliation, he neither became angry with Sītā nor did he find fault with her.
Rāvaṇa said, "O deer-eyed one! Why are you angry without cause at me, who desires to see you? To gaze at the wives of others is the inherent nature and duty of the Rākṣasas."
"O timid one! Middling men respond to those who ask, but the best do not. Others, whose goals are unfulfilled, echo those who praise them; men like me do no such thing."
"Shining with affection, desire me—the lord of the world—and all worldly pleasures. Purchased by you for your enjoyment, I shall never do anything unpleasant to you."
"Reside with me in the palace; do not stay in this lonely forest. Do not dwell on the bare ground; instead, longing for love, rest upon a luxurious bed."
"Just as you have entered my mind without any obstruction, do not obstruct me from dwelling within your heart as well."
Rāvaṇa addresses Sītā as an expert in worldly affairs, urging her not to despise him, the lord of the world. He asks which woman would desire the wretched Rāma (Kākutstha) once they have seen him.
He remarks that someone expecting prosperity from Rāma is like one trying to milk a stone. He tells her to offer her love to him, as he is advising her on what is beneficial and harmful.
Rāvaṇa promises that Sītā will enjoy the three worlds if she is pleased with him. He asks why she laments so much and invites her to let him rest by her side.
He tells her to command the demons and accept pleasant gifts. He asks who would not desire the respect shown by Indra (Śakra), who bows his head in salutation before him.
Hearing the words of the lord of demons, Sītā, who is devoted to her husband, spoke angrily to Rāvaṇa, whose speech was permeated with sin.
Sītā challenges Rāvaṇa, stating he is neither equal to Rāma nor among the brave. She asks why he abducted her by trickery after luring the two heroes away.
She tells the lowest of night-wanderers that his conduct is not heroic. She points out that he now dwells in Laṅkā out of fear of the judgment of the worlds.
She tells the sinner to shine before women only until he sees Rāma. She calls him wicked for desiring another's wife and merely imitating the behavior of the virtuous.
She predicts that Rāma, who is equal to Nārāyaṇa, will soon outshine Rāvaṇa in battle with his raised arrows.
Sītā asks the cruel and arrogant Rāvaṇa where he will flee once struck by Rāma's arrows. She rebukes him for his harsh and improper words against Rāma.
The lord Rāma will not leave even a trace of Rāvaṇa's name. If Rāma can conquer even Śiva (Sthāṇu), then capturing Rāvaṇa is of little consequence.
Sītā tells the man-eater he may praise or restrain her, but she speaks the truth. She says his lustful pride towards her is as futile as pouring water on fire.
She asserts that Rāma will display superior prowess and bring about Rāvaṇa's destruction. Having said this, the princess of Mithilā sat silently before the ten-headed demon.
Then Rāvaṇa, of cruel form, raised his sword in anger. Sighing deeply, he spoke to Sītā (Vaidehī) while standing near her for a moment.
He says that though she has been spoken to kindly for a long time, she remains averse to accepting him. He threatens that if she does not accept him within a month, she will die.
Returning to his palace, he commanded the fearsome demonesses to instill fear in Sītā for his sake.
After he left, the demonesses approached Sītā to frighten her and please Rāvaṇa, repeatedly speaking harsh and cruel words.
They told Sītā to bow to Rāvaṇa for her own well-being; otherwise, they threatened to turn her into their morning meal.
Treating their words as insignificant as grass, Trijaṭā spoke, telling the wicked demonesses to destroy themselves and eat their own flesh.
Trijaṭā describes her dream where she saw Sītā, slender, dark-complexioned, and beautiful-eyed, touching the sun and the moon with her waist.
All those terrifying ogresses, threatened by Sītā with her fierce words and actions as they approached, returned to their beds desiring sleep.
After they had left, the son of the Wind (Hanumān), who had remained hidden for a long time due to the arrival of Daśāsya (Rāvaṇa), made himself known to Maithilī.
Released from the presence of the enemy of sacrifices (Rāvaṇa) like one freed from debt, he commenced the narration of Rāma's story for the purpose of awakening Maithilī's hope.
Seeing him, Sītā thought, "For what reason has this Rāvaṇa, assuming the form of a monkey, descended from the tree and approached me?"
"Praising the son of Daśaratha, he seems different from his earlier nature. Having approached without cruelty, is he perhaps trying to gain my trust?"
"If he is someone other than Rāvaṇa and a follower of Rāghava, then my pre-dawn omens have indeed become fruitful."
"How did Rāma, residing to the north of the ocean, come to know of the city of the Rākṣasas situated to the south of the salt-water sea?"
"I was abducted and brought to this place, inaccessible to men, crossing the rivers, mountains, and forests south of Daṇḍakā, and even the ocean itself."
"Except for the fierce Wind or Vainateya (Garuḍa), no one dares to come here; how then could a monkey reach this place?"
Approaching her while she was thus worried and briefly left alone by the Rākṣasas, the elephant among monkeys said with difficulty, "I am a servant of Rāma."
"Your beloved Rāma resides on Mount Mālyavān, which is far from Mahendra, not distant from the Vindhya mountains, and near the ocean."
"I entered this grove before Daśagrīva (Rāvaṇa) arrived. Once he departed, I approached unnoticed to see you."
"O Queen! While he was speaking, though I was enraged, I did not display my prowess, considering the consequences for the sake of the mission's success."
"Sugrīva, the lord among monkeys, has become a friend of Rāma, the lord of men; therefore, I have come as a messenger."
"Having observed the entire city of the lord of the night-rangers, I, being skilled in searching, have been appointed to this messenger's task."
"Seeing women more beautiful even than divine ladies, and pushing aside Rākṣasas more vicious than serpents, I have reached here."
"Rāma, longing for you and devoted to your reunion, sent me after performing the funeral offerings for his ancestors during the Maghā asterism."
"O Maithilī! This signet ring, a token of recognition from the descendant of Kakutstha who remembers you intensely, was respectfully entrusted to me."
"Lakṣmaṇa, sympathizing with Rāma, remembers you. The lords of kings have prepared themselves; do not fear regarding their arrival here."
"O Vaidehī! Monkeys of terrible prowess will besiege Rāvaṇa here. Seek refuge in fortitude and destroy your grief."
Hanumān says, "When I depart, Kṛṣṇa will destroy the demons. By bringing you here, this Rāvaṇa has staked his very life."
Rāvaṇa has gambled away the enjoyments of his kinsmen and his own wealth. Meanwhile, the best of the Raghus, Rāma, remembers you alone a hundred times a day.
O Maithilī! While the female demons sleeping near you are still unaware, please send back a message for your husband, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Recognizing the monkey's miraculous entry into the city, she gave him her crest-jewel, a token of recognition dear to Rāma.
Having repeatedly asked about Rāma's sleeping, eating, talking, laughing, staying, and walking, she finally sent Hanumān away.
Carrying the token and desiring to perform a formidable deed, even as he was about to go to his master, he thought for a moment in his mind.
They say that he is the best messenger who, after completing the assigned task, performs an additional deed that does not conflict with the primary objective.
"Having seen Vaidehī and performed a feat difficult even for others, I shall attain glory by bringing back news and being the messenger to my lord."
Deciding that the grove protected by the lord of demons must be destroyed, the monkey made it resemble the ravaged Nandana garden.
Proclaiming, "Welfare to the two Raghus! I am their messenger," and acting in the interest of Rāma, Hanumān began destroying the garden, daring any demon to oppose him.

The son of the Wind destroyed the enemy's grove, which turned brown with pollen, its ground colorful with fallen blossoms, and its birds agitated by falling trees. Deer fled in terror as the directions echoed with the cries of birds in that residence of the deer-eyed Sītā.
Agitated by the sound of breaking trees and the chaotic cries of birds, the female night-stalkers reported the situation to Rāvaṇa.
A monkey is destroying the grove that even the sun heated gently, where the wind blew moderately, and which was nourished by the cool rays of the moon.
Then, overwhelmed by anger, the father of Indrajit (Rāvaṇa) ordered eighty thousand Kiṅkaras to destroy the son of Marut (Hanumān).
Holding spears, swords, iron clubs, lances, maces, and hammers, and resembling venomous-eyed serpents, they spread through all directions and reached the forest.
Taking up an iron club, the monkey roared terribly like a thundercloud; they too, with their shining weapons, roared like clouds filled with lightning.
The Rākṣasas clashed with the monkey, who was firm like the ocean, just as rivers with swollen waters merge into the sea during the rainy season.
Shaking his raised tail and wielding a heavy iron club, he climbed the archway and stood there; he did not strike first.
The Rākṣasa-clouds showered streams of arrows upon him, but the monkey-mountain neither wavered nor felt any fear.
The monkey shouted "Wait!" and wielded the iron club in such a way that he seized the lives of many enemies in the battle.
Some vomited blood from their wounds, others covered the ground with their bodies, and yet other fear-stricken Yātudhānas fled in all directions.
Their courage lost and bodies broken, those who cherished their lives screamed; they were terrified by the monkey's roar like deer by the sound of a lion.
Even those masters of illusion, weapons in hand, returned on chariots to kill the monkey, but they were destined to be slain by the son of Marut again.
Stationed on the archway, the monkey brandished his club and slew the assembled attackers who wished to capture him and were now fit to be piled up on the ground.
Then, wishing to protect their lives and desiring to retreat, the surviving night-stalkers went to the presence of Rāvaṇa.
In the presence of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), they cried out, "Though we are many brave and famous warriors, we were forced to turn our backs by a single one, as if intoxicated."
Noticing that those who had grown stout by consuming meat were now agitated, Rāvaṇa, with rolling eyes, dispatched his friendly ministers.
Well-nourished, accompanied by their sons, cheerful, possessing great prowess, and uttering clear roars, they went out with various weapons held in their hands.
Seeing those arrived by the lord’s command—extremely firm, bold, roaring terribly, cruel, and with hands resounded by weapons—the monkey prepared himself.
Unperturbed, he quickly struck those who resembled mountain peaks, who had approached him with raised weapons, and who were capable of great undertakings, having even subdued the gods.
Having subdued enemies before, with his splendor now calm yet filling the quarters with his roar, the enraged and swift monkey slew those angry ones who had rushed quickly toward him.
As those demons were being slain, the world and all directions echoed with their ear-piercing cries, filled with unmitigated terror.
Then, with their hair standing on end due to fear and their enmity diminished, those demons, whose valor vanished in an instant, were brought to destruction by the monkey (Hanumān).
Having killed the demons and defied the enemy's command, Māruti (Hanumān) proceeded again to devastate the Aśoka grove.
The son of the Wind God (Hanumān) showed no mercy while destroying the forest, which seemed to rise up as if to cover the sky or to protect the birds.
May he choose the welfare of Maithilī (Sītā) while uprooting the celestial-like trees. The trees thrown all around seemed to cover the earth like a garment.
Desiring to conceal his intent and quickly issue a command, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa chose Akṣa to kill the monkey, who was performing intolerable deeds.
He said: "May you restrain yourself and go. May you frustrate the enemy's valor. In battle, move quickly against the enemy using your illusory powers."
"May you quickly hasten, fearless in the great battle." That Akṣa, the producer of illusions, went forth to dim the luster of the monkey (Hanumān).
Having deeply entered the forest and harassed the enemies, the monkey (Hanumān) began to torment Akṣa, who had been obstructed by the inhabitants of Laṅkā.
Having uprooted trees from the forest, he stood ready with an iron club to extract the life-breaths of Rāvaṇa's son, which were destined to be extracted.
In the battle, the angry Akṣa, the seeker of combat, hurled masses of weapons at the monkey, who was the withstander, the causer of injury, and the one sought for conflict.
Desiring to play with his iron club against the one wishing to play with weapons in battle, the monkey, seeking glory, struck with trees the one desiring fame.
Wishing to deceive the prince who desired to harm him, the monkey challenged him and struck; then, becoming faint, Akṣa sought refuge in his chariot's banner.
Recovering in a moment, Akṣa, as if wishing to consume the worlds with his brilliance, covered the monkey, who shone like Indra, with a shower of arrows in anger.
While Akṣa wished to join the directions with arrows, the monkey, wishing to ward them off with trees, displayed such valor in battle that it seemed like an illusion.
Akṣa shone while wishing to cover the monkey with weapons; the monkey looked radiant while wishing to cover him with stones and trees.
Those two in battle acted upon the minds of the onlookers, as if wishing to make their strength known or as if wishing to support the worlds with their weapons.
After having struggled for a long time with his illusions against the monkey of unwearied action, the demon (Akṣa), struck by the iron club, fell to the ground.
Purified by favorable cool winds and having cleansed himself in the ocean, the monkey, being hungry, again devastated the forest inhabited by birds.
With his tail curved high, carrying his head as if slightly bent, he bore his mane, which was reddish-yellow like fire and tossed about by the winds.
Due to his speed, other trees fell down as if they had aged. He forcibly felled other helpless trees by uprooting them.
Even after subduing the groups of enemies, the lion among monkeys (Hanumān), unwearied and unrestrained, roamed the forest as if cutting it down or dancing.
Then, wishing to reach the end of his task, he sported in the forest of the Laṅkā-dwelling enemies, who were likely to return, like an intoxicated elephant.
"If the Lord of the Rākṣasas himself had intended to fight, I would have cut him down today as well," saying this, the monkey moved about.
"Once he is killed and the pleasant news is heard, my Lord (Rāma) will attain supreme joy. And today itself, a great satisfaction will arise in Sītā's heart."
Then Rāvaṇa summoned Indrajit to his side and said: "Roaming in the forest and in battles, this one is like a furious, intoxicated elephant."
"You have gone to the end of your enemies and will go repeatedly again. You were able to conquer the gods and remembered your illusions in battle."
"You created weapons and beheld unbearable enemies. You alone destroyed even the weapons of the greats with your own weapons."
"Therefore, go by my command to kill this wicked monkey. Do not fail to manifest your Rākṣasa illusions; do not fail to exhibit your prowess."
"Do not fail to discharge your great missiles; do not fail to attack the enemy in battle. Do not fail to restrain the monkey; go quickly without hesitation."
Leaving the palace, Indrajit bowed at his father's feet, and having received his blessings, he attained great joy.
Once he had gone, the Lord of the Rākṣasas, knowing Indrajit's prowess and considering the monkey already conquered, ceased his agitation.
Desiring to display illusions and surprise the enemy, Indrajit went forth like the irresistible wind at the end of an eon, wishing to purify the world.
Like Death wishing to consume the worlds during the dissolution, he went forth, desiring to swallow the strength of the monkey who wished to destroy the trees.
As he approached, the flocks of birds seemed to wail aloud in grief, as if seeing their slaughtered kinsmen—the trees—upon the arrival of a relative.
Struck by the wind of his speed, the forest, shining with various clusters of flowers and shaken leaves, seemed to sigh as he approached.
"O wicked one! If you do not praise the descendant of Kakutstha (Rāma), you shall not live, nor shall you master your illusions," the monkey spoke these words to him.
Accompanied by his army, Indrajit proceeded in battle, repeatedly covering him from all sides with hundreds of arrows, crescent-headed shafts, and illusions.
Resembling a great mountain and desiring fame, the monkey, having endured the spray of weapons, put to flight the Rākṣasa snares that were like darkness.
He, whose great mane was like light, shook off those who held bows and snares, were led by the lord of Rākṣasas, and were devoid of respect.
Having manifested his strength and being free from evil deeds, the monkey Hanumān shone in battle while slaying enemies to repay his master's debt.
Hurling trees in the four directions and defeating enemies in battle, he was seen roaming in various ways, obscuring the vast expanse of the quarters.
Tawny like fire, doubling the fourfold impact on enemies by the men, he was about to expel the foes from the battlefield.
Alone, he roamed the battle like an excellent being, as if creating light. The enemy of Indra (Indrajit), holding his bow, reached him who brought misfortune to his foes.
With brilliance equal to the sun, the fame-bestowing Indrajit, discharging painful arrows, struck the fame-seeking monkey with his shafts.
Moving in the sky, Hanumān did not descend even when pierced many times by darkness-like arrows that struck his vital spots.
The son of the Wind God (Hanumān), having struck the horses yoked to the poles of Indrajit's chariot and piercing their skins, released their lives.
When those horses slept on the ground in death, the son of Rāvaṇa (Indrajit), harsh and devoid of fear, commanded his charioteer to bring others.
Wishing to resume the battle and desiring to inflict fear, he mounted his chariot as if to encourage his own people.
Desiring victory, Indrajit again formed an invincible battle array against the monkey-cloud who was about to shower the armies with trees.
Flowing with their own warm blood arising from the battle and trickling from wounds, the enemies, out of anger, seemed to bathe the monkey.
Intending to dominate them in battle, sitting on the city gate without despairing, he checked the obstructed cries of the men.
The angry Rākṣasas, having endured, showered a multitude of weapons. Even that which Indra could not endure, the monkey completely withstood.
With blood flowing, the unswerving monkey, striking with an iron bar, killed the enemies who were pale from the flow of blood.
Quivering and leaping about, Meghanāda quickly bound the leaping enemy with the Brahmapāśa, rendering him motionless.
Captured by the quivering cannibals, Hanumān, though motionless and capable of obstructing them, did not move out of respect for Brahmā.
Indrajit loudly said to his men: "Create joy for the master. Do not fail to traverse the sky quickly to carry the monkey."
The enemies carrying Hanumān said: "We will eat you, who have come here from a place of fear and have reached the state of being held between fingers."
They also said: "This is the messenger of that mortal who protected the Brāhmaṇas in sacrifices like Agniṣṭoma and Jyotiṣṭoma."
They continued describing Rāma as the one who cut off the nose of Rāvaṇa's maternal cousin and killed the sons of his mother's sister, like Khara and others.
This spy of that evil offspring of the Kṣatriyas has arrived, in whose encounter with the Rākṣasas no fears manifest.
Having seen the Lord of Kings fast asleep, this wicked one of evil intent, an expert in espionage, entered the Pramadāvana grove.
At night, he beheld Maithilī, who remained steadfast in the conduct of the twice-born, whose scriptures are well-purified and who possess a luster like that of the sage Kapiṣṭhala.
He saw her, the foremost in all feminine virtues, seated on a mat, firm in speech, and lying on the bare ground like a stainless star situated in the heavens.
He saw the auspicious and slender lady, who was most soothing among all splendors and highly luminous, appearing as if scorching herself and turning the forest into pure light.
He saw her appearing like a sacred creeper made of gold and gems, crowded with bees turned tawny by the filaments transformed into honey, and adorned with blooming flowers.
He saw that lady of supreme vows shedding tears, as if performing a continuous sprinkling over her heart scorched by the fire of grief.
Enraged upon seeing her, he broke the trees while slaying the opposing enemies, scattering them all around like the wind god Vāyu himself.
In the great battle, Indrajit, remaining unyielding, paralyzed the one of irresistible prowess who had endured various weapons.
The distressed Rākṣasas, realizing he was about to be bound by the ropes, further bound him with long leather straps, chains, and other materials.
Indrajit became despondent upon realizing another binding was being applied over the current one, for a divine bond does not tolerate any additional shackle.
The Rākṣasas, capturing the monkey, approached the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, who possessed a broad chest and appeared as if stealing the luster of everything before him.
While the lunar disc was in the west, the terrifying Rākṣasas like Kharaṇasa, whose vital parts were mangled in various ways, stood at the front of the forest.
The enemies of the monkey said, "By this creature, the garden has been made forestless, including the mango groves and the unmixed cedar forests."
Taking the monkey, the Rākṣasas joyfully approached the lord of the blood-drinkers, who was a vehicle of wrath, during the forenoon.
The wine-drinking Rākṣasas spoke with manifestation to Rāvaṇa, who was intoxicated by wine, the destroyer of enemies' pride, and the abductor of others' wives.
The enemies of the gods, engaged in rivalry, bowed at Rāvaṇa's feet while handing over Hanūmān, who was destroying the intellect of his foes.
The enraged lord of the Rākṣasas addressed the assembly, saying, "I shall throw the head of this forest-destroying monkey onto the ground."
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, focused on his purpose, addressed the King of Rākṣasas who was striking out in anger, sounding like a thundering cloud.
"O Ten-headed One! Calm down. Desist from proceeding with anger. Please understand that envoys are not to be killed even when no fault exists."
Rāvaṇa spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa, who was trying to pacify him: "This sinner, who has destroyed the pleasure grove, does not deserve to live."
"Since he has killed my trusted demons in the forest, tell me why we should not slay this sinful creature who has committed such prior offenses?"
"Do not obstruct me as I, in my anger, prepare to kill my enemy within my own palace; know that he is fit for his final departure to death."
"Those who do not strike down an enemy present before them soon cause the destruction of even their rightfully earned prosperity."
"What wicked person in this world, even if he were Indra himself, would be able to protect his own life after inciting the wrath of Rāvaṇa?"
"This sinner, who roams the forest edges and destroys fruits, will no longer be able to abuse us or consume the forest honey."
"In the forest protected by me, the sun does not traverse freely, the fire does not shine with heat, and even the wind does not blow violently."
"Henceforth, this ill-mannered monkey will find it impossible to drink the superior, sweet nectar gathered by bees in my forest."
When the agitated Rāvaṇa spoke thus with a face terrifying in rage, the monkey Hanumān addressed him with conciliatory words to achieve his purpose.
"O Lord of the three worlds, why is your anger, upon seeing a single bound monkey brought to your palace, as disproportionate as if directed at a trivial blade of grass?"
"Why does an expert in policy like you display such fury toward an ascetic who is humble before sages and indifferent to conquest?"
"There are no perpetually beautiful women or jewel-laden lands to be gained by defeating him; who then would choose to wage war against such a person?"
"For the prosperity of the entire world, unite with Rāma and Sugrīva, just as the Himālaya connects the eastern and western oceans filled with gems."
"Rāma and Sugrīva will become your friends and the monkey chiefs your servants only by the return of another's wife; therefore, release Maithilī."
"By returning Sītā, attain Dharma; through friendship with Rāma, obtain Artha; and by living in security, satisfy Kāma. Attain all three goals by giving her up."
"Has the true nature of your enemy not been made known to you through the fates of Virādha, Tāḍakā, Vālī, Kabandha, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and even Mārīca?"
"Do not consider the death of Khara and others as a cause for enmity, because that was done for self-preservation and not out of a desire for conquest."
Then Rāvaṇa, his collection of lotus-like faces trembling from the blast of the wind of his anger, agitated like a great lake, spoke to the monkey.
"For you, who have killed demon warriors and broken the branches of the royal garden, yet claim to be a messenger, what part of your conduct is actually like a messenger?"
"If the descendant of Kakutstha, who kills the deformed, children, and women—the slayer of Kabandha, Khara, and Tāḍakā—is called an ascetic, then tell me, what does a sinner look like?"
Recognizing the greatness of kings, how can you claim that the conflict with Rāma is fruitless simply because it lacks gains like jewels, when the true fruit of such a war is prestige?
Seizing and enjoying another's wife is indeed the duty of man-eaters. You only spoke thus because you have a mouth to speak. What doubt could I possibly have regarding your character?
Tell me, Hanumān, what kind of friendship can exist between humans, monkeys, and Rākṣasas, who differ so vastly in prosperity, character, conduct, and lineage?
The lone Virādha, though defeated by the two brothers, is not even worth mentioning. That fool was killed through deceit. Even so, why do you take pride in that?
And Mārīca, acting on my command, was intent only on fleeing and had no desire to fight; he died in the forest while merely luring Rāma away.
It is true that Rāma killed the monkey Vālin while he was preoccupied with someone else. You yourself reflect and say if such an act is appropriate for the great.
Will the ten-faced Rāvaṇa tolerate the killing of his relatives by a man who is mere food, just to save your own life? From where has this wicked thought of yours originated?
The monkey Hanumān replied: I am a messenger. I deliberately carried out the destruction of the trees and the Rākṣasas as a calculated means to secure an audience with you.
O Daśagrīva, how can you claim that those who, because of you, rendered the world up to Trikūṭa devoid of living beings, are not to be executed by the King Rāma?
Regarding what you said about the fruit of war with Rāma being prestige, it is because of that very pride that hundreds of clans of Asuras and Rākṣasas have already perished.
That you consider your own duty as non-duty and weak, and remain fearless toward your enemy Rāma, will not result in your welfare for long.
Just as friendship is not desired among those who differ in lineage and traits, you should likewise not have sought enmity with humans and monkeys.
If the one you call defeated killed Virādha, the obstacle to penances, then how is that foremost of archers, Rāma, not worthy of mention?
As you yourself stated, even the highly deceptive Mārīca, while fleeing, was unable to escape the range of the arrows of the elephant-like Rāma.
Do you not remember the prowess of Vālin while he was occupied with another? Surely, squeezed by his arms while you were performing evening prayers, you had fainted.
Abandon this war against the strong, which was suggested by evil-minded relatives. Surrender Sītā along with your treasury, army, self, and lands to the one who deserves to be honored.
Thus addressed loudly in the assembly by the son of Marut with clear, harsh, and unbearable words, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa looked at his attendants and ordered the burning of the monkey.
Then, wrapped in bark, silk, and blankets, with his tail blazing and uplifted, Hanumān soared into the sky while being watched by the agitated-eyed demons of the court.

Skilled in battle and honored by Rāma, he incited strife in the city of the chief enemy of the gods. Then, resembling the fire of Indra’s weapon, he forcefully rendered Rāvaṇa’s palace into a state of ruin with blazing fire.
Due to the spreading fire, the city did not remain intact. As the women fled through the sky, the city attained a state similar to the destruction of Tripura, losing its mountain-like stability.
As the demons abandoned their sap-filled bodies and fell in various directions, the sky seemed filled with the rising, piteous, and indistinct cries of those who were weeping.
There was no collection of golden dwellings that the monkey did not consume with fire. Everywhere, the melting caused by the heat did not fail to turn things into liquid.

Laughter ceased; the playful sport previously pursued with joy diminished, as did the brilliance of love. The passionate women lost their delight, and the welfare desired for the city was no longer achieved.

Laṅkā, with its dwellings ignited and ruled by a proud lord, burned. The city, where the fire of desire was once prominent, now saw its glory consumed by the brilliance of the blazing sacrificial-like fire.
Among the flesh-eating demons, in every direction, a clear and overwhelming agitation spread. The great people, now staggering, performed many actions that were devoid of their usual dignity.

Mountain-born elephants were not spared, nor were beloved ones protected. Every kind of charm vanished completely. Driven by great frenzy and afflicted by pain, the women reached a death that was not in battle.
The monkey burned the city, which had never been attacked by great monkeys of terrifying prowess, nor had it ever been invaded by men.
The city, filled with great splendor and never before repulsed even by the most distant enemies, was met with fire. It quickly crumbled to the earth, its gates destroyed on all sides.
The lord of monkeys saw the vanishing multitudes of women, who were captivating and wore attractive necklaces, as they perished in the disaster.
The golden ponds with pure water could not remove the bodily distress of the women, nor did the demons find any peace by approaching the trees whose leaves and flowers were engulfed in flames.
Then, he went straight to the grove where the rows of birds were disturbed and the Asana, Bāṇa, Keśara, and Tamāla trees were broken, in order to see Sītā.
The daughter of Janaka, respected by all, with eyes like lotuses and resting on the ground beneath a tree, was seen by the monkey who was capable of leaping over massive mountains.
The beloved of Rāma was seen, deprived of her ornaments, enduring great sorrow, yet maintaining her dignity despite the separation.
Hanumān spoke measured words to her: "O Goddess! Having witnessed your grief and seen all the demons, I shall now joyfully and quickly go to the presence of Rāma at Mount Mālyavān."
Inaccessible to enemies, he assumed a form that struck fear into his foes. Possessing great strength and stature, he leapt into the sky, which was fitting for his lofty and powerful nature.
Hanumān, bearing the signet ring and the power of the wind, shone brilliantly in his transformed state, as did the ocean agitated by his flight, while he joyfully proceeded as a messenger.
He proceeded toward the excellent, lofty, and beautiful mountain ahead, which was firm, famous, a source of light, full of living beings, and possessed of lotus-like lakes.
Hanūmān beheld ahead of him the lofty, beautiful, and firm Mahendra mountain, abounding in living beings, which appeared like a divine station established for a moment in the sky.
Upon reaching that wondrous mountain, which looked like a variegated painting, the monkeys, terrified by Hanūmān's immense speed, were repeatedly bewildered.
Moving along, he scattered the waters of the ocean and shook the trees standing on the shore. Those trees spread comfortable beds of flowers, upon which love-stricken kinnaras reclined.
That monkey, having quickly reached the mountain adorned with clusters of trees, revealed the success of his mission through a smile and graced the mountain along with the joyful monkey army.

Although Garuḍa, the wind, and the sun are renowned for their speed among those who fly, they nonetheless considered Hanūmān to be exceedingly swift as he returned having accomplished his goal so quickly.

Then, Hanūmān, the monkey-mountain, shone brightly; his wounds were like caves inhabited by snake-like weapons, his broad chest and thighs like hard rock walls, and his flowing blood like the red hue of minerals.

Upon the arrival of the son of the wind, the monkeys shone like the golden peaks of a mountain, their moving reddish hair resembling golden creepers and their bright eyes appearing like clusters of gems.
Hanūmān, the moon among monkeys, delighted the ocean-like monkey hosts with his sweet appearance. Spreading the nectar-like rays of his words, he caused their eyes to overflow with tears of joy.
Then, those elephant-like monkeys, who had trampled the creepers of the Vindhya and drunk the pure waters of its streams, ravaged the Madhuvana forest under the command of the joyful Aṅgada.

The monkey-sun, dispelling the darkness of the monkeys' sorrow and blooming the lotus-like purpose with the rays of his sweet words, left the mountain as if it were the Eastern peak and soared into the sky, destroying the darkness of delusion in the King's heart.

Hanūmān reached the son of Raghu, who was in the forest penance grove, wearing matted hair, deerskin, and bark garments. Accompanied by his younger brother of equal tranquility, attire, and meditation, he appeared like the Supreme Being with Nara.
Holding the jewel in his cupped hands, its faint light escaping through the gaps in his fingers like the moon behind a thin reddish cloud, he bowed to the King with bent knees and head.
That crest-jewel, possessing the weight and beauty of a noble gem and looking like the full disc of the moon, was seen by Rāma along with the hope for life.
Rāma saw the jewel, which had come from the forest, its luster faded and dusty from lack of cleaning, deprived of Maithilī, yet retaining its dignity like himself.
At that time, King Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa and the leader of the monkey army thought: "How can Hanūmān, who by his prowess has achieved the desired goal, not be the wish-fulfilling gem?"
Hanūmān said: "The wicked enemy, unaware that you are like the winds of destruction, has seized the spark that is Sītā and lies in the forest of Laṅkā like a lion, only to meet his death."

"I have returned after seeing him, the master of illusions, who seized the wealth of Kubera in battle and fought the gods. Does not wealth acquired by straying from the path of righteousness distress everyone when coupled with the arrogance of power and loss of shame?"
"The prosperous demon is a fool; it is no wonder that he is arrogant. What reason could there be for the ignoble to walk upon the path of righteousness?"
"O Lord Rāma! In his abode, I saw that slender lady, anxious and sorrowful. This is the essence of the matter told to you; what is the use of further elaborate speech?"
"If only the spot were removed from the crescent moon and no future one appeared, then the pure Sītā, made slender by her wasting grief, might be compared to the digit of the moon."
O King! Strive hard to rescue your virtuous wife, who has been seized by one who acts without reflection, has not served wise elders, and is cruelly unyielding.
Rāma became like a great lake teeming with agitated creatures and drying up. Overwhelmed by grief on all sides, he appeared as though desiring water fallen from a cloudless sky.

Then the monkeys assembled and followed Rāma, who bore an appearance and attire similar to Lakṣmaṇa. Rāma signaled the departure with his hand, and his command was respectfully received by the bowing Sugrīva.
Then the two kings, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, mounted the backs of monkeys. The monkeys, with eyes reddish-yellow like blazing fire, left the earth, sky, and mountains, and swiftly reached Mount Mahendra.
Mount Mahendra stood as if to protect the earth on all sides from the flooding waters of the ocean, stretching its body between the sky and the earth, capable of withstanding the ocean's force.

Its roots reached the abode of serpents, while its hundreds of peaks touched the celestial world. Its massive and thick ridges filled the directions, and its beautiful bowers were filled with trees laden with fruits and flowers.

The mountain clearly imitated the sounds of beloved women through the humming of bees and the beauty of his beloved's smile through the lotuses, suddenly bringing supreme joy to the lord of men, Rāma.

With its peak-like hands, the mountain seemed to touch the broad hips of the sky out of passion—the sky whose girdle was the jewel-like planets, whose cloud-garment had fallen, and which possessed unsurpassed brilliance.
Having avoided fickle, light, weak, and powerless people, the mountain seemed to have made its home by the seashore—firm, of incomparable height, and supporting tall clouds.

With its crystal houses equipped with jewel-lamps and the songs of young Kinnaras, it created an impression of the city of gods for celestial nymphs; it was free from sorrow and filled with numerous Kalpavṛkṣa trees.
Then the monkey armies, along with the sons of Raghu, looked up and saw the direction where Sītā was, separated by the ocean, smoky with rising fumes, as pointed out by Hanumān's finger.

From the bowers of Mahendra, the monkeys, whose brilliance obscured the rays of the sun, reached the ocean—which was capable of supporting the world's weight with its vast waters and waves, yet remained within its shores.
The ocean's light from gems within large oyster shells dispelled the darkness of the underworld, while nets of floating diamonds high above obstructed the path of the sun's rays.
Its waters increased at night by the growing flows of pure rivers, making the peaks of Mahendra, made of moonstones and bearing water, clearly visible.
The ocean held mountains and serpents that support the earth, which were of unassailable power and bore many brilliant gems, along with tortoises and crocodiles exhausted and hidden from fatigue.
They saw great waves releasing massive sprays of mist, creating rainbows from the brilliance of pure gems. These waves, with deep rumbles, removed the earth's heat like rain-bearing clouds.
There, the trees on the shore-slopes, broken by sea-elephants, shone bright, adorned with ornaments of coral and colored by heaps of pearls.

Filling the entire subterranean world, filled with gems, and hiding the sky with mountain-like waves—where could such a mass of water truly come from? Thus approaching, they considered the ocean an illusion.
Though without a moon, it possessed great brilliance; though its wealth (Lakṣmī) was taken by gods, its beauty was not lost; though churned by gods, it surpassed the heavens with its waters.

The ocean carried the earth, the principal mountains, Śeṣa, and the elephants of the quarters like a boat. By its actions, it surpassed even the Great Boar, who held the distressed earth on his mountain-like snout.

Beholding Rāma, the ocean, which appeared like a white silk garment slipped from the mountain-breasts of the Earth, held a collection of water delightful to the mind and was fringed by the ends of flickering rivers flowing from the mountains.

The ocean, variegated with infinite great wonders, free from impurity, pure, and vast, shone intensely when approached by the king of monkeys, Lakṣmaṇa, and the lord of the earth Rāma, who were themselves insurmountable.

As if instructing observers that greatness does not exist without adversity, the ocean constantly fluctuated every moment, with its waves rising as high as mountains and then subsiding into tranquility.

Love, skilled in causing distress, pierced the son of Raghu with even soft flower-arrows and scorched him with even flickering cool breezes, yet he neither inflicted a visible wound nor produced a flame.
At the close of day, having reached the shore of the ocean and surpassed the common world, the sun and the son of Raghu, both possessing a soft and faded luster, mirrored each other’s appearance.
Then, as if stealing away all diversions and compelling a singular focus on the beloved, a dense darkness increased along with the rising of Love in the son of Raghu.
Then the moon appeared over the ocean, dispelling darkness and providing scope for vision, as if recreating the dissolved world; indeed, the great exist entirely for the sake of others.

Overpowered by Love, the son of Raghu repeatedly doubted, asking, 'Whence this lightning in a cloudless sky? This rain of sharp arrows is impossible without a bow.' Thus, he failed to recognize the moon.
The moon shone in the clusters of night-lotus, upon the faces of the directions whose darkness was destroyed, and in the sky, in a manner that none other than the moon can shine.

Having the luster of a water-laden cloud, the darkness settled in the bowers as if seeking refuge from its enemy, the moonbeams, which were warded off by trees; it crouched like one terrified within the gaps of large, uneven rocks.

Then the younger brother of the son of Raghu, who was pleasing to the eyes and mind, though born from the heart was of noble character unlike Love, spoke with a voice like the thundering of a rain-cloud.

'Make the wives of the enemies such that their hair is disheveled by the death of their husbands and their cosmetics are washed away by tears. Abandon grief; where are you, the refuge of the worlds, and where is delusion?'
'Alas! In the human world, a great man who becomes heedless sinks deeply. A heavy lord of elephants, with a body like a mountain peak, sinks when stuck in mud, but a piece of wood does not.'

'What is there to be known that is not known by you? Or is even a blink of your eye without intelligence? Nevertheless, a flood of affection, which has gained a soul through your good deeds and fears the undesirable, impels me to speak.'
Hearing these words of the son of Sumitrā, Rāma, yawning and stretching his arms, assigned monkeys to every direction for protection and, desiring sleep, lay down upon a bed of sprouts.
As the moon, the treasure of arts, lost its luster and set like one whose merit is exhausted, the lilies—resembling enemies—embraced sorrow, while the lotuses—acting as friends—bloomed with laughter.

Having ascended high into the sky and now falling like a king from a precipice, the moon, who had bestowed favors, was quickly followed by the host of stars, whose white fame was gathered and whose devotion was firm.
Wondering where those side-glances or playful words meant for him had gone, the moon set before the women of Laṅkā awoke, without even reaching the beauty of their foreheads.
Women who spent the night feigning sleep with faces turned away out of pride, grew anxious as night ended; they reconciled with their husbands even though their faults were clearly seen.
The trees of love belonging to the beloveds, though withered by jealousy, had firm roots; having lost all auspicious sprouts, they grew once more, nourished by the sprinkling of tears.
With the fear of separation and passion renewed, the people—never satiated—did not realize the repetitive nature of Kāma as he returned with ever-fresh flavors of love.
When consciousness dawned in the heart along with the pleasure born of all senses, the eye, unable to bear its closure, remained open, feeling cheated like a weakling.
The slender-waisted woman, seeing her own thin nails broken upon the soldier's broad chest, felt distressed by her frustrated desire and long remained angry with both her husband and her nails.
With limbs motionless and eyes closed, their life evidenced only by sweat and horripilation, people held in deep embrace by their beloveds lost all sharpness of intellect.
Was it darkness, sleep, death, bliss, fainting, or the illusion of Manobhava? Regaining consciousness, they pondered what and how it was, yet could not truly comprehend it.
Pressing chest to breasts, face to face, and limbs to limbs intensely, those afflicted by love were never satisfied; for in love, the concept of sufficiency is a contradiction.
The newlywed bride, with her slender limbs limp while being embraced, kept her eyes closed even when gazed upon; devoid of pride, she remained as if her sole essence was to benefit another.
In the bride suddenly embraced at the start of lovemaking, passion was bashful and accompanied by both fear and desire; once reassured by her lover, it became delightful through their union.
Another woman, scratched by her lover as he sought reconciliation, betrayed her softening by horripilation; her inner anger vanished, and she was won over by his prowess alone.
Another woman, though initially firm and harsh, was touched by her lover—who was like the moon—and quickly became delighted, perspiring from agitation like a moonstone oozing water under moonbeams.
As the moon, the lord of the night, departed, the sky turned dusky and seemed to faint in confusion; then the sweet beauty of Aruṇa, like a devoted friend, woke the sky.
With their mutual thirst unquenched, and the night ending as if in a second, the eager people reluctantly left their bedrooms, appearing as if they were under the control of another.
One man, partially rising, was embraced and sank back; another was stopped while leaving, unwilling to go; another left on a pretext and returned, abandoning all other duties just to stay.
In the morning, at the royal palaces, auspicious young women sang with rhythm providing balanced beauty, careful attention, melody, and words that clearly conveyed their meaning.
Then the rising Vivasvān, with his continuous ropes of rays, seemed to pull out the world which was submerged in the darkness—as if in impassable mud—where all distinctions of form had been lost.

The faces of the women, with their lip-color kissed away, collyrium removed, and shining with disheveled locks, appeared more beautiful in the morning after fulfillment than they did the previous day when fully adorned.

With the corners of their eyes reddened from staying awake, decorative markings of collyrium and red lac washed away, and bodies slender from exhaustion, those women resembled those who had just returned from their lovers' dwellings.

Though beautiful, the lower lips of the women—smeared with traces of collyrium from the eyes and bearing intense stains of betel—diminished their dignity by betraying the intimate night spent with their husbands.

By applying collyrium to their lovely eyes, reddening their lips with betel, and perfuming their mouths with fragrant substances, the people showed a distinct partiality toward enhancing their physical charms.
Due to intense passion, the couples—who were never apart—did not resent the pain from tooth-marks received during lovemaking and only noticed in the morning; they felt no offense toward one another.

The victorious women, like chief warriors, moved about with arrows of eyes drawn to the ears and feathered with lashes, possessing spears of long hair, wheels of breasts and thighs, and nooses of expanded ears.
Seeing their rivals' breasts smeared with sandalwood paste and their garments soiled from the night's dalliance, the co-wives rejoiced in the morning, their hearts heavy with lingering jealousy.
Passion, born in hearts sick with love, though fickle, remained captivated by virtue; it shone as if peering through the windows of the eyes to gaze upon the faces of the beloveds out of curiosity.

When love reached its zenith, people overwhelmed by passion lost all consciousness of their surroundings and could not even remember the endearments and services they had instinctively offered or received.
Through garments of pleasing but subtle colors, fragrant unguents, and faces radiant with satisfaction, the people indicated that their secret desires had found fulfillment.

In the early morning, young men with bodies anointed with sandalwood, covering their bitten lips with their hands while speaking, and with sleepy, unblinking eyes, inadvertently revealed the secrets they intended to hide.

O beautiful one! Since the world is already conquered by your gentleness, why is the bow of your eyebrow raised? Is it to strike forcibly? Tell me, is the arrow of your glance smeared with collyrium as if with poison?
Filled with love, young men said to young women in assemblies: "Why has the betel-stain, like a pile of grass, been placed upon your lip which is like a blazing fire?"
The houses in the morning shone like lakes; they were pleasant to enter, possessed of beauty, pure, removers of distress, spacious, and filled with the lotus-like faces of awakened women.

The splendor of the celestial Nandana grove, served even by gods, was surpassed by the houses which were swept, sprinkled, adorned with beautiful flowers, scented with fragrant substances, and frequented by bees.
A bee, falling upon the eyes out of greed for blue lotuses, was brushed away by a hand; mistaken for a red lotus and driven by thirst, the bold creature then bit the palm of the hand.

Like a dance master, the bee orchestrated the trembling of the eyes, the shaking of the hands, the knitting of the eyebrows, the heaving of the breasts, and the tinkling of ornaments as the woman tried to ward it off.
Then, on that auspicious day, the city folk dressed in attire suited to their family traditions and status, and set out toward the royal palace at the time the enemy of Śatamanyu awoke.
Like torrents of water rushing from the peaks of great mountains, the crowds of people pouring out from the city mansions filled the street-rivers and flooded the ocean-like courtyard of the King.
Before the enemy of Tridaśendra awoke, those waiting, both lowly and great, were parched with anxiety and met with indifferent looks from the doorkeepers, reaching a state of parity.

The rākṣasas attended him with majestic elephants whose trunks, ears, and tongues were large and constantly moving. These elephants, with swarms of bees clinging to their temples, were captured effortlessly and held with just the tips of the fingers in a display of disdain.

Lions, with forepaws that had been released after being smeared with the flesh of slaughtered intoxicated elephants, were brought there; while others were arranged in rows, tied to one another by their tails.
Clusters of flowers along with buds from the celestial trees (sura-drumas), abandoned by the trembling hosts of gods and plucked by the fearless night-stalkers, were seen scattered in that place.

The ten-faced Daśāsya, who rejected the best of the twice-born and considered all virtues as worthless due to extreme delusion, first worshipped the eminent brahma-rākṣasas of sinful intent for the sake of his own prosperity.

Accompanied by trusted followers who were masters of illusion, terrifying to people, devoted to seizing wealth, and finding pleasure only in the destruction of the virtuous, he entered the assembly hall, causing the ground to tremble.

Filled with demons wielding sharpened weapons and crowded with ogresses having large bellies and faces, the assembly hall resembled a forest scattered with hundreds of hunters, where the terrified captive celestial women were like does caught in a snare.

Like a lightning-charged cloud emitting a deep, grave sound toward every quarter, he took his seat upon a high, golden throne, variegated with various gems, resembling a peak of Mount Sumeru and radiant with the brilliance of many jewels.

Then, his mother spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa, who was awake, had performed his worship of the deities, was radiating mental peace through his very glance, and looked beautiful with his limbs adorned with ornaments.

O wise one! You, being a delight to your kin, should quickly bring peace to the dwellers of heaven regarding the poison-like nature of your brother, who is excessively arrogant with pride and is tormenting the worlds, turning it into nectar.

Act in such a way that he releases Sītā, whose form is enveloped by the mist of sorrow, who sits on the bare ground, and who, like a fallen star with extinguished rays, strikes fear into the hearts of people.
O delight of the clan! Strive quickly before this brother of yours, who terrifies the hosts of gods like a mass of poison, is devoured by the lord of men Rāma, just as poison was swallowed by Hara.

The assemblies of Janasthāna have been destroyed, the city has been made like a place with uprooted warrior-trees, and the halls are burnt. Therefore, perform whatever duty a kinsman must undertake towards Rāvaṇa.
Urged repeatedly by his mother, the steadfast Vibhīṣaṇa, with a pure intellect, reflected deeply for a long time on that beneficial course of action which was intended to be performed earliest.
He went to the gate of Rāvaṇa’s palace, where the messengers of Indra were struck back by doorkeepers, where the world-guardians stood with offerings, and where trusted demons entered with fear.

Saluted by the gatekeepers from afar, he entered unannounced while inquiring about the news. With a path respectfully cleared by the demons, he beheld the enemy of Indra, Rāvaṇa, appearing like a mountain peak.

He saw Rāvaṇa seated on a high throne of fiery brilliance, terrifying like the clouds of destruction, naturally fierce, with sparks flying from his eyes, resembling the smoke of the fire at the end of an aeon.
He beheld Rāvaṇa who, even when casting a look of affection, inspired fear like the lord of serpents; though dark in form, he surpassed all renowned luminaries with his inherent energy.
The radiant night-walkers, who had conquered the world of mortals, crowded around him—the bestower of gems—just as the thirsty chief deities approach a cloud that sheds pearls.
Having offered salutations, he sat on a seat prepared by servants who knew his gestures. Resting his beautiful arms on the throne, he sat close to those who had arrived earlier.

Then the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, extending his hand—which resembled an agitated serpent, was encrusted with gems in glowing rings, and had tongues of light from many flickering nails—addressed the assembly.
Success is achieved in well-counseled tasks when undertaken with capable friends like you, who have witnessed many affairs, are well-versed in policies, are intelligent, and know the proper means.
Since the destruction of Vāli and Khara was ignored, the city burnt, Akṣa killed, and the enemy's army now desires to cross the ocean, speak immediately on what is appropriate here.
Touching their arms, shoulders, chests, bows, swords, maces, and spears, the demons headed by Prahasta, renowned for their pride, spoke to the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
O chief of man-eaters! Having shattered the invincible Indra and wielding mighty punishment, why do you, becoming intent on counsel, give such importance to an attack by a human like Rāma?
Tell us! Shall we crush the sun, enveloped in smoke and sparks, onto the earth? Shall we spit out the moon, squeezed by our teeth and drunk dry, like withered sugarcane?
What of those monkeys and the descendants of Raghu? They would not even suffice for a single breakfast. O upholder of Kailāsa! Command us: shall heaven be below and the earth in the sky?
O King! The fire on the tail of that fickle monkey, who deserved to be killed, was fanned by your own men and, through their negligence, it burnt Laṅkā while he was escaping.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, with a broad chest, a raised gaze, and a body inclined to speak, gesturing with his hands, addressed the demons with words full of significant meaning.

What you, well-supported by the king, have said in accordance with your reputation for battle must indeed be fulfilled at the cost of your lives; however, in matters of counsel, wisdom is authorized, not mere valor.
Human effort attains greatness when it follows a policy respected with care. Hanūmān, who destroyed the entire city, provides an answer to the one who has conquered even Indra.
Consider with divine wisdom whether it was by negligence that fire burned Laṅkā, having flared up from the body of one meant to be executed, and if even the binding by the Brahmāstra was a mistake.

The worlds possess immeasurable and wonderful states, and people are diverse with conquered pride. Put forth excellent effort in action, and do not disregard the wise who are full of political wisdom.

Prosperity, even though fickle, does not abandon that king desiring victory who constantly examines the states of progress, decline, and stagnation, and applies himself to the six political expedients like sandhi.

The prosperity of an enemy who has lost his sense of policy, who has not conquered his senses, and who is filled with arrogance should be ignored; in the end, it causes disaffection and destroys him root and branch.

Even one's own decline should be accepted by a wise ruler if it is accompanied by the affection of the people and leads to future fruit; he should seek peace when faced with an overlord who has conquered the six internal enemies.
When a king sees no favorable progress or decline through either war or peace, he should remain quiet, awaiting the right opportunity, and should not engage in useless exertion.

While in a state of peace, a king should increase his own prosperity or strike the enemy through secret means; he should win over the enemy's people or cause dissension among them and make a peace that weakens the foe.

Showing the quality of affection and making the enemy's own people hate him, a king should break the enemy's circle of allies. By employing such means, peace should be made a strategy for attaining prosperity.

Considering his people enduring and not to be bribed by others, and occupying forts surrounded by water, trees, or mountains—impassable and invincible—a king should prosper through conflict with the enemy.
He who cannot destroy his enemies but is also not defeated by even weak foes should instigate a fight like that between a dog and a boar, while remaining secure and strengthening his forts.

If the enemy can be appeased merely by marching, one should proceed with a protected army. If unable to destroy the enemy, one should focus on protecting one's own affairs and seek refuge with a superior power.

A king should make peace with one and war with another, or vice-versa, after carefully considering his growth. Understanding the strength of himself and his enemies, a seeker of victory should employ these policies.
You, O King, have generated disaffection in the world and provoked the circle of kings headed by Indra. I see the opposite in Rāma; therefore, I consider the opponent to be far superior.
The moment Vāli was killed with a single arrow and the monkey Sugrīva was made king—who is now your enemy's greatest friend—at that very moment your cause was lost.

Your power, which became confined merely within your ramparts after the slaughter of Khara and others, is now fading excessively due to the burning of Laṅkā, the killing of Akṣa, and the destruction of the groves.

Enslaved by the six internal enemies, with bewildered kinsmen, lost friends, and surrounded by the worthless, do not engage in a foot-battle with an elephant. Bow down to the lord of the earth, Rāma, who is kind to those who surrender.

Rāma is pained by the abduction of his wife, and we are pained by the death of our kinsmen who were like our very selves. Just as hot iron joins with hot iron, let there be peace between us and the enemy; release Sītā.

O King! Let the kshatriya prowess, intensified by wrath and fanned by the fierce winds of royal circles, be pacified by the waters of conciliation. Be gracious, so that we, along with our kinsmen and servants, may live.
O King! Both equals may perish like unbaked clay pots. However, Rāma is established in valor and possesses the loyalty of his followers, while you have many noble enemies.

Even if you consider yourself superior to the enemy in army and treasury, a full pot's destruction by an empty one is a waste. When something full breaks, much is lost, whereas the empty loses nothing.

A proud man whose servants are distressed and whose wealth is sought after may strive even in risky matters. But if one who has already achieved his ends takes unnecessary risks, Fortune surely does not find delight in him.

A king who has secured the loyalty of his subjects should undertake tasks that are feasible, free from flaws, and yield great results, leading them to completion. In the opposite case, all effort becomes futile.

A well-principled king is impossible to defeat. In conflict, losses like depletion of resources are certain, with no gain or auspicious conclusion. Therefore, abandon enmity with such a popular ruler on this earth.

Your ally was destroyed, and he gained an ally. He now has a gathered army ready for his friend’s distress. The enemy has subdued a territory to be enjoyed through a single arrow. See what objective was not achieved by the killing of Vālin?

The lord of monkeys did not approach Rāghava out of greed or fear, which would make him vulnerable to dissension. Having regained his kingdom and staying on the path of the righteous, he came wishing to return the favor.

Those monkey chiefs subsist on fruits, live in mountain springs and bowers, and are ignorant of the sensual pleasures of divine damsels. Being of a lower species and unattainable by the lure of precious gems, they cannot be bribed or seduced.
Crowned as the prince regent by King Sugrīva, who treats him no differently from a son, how would the son of Tārā, who is devoted to Tārā, ever turn treacherous for the sake of the Rākṣasas?

In this conflict, I see no one superior or even equal to Rāma whom we could seek refuge with. Brahmā regrets giving you boons, and Indra and the other gods have been hostile toward you since long ago.
O Ten-faced King! Even over a long time, there is no cause for a rear attack or any loss for the enemy who is besieging the fortress, while those sheltered within the fort will eventually suffer.

Their weapons are trees and mountains; their drink is water; they live on fruits. They have no elephants, horses, or women to lose. There is no kingdom behind them nor subjects to protect. Tell me, what vulnerability do the enemies have?
Therefore, let there be peace with the enemy; no other remedy is seen upon deliberation. If you remain unconciliatory, these monkeys will surely bring everything here to destruction in no time.
