Deeply respecting Vibhīṣaṇa’s words, the maternal grandfather, whose body was bent by age, whose skin was wrinkled, and whose head trembled with senility, straightened himself and spoke to Rāvaṇa.
A single man on foot, armed with a bow, destroyed fourteen thousand Rākṣasas who possessed many illusory powers and moved in the sky. Given that, why do you still doubt him as a mere human?
Surely, this invincible means, in the form of a human accompanied by a monkey army, has been created for the destruction of the night-stalkers by the distressed Brahmarshis along with the gods.
Just as Mahendra split the head of the demon Namuci—which was not shattered even by thunderbolt strikes—using only soft foam of the waters, so should this mysterious event be understood.

Where are fingernails, tolerable even to women, and where is the chest of the demon Hiraṇyakaśipu, as broad as the slab of a great mountain? Behold the clever policy of the gods: in the form of Narasiṃha, He split that chest with those very nails.
O King of Kings! Negligent and having strayed from the path of righteousness, you have incurred the enmity even of sages. If you value the peace of your lineage, follow what Vibhīṣaṇa has said.
Regaining consciousness from the thunderous sound, his eyes clouded by sleep yet having understood the essence of the matter, Kumbhakarṇa spoke like a water-laden cloud thundering in the sky.

The means to begin an action, the excellence of men and material, considerations of place and time, remedies against calamities, and the successful attainment of the goal—these are called the five limbs of counsel.
O Lord of the night-rangers! A proud man who disregards the determined purpose, time, place, and the means of action will not attain the fruit of counsel when the opportune time has passed.
O Lord of the flesh-eaters! Even the sun at its zenith might abandon heat, or the moon its coolness at night; but I believe that arrogance, which despises the world, is the very root of ruin.
Nevertheless, those like me, wishing for your success, strive to speak forcefully to you despite your contrary actions; though mocked by others, we act out of the blindness caused by deep affection.
O King! Cruel deeds and addiction to vulgar pleasures—said to cause the exhaustion of merit—have been excessively indulged in by you, and they are now surely yielding their bitter fruit.

What has not been given? What pleasures have not been enjoyed? Or whom have I not surpassed to stand high? For me, who has thus achieved his purpose, if death comes for your sake, what is it that has not been attained?

"What is the use of speaking of these false policies? I shall provide the resolution in battle with my prowess." Having said this, Kumbhakarṇa fell asleep again, and then Vibhīṣaṇa spoke to the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
The directions, shrouded in dust without cause and buffeted by unnatural, fickle winds, seem to weep like a husband in distress through the abnormal cries of beasts and birds.
The sun, with a mass of grey rays like a lion with a disheveled mane, rises as if opening a terrifying mouth-shaped portal born of portents to devour the people.
Śukra, the preceptor of the Bhṛgus, has moved toward the path of the Vindhya peaks occupied by Agastya; Bṛhaspati is visible by day, and meteors fall, trembling the earth.
Carnivorous beasts, craving the flesh of slaughtered Rākṣasas, wander fearlessly around our city, howling with cruel voices and possessing mouths that glow like blazing fire.

Cowherds milk cows with large udders, yet obtain only a little, discolored, and tasteless milk; insects and hair appear in the sacrificial offerings, and the fire does not blaze even when well-fueled.
O Rāvaṇa! Being addressed by me out of affection, take remedial action in this matter; indeed, those in the service of another find it difficult to tell the one in power what is wholesome in the end.
Before the man-eaters, shattered, crushed, distressed, split, trampled, humiliated, and cut by sharp weapons, satisfy the carrion-eaters, bow down to him (Rāma).
The haughty enemy of Indra, magnifying his own power, knitted his brows, cast aside patience, and with terrifying, harsh eyes, addressed Vibhīṣaṇa with fierce words.

O grandson of Pulastya! Consider these things equally impossible: a stone floating on water while a leaf sinks, darkness coming from the sun, fire flowing from the moon, or my being conquered in battle by an enemy.
May no one on earth have such wretched kinsmen as ours—discontented, hiding malice at our prosperity, envious even when honored, and inconsistent in their actions, intentions, and words.
Relatives often desire even their own ruin but not the prosperity of those of equal lineage; they bow to enemies but cannot endure the rise of their kinsmen with their tormented hearts.

"Today, out of great joy at the prospect of Laṅkā's defeat, you have revealed your exceedingly wicked inner soul. Shame on you! Your concern for me is false." Saying this, he kicked him with his heel.
Then, suppressing anger with forgiveness, resentment with fortitude, pride with humility, delusion with intellect, and weakness through enthusiasm, he rose up along with his four ministers.

He addressed the lord of the night-stalkers, "O Great King! Live happily without me. If a foolish patient remains diseased by refusing to consume wholesome but bitter medicine, it is not the fault of the physicians."
A self-conceited master who lacks discrimination, harbors enmity when spoken to plainly, and is delighted by unwholesome words pleasing to the ears, is indeed a great disaster for his well-wishers.

Just as someone playing with a serpent while following it into a house lives in constant peril, so too if one survives while serving an utterly foolish king, that survival itself is considered a gain.
While I stood on the path of righteousness, you kicked me due to your own faults. You should contemplate with your chief ministers which of us this action brings disgrace upon.

Boldly addressing the lord of the night-stalkers with these virtuous words repeatedly, he fearlessly departed from the city of the enemies of man to bow at the feet of the king of men, praised even by his foes.

Then, upon his arrival, King Rāma, whose heart was as firm as a mountain, having learned of his good conduct through the words of Hanumān, the son of the wind, delighted him and his happy attendants with offerings of water from the hands of the monkey-lords.
On the delightful shore where the breeze blew pleasantly, the night, beautified by the rays of the moon and causing longing in Rāma, finally came to an end.
At the arrival of day, Rāma suddenly fixed his wrathful gaze upon the restless salt waters, appearing like the sun's orb that had climbed high into the sky.

When Rāma held the great arrow, capable of destroying the waters and emitting smoke due to the deep pressure on its feathers, the earth with its mountains and the assembly of serpents fell into fearful doubt.
The salt ocean, crowded with fierce water-elephants and having its great mud exposed by agitated waters, became distressed as its mighty serpents were pierced by the blazing arrows.
Avoiding the mass of water shining with the movement of great serpents out of fear, the Ocean Lord approached the shore, where the caves were agitated by the arrival of the monkey army.
He reached the shore which was filled with herds of restless deer and trees, where Rāma resided amidst many blossoms, and which was shaded by tall, excellent trees with green foliage.
The Ocean Lord, who prevents the submerging of the earth and mountains by his mass of water and who possesses great treasures, arose, now devoid of his restless speed and high waves.
Then the Lord of Waters, prostrating before Rāma who possessed the dark hue of dense tamāla trees, spoke beneficial and profound words, his arms stretched out like the Gaṅgā.
"The great mountains are tall, the waters are unfathomable, the wind carries away moisture, and the sun's rays are hot—all this is Your supreme māyā, the cause of the universe."
"O Thou, reddened by exertion! Withdraw the arrow that glows like the fire of destruction. Allow the mass of water to return to its ancient and beautiful state."
"Tell me, if the bed of the ocean is devoid of water, would it be easy to cross? It would be difficult for monkeys, obstructed by deep mud, and terrifying with whales, shells, and sea-elephants."
"To reach the shore of Laṅkā, let the monkeys, capable of bearing the weight of mountains, easily carry a multitude of heavy-bodied mountains to form a causeway over the great waters."
"In the great battle, let the arrows of Rāma sever the necks of enemies—white as the laughter of Hara—upon the bridge made of great mountains over my deep waters."
"Let the monkey-warriors, smiling beautifully and devoid of fear due to their heroic spirit, proceed quickly to destroy the strength of the many-armed Rāvaṇa."
Following the will of Dāśarathi, the vast monkey army, eager to depart and aware of the ocean's intent, became extremely agitated as they began to gather mountains.
Rāma's army, capable of carrying heavy mountains and tawny like the fire of destruction, suddenly leapt into the sky that was as deep as the clear waters of the ocean.
They plunged into the range of mountains where the tall peaks obstructed the path of gods, which echoed with the fearless roars of lions and had fragrant waters in deep caves.
They traversed mountains where bees hovered over flowers, and lotuses bloomed amidst intoxicated ospreys and ducks; mountains with caves full of serpents and earth torn up by the tusks of elephants.
They explored mountains with clear waters tawny with lotus pollen and charming with the cries of cranes, where the heat of sun-stones met the fragrant smoke of celestial trees.
The mountains resounded with the deep roars of elephants agitated by lions, and were filled with large boars, strong and heavy, their snouts soiled with mud.
Then, the hosts of monkeys uprooted the mountains, embracing them with their arms—mountains whose peaks remained crushed and which scattered the hosts of the sun's rays and stars with their summits.
Burdened by the weight of lofty great mountains and holding sharp-edged rocks with their arms, the monkeys, desiring to dam the salt ocean, ascended into the vast expanse of the sky in various ways.

The sky, filled with many white clouds and possessing the hue of a large polished steel sword, resembled the Himālaya mountain, decorated with rows of birds and echoing with the cries of intoxicated ospreys.

They climbed into the sky, which was crowded with beautiful swans, filled with the loud cries of moving cranes, carrying the fragrance of flower pollen, and appearing vast and clear due to the arrival of the monsoon rains.

Those monkeys, carrying the weight of mountains for the commencement of damming the salt ocean, suddenly ascended the coastal mountain where the movement of the terrified enemy had been blocked by Rāma’s arrival.
Then, brought by the monkey chiefs and properly placed by Nala (the son of Agni), the mountains, with their stable bases and peaks, entered the great ocean.

The ocean was dammed with mountains and it rose. Rāma was satisfied, and Sugrīva rejoiced. The enemy trembled with fear. Mount Suvela came into view. The far shore was reached, and the monkeys exulted.
The monkeys roamed, skipped, danced, ate, sang, leapt up, sat down, slapped their arms, roared loudly, shone, rejoiced, separated, and came together.

The salt ocean appeared with its body beautified by mountain mud, fragrant with the scent of crushed kakkola and cloves, possessing many thick and large waves, overflowing its shores and surging upwards.
The salt water, restless near the shore, assuming a vast and lofty expanse in the sky, and capable of holding the celestial Gaṅgā, was confined by the excellent dam of mountains.

Rāma's army, terrifying to Rāvaṇa’s mind and possessing reddish-brown flickering manes, ascended Mount Suvela, which was beautiful with its clusters of excellent mountains entwined with rows of trees.

They ascended Suvela, whose deep and large caves and mountain-groves were filled with the tumultuous sounds from the city of Laṅkā, and whose dark tamāla shade was crowded with celestial beings enjoying the melodies of the lute.

They ascended the mountain, which offered dense shade from bakula and hintāla trees thick with fresh leaves, and where the elephants’ excitement was stirred by breezes carrying the scent of Airāvaṇa's ichor.

They climbed the mountain, which had clusters of tender, attractive, swaying leaves growing in the shade of tall trees, and pomegranate groves with swaying blossoms resembling forest fires, terrifying to the deer.

They ascended the mountain, which echoed with the sweet chirping of birds, was crowded with large sāla trees near the great water-dam, and bore clusters of gems made of water droplets clinging to moving sprouts.

They reached the mountain, which possessed tall clusters of gem-rays, produced a deep sound from the collision of mountain water, had beautiful cave assemblies, resembled the city of gods, and was filled with the sweet songs of immortals and bards.

They climbed the mountain, which had peaks of clear large gems and large slopes reddish-yellow with vermilion marks, where the desire for nocturnal roaming was checked by the fear of encounters between brave lions and elephants.

They ascended the mountain, which had fearsome caves with large serpents, resounded with the loud and terrible cries of numerous birds, and was crowded with elephants, boars, lions, cattle, and deer amidst its large sāla trees.

They ascended the mountain, which appeared playful with moving sprouts, whose ground was yellowish with the pollen of beautiful earth-lotuses, which possessed bakula flowers as arrows, and whose bright smile was the young creepers of clove trees.

They climbed Suvela, which resembled Mount Meru with its peaks of pure gems and gold, where the movement of deer herds was obstructed by its lofty slopes, whose borders were frequented by gods, and which was crowded with fresh mandāra trees.

The mountain possessed excellent trees bowing under the weight of fruits and was adorned with attractive flower-wreaths growing nearby. Its deep caves were filled with abundant water originating from moonstones (hariṇa-kalaṅka-maṇi).

It was crowded with elephants seeking water, and its body featured beautiful white caves flowing with liquid gold. The trembling rays of emeralds, resembling the luster of fresh sprouts, were being licked by herds of ruru deer.
It withstood strong winds and the collision of high clouds making fearsome noises. By its connection with rows of white clouds, it assumed the graceful appearance of the Himālaya mountains.

The army of Rāma, eager for battle, ascended the mountain which acted as a barrier to the gates of Laṅkā. They were delighted by the construction of the bridge over the salt sea, and the abundance of fruits from trees alleviated their physical exhaustion.

The enemy's army was prepared for battle, capable of enduring the fatigue of war. It resounded with the terrifying noises of large drums (paṇava), flutes, kettledrums (bherī), large cymbals (jhallarī), and the tumultuous sound of ḍhakkā drums and bells.

The enemy forces were fearsome with arrows drawn. Their stout bodies were concealed in clean iron mail. The army attained a beautiful expansive quality through the dense crowding of restless horses and elephants.

Equipped with swords, javelins, spears, great axes, arrows, and heavy clubs, the army was adorned with the sentiment of heroism (vīra-rasa). The earth shook from the heavy movement of their horses and elephants.
At the start of the battle, those highly restless monkey troops, eager to destroy the mountain near Laṅkā, were firmly restrained by Rāma with a grave voice.
The formidable monkey army, residing in excellent tall trees by the water, in caves, on mountain walls, and in bower-crevices, appeared restless like the rays of the blazing sun (himāri).
To observe the army of Rāvaṇa, which possessed the dark hue of clouds heavy with water, the monkeys climbed upon watchtowers, trees, platforms, palaces, arched gateways, and assembly halls.
Then the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, his soul overwhelmed by lust and being informed of the enemy's strength by his spies, deluded Sītā with a magically created head of Rāma and dispatched his army to battle.
Then the conches were blown, the kettledrums were struck with sticks, the flutes were filled with breath, and the hand-clapped instruments resonated.
Large drums were sounded, the struck small drums echoed, the trumpets were filled with air, and the horns, once full, resounded.
The mṛdaṅga drums resonated deeply, the struck gomukha instruments sounded, the bells chimed long notes, and the kettledrums produced a great roar.
The horses neighed with joy, the elephants roared deeply, the terrified young camels wailed, and the rows of foot-soldiers shouted.
The frightened horses trembled, the bulls throbbed excessively, and the women became agitated, fainted, grew deluded, and grieved for their husbands.
The heroes roared, rejoiced, and shone as they were praised by others; they tied their finger-guards, prepared themselves, and marched out.
They strung their bows, climbed into chariots and other vehicles, unsheathed their shining swords, and lifted their heavy clubs.
They whirled their spears and took up auspicious arrows; the infantrymen moved about, leaped, shouted, and bounded forward.
The horses leaped at the whip-strokes, slowed when the reins were pulled, galloped when released, and spat out blood-stained foam from exhaustion.
They provided armor for the elephants, spread blankets over them, fastened the girths and banners, and raised the tall, pointed standards.
Those who loved their children reassured their wives and embraced them; they patted the children on their heads and kissed them.
The uninjured elephants, sensitive to deep goading, understood the signals; their rut increased and shone, and they were mounted by joyful riders.
The deer moved to the right, the she-jackals howled auspiciously, the favorable right sides of their bodies throbbed, and their minds became calm with confidence.
By the command of Rāvaṇa, Prahasta desired to march out extensively, while Mahāpārśva and Mahodara rushed toward the southern gate.
Indrajit set out towards the west, Rāvaṇa himself went to the north, and Virūpākṣa desired to occupy the interior of the city with his troops.
Rāma heard all those sounds and set out with his army; he brandished his divine weapon and then fastened his quiver.
Then he looked at Saumitri, gave orders to the forces, offered salutations to the gods, and left his bed of leaves.
The Vānaras shone, rose up, shouted, and pervaded all directions; they climbed the mountains and then broke the trees.
The earth cracked, the sky rained blood in puddles, deer moved to the left, and birds chirped inauspiciously, signaling bad omens for the demons.
Blazing meteors were seen, and jackals howled inauspiciously. The earth trembled, and Rāma sensed the arrival of impending misfortune.
Having heard that the enemies had approached the demons, Rāvaṇa, seated on the top of the ramparts, personally prepared himself for battle.
The Rākṣasas discharged arrows, threw spears and battle-axes, wielded swords, and dragged enemies with outstretched nooses.
They pierced with sharp arrows, struck with various javelins, crushed with maces, and cut down with sharp discs.
The monkeys struck with their fists and bit with their teeth; they hurled lofty mountains and uprooted trees.
They rolled enemies with their tails, brought them to destruction with their palms, tore them with nails in anger, and crushed them forcefully on the ground.
Beheaded trunks arose, and rivers of blood flowed. The lotus-like faces of soldiers floated, while banners appeared like foam on the water.
Elephants got stuck in the mud of blood, chariots failed to move, horses sank, and soldiers did not dare to advance.
Each city gate of the enemies was besieged by ten million monkeys, while thirty-six crores of monkeys surrounded the monkey king, Sugrīva.
The wounded groaned, staggered, fainted, languished, and rolled about. They swooned, vomited blood, and soldiers from both sides felt parched with thirst.
Prajaṅgha fought with Sampāti; struck by a tree, he trembled, screamed loudly, and perished, losing his life.
In the battle, Nala gouged out the throbbing eyes of Pratapan; Jambumālī gave up his life after being struck with a rock by Hanumān.
Vibhīṣaṇa crushed the limbs of Mitrighna with a mace. Sugrīva overcame Praghasa, and then Rāma slaughtered many others.
Struck by Mainda, the head of Vajramuṣṭi was severed. Nīla cut off the throbbing head of Nikumbha with a disc.
Virūpākṣa, pierced by the arrows of Lakṣmaṇa, lost his life, while Dvivida caused Aśaniprabha to give up his breath.
Indrajit hurled a mace, which Aṅgada intercepted. Then, Aṅgada crushed Indrajit's chariot along with the horses using a tree.
Seeing that feat of Aṅgada, the whole world was amazed. All the Rākṣasas were terrified, and Rāghava held him in high regard.
Sugrīva rejoiced, and the gods, filled with wonder, exclaimed, "Excellent!" Vibhīṣaṇa praised him, and the monkeys applauded.
Oh, wonder! When Lakṣmaṇa rose, the son of Rāvaṇa vanished. Then Rāma discharged his arrows, and the enemies were terrified.
The wounded groaned horribly. Flesh-eaters devoured the slain. Blood oozed from the wounded, and severed arms quivered for a moment.
Even with their heads severed, the fierce anger of the warriors did not vanish. The remaining soldiers fled the battlefield, while those who prided themselves on their bravery were filled with shame.
Rāghava showed no mercy in the fight. None of the enemies could maintain their courage; they perished like moths before the heroes. A great cry of "Ha! Ha!" resounded everywhere.
The sun disappeared and night took its place. Like the night of universal destruction, that darkness seemed to swallow both the monkeys and the Rākṣasas alike.
Indrajit became exceedingly furious and summoned the serpent-missile. Becoming invisible, he challenged the opposing army and mocked them with laughter.
He oppressed the entire army and restrained them with his arrows. The shafts he released turned into actual serpents upon reaching the enemy.
He covered the whole army and the two Rāghavas with those serpent-arrows. He boasted, "Even Indra could not conquer my illusory power; what hope is there for mere humans?"
The two Rāghavas were once again bound by him with serpents. Overwhelmed and distressed, they lost consciousness and fell to the ground.
Then the soldiers cried out "Rāma!", trembled in fear, and lamented. The army commanders sighed deeply and cursed themselves in despair.
They could neither restrain their grief nor stop the falling missiles. The monkeys could not discern the path of the invisible Indrajit and wandered about aimlessly.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa washed Sugrīva's eyes with water. With his vision cleared, Sugrīva perceived the enemy in the sky and let out a great roar.
Then the monkey chief Sugrīva raised a mountain peak to strike Indrajit. The son of Rāvaṇa abandoned the spot and fled to his father's side.
He related the events to Rāvaṇa, who rejoiced greatly. Rāvaṇa embraced his son tightly and affectionately smelled his head.
The gratified night-stalkers raised high banners, feasted excessively on meat, sang, drank, and dallied with their beloved wives.
By the King's command, they showed the fallen Rāma to Sītā. Her eyes closed in shock, and she rolled in grief on the floor of the Puṣpaka chariot.
Believing her beloved killed, her breath seemed to fail and her body became paralyzed. After a long time, the miserable Sītā sighed, wept bitterly, and shrieked.
"Is my heart bound with iron bands or was it fashioned from a thunderbolt, since it has not burst into a thousand pieces without Rāma?"
"You crossed the ocean for my sake and destroyed the enemies. Now you have left me in this terrible state; fie on me, whose life has become so wretched and trivial."
"Your father, overcome by sorrow, did not survive without you. What is the use of me, a worthless wife, continuing to live while you are dead?"
She loathed her very life-breaths and blamed her supposedly auspicious physical marks. She tore at her hair and rolled on the ground repeatedly.
She grew weary, brooded, and fainted; for a moment, she neither breathed nor felt pain. She cursed fate, cried out, and burned intensely with the fire of grief.
Then Trijaṭā comforted Sītā and led her away. Subsequently, the Vānaras, along with Vibhīṣaṇa, kept a vigilant watch.
Rāma became aware of the dire situation and was consumed by grief. His anger intensified, and he lamented over Lakṣmaṇa.
Desiring death, Rāma honored the entire army with his words. He took leave of Sugrīva and dismissed him to return to his own land.
He commanded Aṅgada to escort the two Rāghava princes to Kiṣkindhā. However, Sugrīva himself vowed to slay the demons.
Hearing from Vibhīṣaṇa that this was the serpent-missile and its remedy was the remembrance of Garuḍa, the best of the Raghus meditated upon him.
Then the mountains shook, the ocean overflowed its boundaries, flowers fell from the trees, and the radiant quarters of the sky shone brightly.
The serpents plunged into the ocean, and a pleasant wind blew. The fierce lights subsided, and the bonds of the arrow-serpents began to loosen.
The warriors shone as if unhurt, and Lakṣmaṇa regained consciousness. Vibhīṣaṇa also looked radiant as Garuḍa approached them.
Garuḍa touched the two descendants of Kakutstha, and they became free from pain. He identified himself to them and then departed as he had come.
The Vānaras shouted, shone with brilliance, rose up, and uprooted mountains and trees. Then they ran about and yearned for battle.
They approached Laṅkā again, and the ten-faced Rāvaṇa noticed them. Learning that his enemies were alive, he lost his fortitude.
"They have escaped the divine arrow-bond," he lamented. He then fell into great delusion and could no longer foresee victory.
Then Dhūmrākṣa, favored by Rāvaṇa, set out for battle. His chariot was yoked with birds having the faces of lions and wolves.
The man-eaters covered their bodies with armor and mounted their steeds. They honored their weapons and proceeded to the battlefield.
Dhūmrākṣa mounted his chariot and sneezed inauspiciously while leaving the city. He proclaimed his name and hurried forward.
A vulture perched on his head, and cruel crows croaked. The sky drizzled blood, and the earth shook.
Then the battle began, and weapons were hurled at each other. They cut, whirled around, flowed, and leaped.
The monkeys and demons struck each other, shone, and shrieked in many ways. The heroes did not fear but terrified their enemies.
Those who were crushed bled, and those wounded by arrows swelled. The arms of those shooting, with fists including thumbs, discharged arrows.
Dhūmrākṣa sported in the battle, and Hanumān rebuked him. He took up a rock and crushed Dhūmrākṣa's chariot along with the horses.
The demon fell to the ground and shrieked terrifyingly. He struck the enemy with a mace, and the monkey shook him with a mountain.
Then, by the command of Rāvaṇa, Akampana desired to fight. He charged forward on a chariot and roared extremely fiercely.
His left eye throbbed, and inauspicious birds shrieked. Ignoring these omens, he proceeded and shone in the battle with his arrows.
Arrows, stretched like ropes, filled the sky and covered the earth. Because of this, the armies shrank in fear; no one could withstand him.
He reduced the enemies to ashes and distressed them like Kṛtānta. Māruti became enraged and uprooted a great-topped palmyra tree.
With that tree, he offered Akampana like a great sacrificial animal to Yama. When he was slain, grief scorched Rāvaṇa like fire.
He trembled, ground his teeth, and bit his lip. He quickly and diligently arranged for the protection of the city on all sides.
He requested Prahasta, who possessed wondrous valor, to fight. Prahasta replied, "O King of Kings, what is the use of deliberation? We exist for the sake of war."
The fearless great warrior, making a sound, prepared to fight. His soldiers were marshaled, and the horses and elephants were readied.
They yoked the chariots with horses, and the priests offered sacrifices to the gods. They honored the Brāhmaṇas properly, who then pronounced blessings.
White mustard seeds were placed on heads, and cows were touched by the warriors for luck. They sharpened great weapons and tested the horses.
The soldiers brandished and polished swords and wiped battle-axes. Prahasta adorned himself, applied ointments, dressed, ate, and drank.
He laughed for a moment and then set out with warriors and vehicles. Prahasta honored the Vipras and offered oblations to the fire.
He gathered his trusted companions and anointed himself with sandalwood paste. He sipped honey-wine and fastened his excellent armor.
He put on a beautiful turban and occupied a splendid chariot. Taking up great weapons, he then set out to depart.
They struck various musical instruments, and the followers chanted praises. A terrible dust rose up, and the roar filled the directions.
Vultures followed him as he went, and carnivorous beasts attended him. Terrible winds blew, and meteors fell from the sky.
The sky dripped blood, and the battleground glowed. Chariots with horses stumbled, and the horses and elephants did not move swiftly.
Whips fell from hands, and sacrificial animals turned to the left. The earth cracked, and the sky was filled with the roars of the monkeys.
The elephants and horses passed blood, and the demons spat repeatedly. Then the two armies looked splendid and struck each other mercilessly.

In the battle, the warriors hated one another, gambled with their lives, leaped about, and fainted. Some lay dead, some were devoured by scavengers, others devoured their enemies, and many lamented aloud.
The vānaras attacked and insulted the ministers right in front of Prahasta. The commander of the rākṣasas could not tolerate that bold and insolent action.
He covered the army of the vānaras with a deluge of weapons. He punished many warriors and separated them from their lives on the battlefield.
He struck terror into them and blazed like the sun. He did not grow weary despite the heap of enemy bodies and his presence pervaded all ten directions.
Frightened, some warriors cowered and shrank; others, being defeated, felt ashamed. Some fled from the battle, while others begged for protection and safety.
Thus Prahasta conquered that army and grew immensely arrogant. Filled with rage, he did not find peace but continued to protect the night-wandering rākṣasas.
There, Nīla became enraged and hurled a massive tree. Struck by the tree, Prahasta responded by discharging a multitude of arrows.
The monkey endured the onslaught of the enemy's chariot and horses and crushed them with a tree. Armed with a mace, Prahasta reached the ground but showed no sign of exhaustion.
The anger of both warriors was kindled, and their skill and speed with weapons increased. Nīla hurled a tree, while the mace-bearing Prahasta warded it off.
The two heroes leaped into the sky and moved in circles upon the ground. They rushed at each other with great speed and did not tire.
Then the monkey hurled a massive rock at the rākṣasa. Struck by that stone, he died and fell prostrate upon the surface of the earth.
All the vānaras rejoiced, while the various night-wandering rākṣasas perished. The hopes of Daśāsya were shattered, and the monkey army praised Nīla for his victory.
When the desires of the night-wanderers failed during their attack on Rāma's army, they retreated to Laṅkā in deep distress and loudly announced that Prahasta had been slain.
Then the Lord of Rākṣasas became afraid and looked around the city. He dispatched Rākṣasas to awaken Kumbhakarṇa.
They reached his palace and saw him asleep. They made tumultuous noises and quickly struck him with sticks to wake him.
They pulled his hair, made elephants walk over his limbs, sprinkled cold water on him, and even prodded him with burning torches.
They scratched him with sharp nails, bit him with their teeth, poked him with sharp spears, and sounded auspicious kettle-drums.
He paid no heed to all those attempts and woke up on his own accord. He then asked the night-walkers, "Why have you woken me up?"
"O night-walker! The King wishes to see you," they replied. He bathed, anointed himself, ate meat, and drank Vāruṇī.
He then dressed himself and set out from his house to see Rāvaṇa. The King saw him coming and rose slightly from his seat.
The King pointed to a nearby golden seat and was pleased. Kumbhakarṇa smiled slightly and then sat down near him.
Kumbhakarṇa asked, "Why did you call me?" The King replied, "You were happy in sleep and did not know what that Rāma has done to the Rākṣasas."
"He has crossed the ocean, besieged our city, shone with weapons in battle, and led the Rākṣasas to their destruction."
"As long as I have lived, I have not spoken anything pleasant. As my honored brother, do not fail to slay my enemies out of affection."
"Do not fail to show your prowess; do not fail to protect this wounded city. We have seen your valor; in the past, you conquered the gods."
Kumbhakarṇa said to him, "You did not listen to everything we said in the council. This is the fruit of that negligence."
"You held the words of the wise in contempt and relied on the words of fools. Although you studied the scriptures, you did not recognize what was beneficial."
"Those fools who incited you to war have deceived you. Mālyavān spoke reasonably, but out of arrogance, you did not endure his words."
"You stole the wife of Rāghava and did not return her even when advised by trustworthy friends. Now, do not fail to experience your own faults; do not be deluded, and do not be angry."
"The time for what I spoke then has also passed. The Rākṣasas have been slain by the enemies, and you have exhausted the treasury."
"Your power to make a peace treaty has diminished. You have acted in such a way that you have wasted your enmities, treasury, and army together."
Daśānana became angry and spoke to Kumbhakarṇa: "Why have you censured me? Have you not kindled your own prowess?"
"Do not harp on policies of good conduct; do not fail to advance in battle. Do not reproach me for past mistakes; do not fail to perform what is supremely beneficial."
Then Kumbhakarṇa roared and turned back the other soldiers. He took up great weapons and went out quickly to the front.
He seemed to scrape the sky with his head and filled the atmosphere with his broad body. He appeared to crush the earth with his feet and burn the enemies with his sight.
Shining like a burnt mountain, he moved like the cloud of destruction. He shook the ocean and terrified even the Rākṣasas.
He moved like a winged mountain and breathed like the gale of dissolution. He filled the worlds with his roar and shone like the fire of destruction.
The earth bent under his weight, and trees fell due to his speed. Terrified lions fled, and the great mountains were shaken.
Portents appeared as the sky rained blood. Terrible winds blew, and cruel birds uttered harsh cries.
His left eye twitched, and fierce jackals howled. Vultures alighted on his mace, and a blazing meteor fell.
Disregarding those portents out of pride, he reached the battlefield. He roared, rejoiced, and challenged the enemies to combat.
The cruel one ate but was not satisfied; his hunger increased as he fed. He swallowed the fat and drank the blood of the forest-dwellers.
His sides swelled with flesh and his belly distended. He stole the lives of many, and his fame shone in the battle.
He paralyzed their strength, but they could not stop his valor. Some monkeys climbed trees, while others dived into the ocean.
Some crossed mountains, while others hid in caves. Some sat paralyzed with fear, and others fainted.
Other monkeys fled across the ocean by the bridge. There, Aṅgada felt ashamed and stood firmly with great energy.
Aṅgada kindled the courage of the monkeys and fought. They threw rocks and raised trees to strike back.
The tiger-like monkeys roared and fought well. Kumbhakarṇa crushed them, ate them, and threw them away after striking them with his palms.
Kumbhakarṇa crushed the monkeys with his feet and terrified them. He pierced them with his spear.
He struck them hard with his mace and crushed them in his embrace. He tormented others with his knees and twisted them with his hands.
Rocks thrown at his body split, and great trees were reduced to powder. He did not even notice them, nor was he disturbed.
The two tigers of the Raghu dynasty saw him, and Vibhīṣaṇa said: "This one conquered Indra, the lord of gods, and did not fear the Sun."
"He destroyed the power of the lord of Yakṣas; no one could resist him. O Princes, do not fear Kumbhakarṇa, and do not fear for us."
Rāma commanded the monkeys not to neglect the attacking demon and to act with diligence. He urged them not to hesitate in their attempt to slay him.
The monkeys roared, challenged the Rākṣasa, and leapt about. They demonstrated their strength and began hurling trees and mountain rocks at the foe.
They struck him and scratched him with their feet and teeth. Śarabha cast a tree at him, while Nīla hurled a massive mountain.
Ṛṣabha threw mountains, and the monkeys used them to pierce the enemy. Gandhamādana roared and released jagged mountain peaks.
Gavākṣa jumped and scattered many mountains. However, the heroic Kumbhakarṇa did not care for them, nor did he feel any pain from the assault.
Unrestrained, he crushed and scorched the enemy forces. He rushed to slay the foes and devoured those who fell into his lap.
He roared at the monkey host, who fled as he approached. He grabbed the fleeing ones with his hands and thrust them into his terrifying mouth.
He drenched the ground with blood and covered it with the bodies of the slain. The cruel demon was never satiated by eating, nor exhausted by killing monkeys.
Some could not fight, and others dared not approach. The forest-dwellers who were swallowed managed to escape through his nostrils and his mouth.
Others were digested within his belly, which was like the underworld. They cried out, called to friends, tried to flee, and broke into sweats.
Crushed and wounded, the monkeys bled and grew thirsty. The broken army approached the King (Rāma), who then urged Sugrīva forward.
Enraged, Sugrīva also prepared to fight and hurled a giant tree at the enemy. The foe endured the strike and seized a fierce spear.
He brandished the terrifying spear and threw it at the lord of monkeys. Hanumān rushed there and caught the weapon while it was in the air.
The hero Hanumān shone as he broke the spear without fatigue. The demon lamented that his weapon, forged from a thousand loads of iron, was destroyed.
The Rākṣasa became extremely angry and uprooted a heavy mountain. He hurled it at the king of monkeys, who fainted upon being struck.
Sugrīva rolled on the ground as his blood flowed. The Rākṣasa picked him up and fled, appearing glorious in his victory.
The monkeys were terrified, but the son of the Wind followed Kumbhakarṇa. Sugrīva slowly regained consciousness and bit off the demon’s ears and nose.
The demon did not fear but tried to escape. Enraged, Kumbhakarṇa began to crush Sugrīva against the ground.
Sugrīva slipped from his hands and ascended into the sky. He quickly returned to Rāma and brought joy to the assembly of monkeys.
He urged them to fight and incited the two Rāghavas. Kumbhakarṇa returned to the battle, and the monkeys fought on.
Following the king's command, the monkeys surrounded the demon and quickly climbed upon him. He rushed at those who had mounted him, and they, becoming agitated, fell off.
He swallowed, pierced, and mercilessly crushed them. They suffered terribly and vomited blood from their mouths.
Intoxicated by blood, he showed no mercy even to his own kind. He took the lives of others and obstructed their prowess.
The courage of the terrified forest-dwellers was snatched away. Lakṣmaṇa then cut off the demon's crown and his armor.
His body was pierced with arrows, yet the night-stalker praised Lakṣmaṇa. He then vied with Rāma, who struck down his incoming arrows.
Out of pride, he held in contempt those by whom Khara, Vālin, Mārīca, and Dūṣaṇa were slain, and he raised his mallet high.
Rāma severed that hand along with the weapon using the Vāyavya missile. Now holding a tree in his other hand, the demon blazed with rage and rushed toward his enemy.
The king Rāma cut off his other hand, along with the tree, using the Śakra weapon. He shredded the demon's shanks with arrows and filled his mouth with shafts.
Rāma pierced his heart with the Indra weapon, and being slain, he fell upon the earth. Two thousand forest-dwellers were crushed under his massive falling body.
The gods praised Rāma, while the night-stalkers fled in all directions. The earth, with its mighty mountains, trembled, and the lord of the waters was greatly agitated.
The demons informed King Rāvaṇa that Kumbhakarṇa was slain. Rāvaṇa wept, grieved deeply, and fell into a profound swoon.
He extolled his brother's virtues and celebrated his valor. He wondered how the enemies, whom the enraged Kumbhakarṇa hated so much, could still be alive.
"How indeed did they survive, while that mighty one died?" Then, the princes, having consoled Rāvaṇa, desired to enter the fight.
Devāntaka, Atikāya, Triśiras, and Narāntaka—those powerful sons of Rāvaṇa—hurried to the battlefield.
For protection, the king sent Yuddhonmatta and Matta. Those two demons, experts in warfare, went out following the princes.
They defeated the armies and threw the enemies into confusion. They piled up the best of the monkeys on the ground like heaps of mountains.
Narāntaka strove to fight with Aṅgada. The demon hurled a spear, which shattered against Aṅgada's chest.
The son of Vālin killed the horses and struck the demon with his fist. The son of Rāvaṇa, undaunted even on the ground, began to fight on foot.
The son of Vālin snatched away Narāntaka's life with a powerful fist-blow. Then all the sons of Rāvaṇa, enraged, rushed toward Aṅgada.
Then Nīla and Hanūmān surrounded the sons of Rāvaṇa. They used high mountains as weapons, but Triśiras countered them with his arrows.
Then the powerful Devāntaka struck in battle with an iron club. However, Hanumān, the son of Marut, split Devāntaka's head with his fist.
Then Devāntaka displayed his valor and tormented Nīla with arrows. But the battle-crazed demon was ultimately brought to destruction by Nīla with a mountain peak.
Next, Triśiras brandished a spear against Hanumān. In the ensuing battle, Hanumān struck the demon's horses, which then perished.
Struck on the head, Triśiras stumbled and was deprived of his sword by his enemy. With that very sword, his heads were severed, and he surrendered his life.
The intoxicated Mahodara was killed after being struck by the great mace thrown by Śarabha. Subsequently, Atikāya began to sport in the battle with a chariot drawn by a thousand horses.
Atikāya tormented his enemies with his chariot and roamed unrestrained. Vibhīṣaṇa identified this great car-warrior to Rāghava.
"He paralyzed the Vajra, pleased the self-born Brahmā, learned the use of great missiles, and protected the Rākṣasas in battle."
"He studied the treatises on statecraft and challenged the prowess of Yama. He shone in battles against the gods, and no fear ever arose in him."
"This son of Rāvaṇa, a terror to the Vānaras, has arrived." Then he challenged Lakṣmaṇa and vibrated his heavy bow.
In the great battle, Lakṣmaṇa attacked that lion-like demon as a serpent would. Both discharged numerous nets of arrows to conquer each other.
The two high-souled warriors cut down each other's weapons and did not tire for a long time. They discharged arrows in such a way that they spread darkness everywhere.
The Rākṣasa and Lakṣmaṇa employed the solar and fire missiles. Upon meeting each other, those weapons were neutralized and destroyed.
Then the Rākṣasa brandished the Aiṣīka weapon in battle. That too was destroyed upon encountering the Mahendra weapon discharged by Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Lakṣmaṇa remembered and invoked the invincible Brahmā weapon. With it, he shattered the head of the enemy of men.
Then Rāvaṇa wailed, and Indrajit consoled him. Enraged, Indrajit went forth and worshiped the self-born Creator, Brahmā.
He offered oblations to the fire and consecrated the group of missiles. He obtained the weapon of Brahmā and a chariot that brings victory.
The son of Rāvaṇa mounted that chariot with its flaming front and rejoiced. Then, assuming an invisible form, he mangled the bodies of Rāvaṇa's enemies.
The enraged son of Rāvaṇa put sixty-seven crores of monkeys to sleep with his arrows. At the end of the night, he also caused the two Raghus to faint.
He expanded his prowess and covered the directions with arrows. He roared a terrifying roar and, having gone, informed Rāvaṇa of his deed.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa perceived that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were still breathing. Holding a torch, he went across and comforted the surviving monkeys.
Saying, "O Tigers of the Raghu dynasty, do not grieve; they have not died," Vibhīṣaṇa identified Nīla and other slain monkey chiefs.
There, Jāmbavān breathed slightly, opened his eyes, and asked the descendant of Pulastya, "Is the son of the Wind-god, Hanūmān, alive?"
"O Great King! If he is safe, then none of us are dead." Then Vibhīṣaṇa informed him that the son of the Wind-god, Hanūmān, was indeed alive.
Hanūmān arrived there, and both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa rejoiced. Then they dispatched him to the mountain of all medicinal herbs on the slopes of the Himālaya.
They sent Hanūmān to fetch the herb Mṛtasañjīvanī, which restores life, as well as Sandhānakaraṇī for healing and Viśalyakaraṇī for removing weapons.
He flew into the sky and reached the great mountain where thousands of potent medicinal herbs glowed brightly during the night.
When Hanūmān could not distinguish the specific medicinal herbs, he carried away the entire mountain containing the potent plants.
Some of the slain regained life, some opened their eyes, other warriors cast off their unconsciousness, and still others yawned as they revived.
Similarly, they made others smell the herbs and applied them as ointments. Thus, they all regained consciousness and attained greater strength.
Hanūmān delighted the two descendants of Kakutstha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, and revived the remaining monkeys. Then they quickly set Laṅkā ablaze with fire.
Then the army prepared; they wiped their spears and lances, polished their sword-blades, and made their battle-axes shine.
There, the two mighty sons of Kumbhakarṇa, Nikumbha and Kumbha, geared up for battle and attacked the monkeys.
They protected the city of Laṅkā, guarded the Rākṣasa army, wielded their array of weapons, and brought destruction to their enemies.
The enemy army cried out repeatedly and fled in confusion. Blood dripped from wounds, and the slain lay prostrate upon the earth.
Akampana and Kampana were struck down in battle by Aṅgada. However, the envious Prajaṅgha then attacked Vālī's son, Aṅgada.
Aṅgada repeatedly struck his head with a fist and, remaining unperturbed, quickly cut off the head of Yūpākṣa.
Then Dvivida broke the body of Lohitākṣa. Subsequently, the enraged Kumbha pierced Mainda along with Dvivida using his arrows.
Both of them reeled and fell to the ground, wounded. Seeing his maternal uncles distressed, Aṅgada attacked Kumbha with trees.
The night-stalker Kumbha covered him with a shower of arrows and drove the trees away. Rāma urged the monkeys to quickly go and protect Aṅgada.
Sugrīva quickly rescued his nephew from the danger posed by the enemy. Enraged, he struck the son of Kumbhakarṇa with a fist and deprived him of his life.
Then Nikumbha hurled a mace at the leader of the monkeys. Hanumān broke that approaching weapon, which was as terrifying as a serpent.
Hanumān overwhelmed the enemy with his splendor and let out a terrifying roar. He seized the foe's neck with such force that he did not leave him alive.

Hanumān, the lord of the monkeys, united the army with immense joy and attained lasting success. The mind of King Rāma rejoiced in delight as though his objectives were attained, while perpetual sorrow spread among the lords of the Rākṣasas.
Then, the King of the Rākṣasas, whose kinsmen were slain, wept and said: "What will I do with the kingdom? What purpose will be served by Sītā?"
Now that the heroic Atikāya is slain, I do not wish to live. Who will put the enemies to shame? Who will conquer Yama?
Without Atikāya, who will sever the noose of Varuṇa? Who will respect Rāvaṇa? For whom will Svayambhū be pleased?
By whom shall I be praised? Who, being exalted, will lead his kinsmen to greatness? Who will satisfy the ancestors at the right time? Who will not boast after performing great deeds?
Hari (Indra) will now raise his thunderbolt and roam without fear; he will enjoy the sacrificial offerings and display the pride of a hero.
The sun will burn without fear, and the wind will blow unrestrained. The sequence of seasons will rotate freely, and the moon will rise according to its own will.
The clouds will pour down fiercely, and Yama will behave sternly. With the death of Atikāya, why would they not act otherwise than before?
My eyes will open in vain, for they shall no longer see the humble Narāntaka, who was always eager and modest to receive my commands.
Shame on me, for I shall never see Triśiras again. Now that he has met his death, by whom will the enemies be slain?
Since Matta is killed by the enemies, how shall I find happiness in battle? Without the one intoxicated by war, who will attack the enemies in the field?
Śatakratu (Indra), ready for battle, will now challenge me without hesitation. Since the invincible Nikumbha is killed, Indra’s purpose will be fulfilled.
The pleasure of Hari (Indra) will be secured, and Laṅkā will be destroyed. O Devāntaka! Abandoned by you, I shall fall under the enemy's control.
If my sons are killed, I shall either die or conquer. I will swiftly destroy the enemies; I will not live in sorrow.
Sages and gods will smile and constantly say: "Due to the misconduct of Daśagrīva, the race of Rākṣasas has been destroyed."
O dear one! Who could have imagined that Rāghava would sever the limbs of Kumbhakarṇa in battle and pierce his vital organs?
The sun will fall to the earth, the earth will be weighed, the wind will be broken, and the sky will be struck with fists.
Fire will flow from the moon, the ocean will dry up, water will burn from the sun, and masses of darkness will shatter.
That the enraged Kumbhakarṇa would be defeated in battle by a mere man—these things were never imagined by anyone among people.
With Kumbhakarṇa slain, the monkeys will scale the walls of Laṅkā. Arrogant, they will bite the Rākṣasas and destroy my retreats.
They will injure children and the elderly, and dance filled with joy. Without that chief of Rākṣasas, who will restrain them?
Rāvaṇa expresses his profound indignation that Rāghava desires Sītā. He mockingly questions what happiness that prince, who has fallen from his kingdom, could possibly obtain from her.
I shall kill Vaidehī, the root cause of this ruin; I will either have the Rākṣasas devour her or bury her deep within the earth.
I will no longer seek the sovereignty of the world, nor shall I strive to live. In a palace devoid of my kinsmen, I will find no pleasure in sensual objects.
In whose happiness shall I rejoice, and who will rejoice in mine? O Kumbhakarṇa, without you, for what purpose should I accept any enjoyments?
The riches that come to me while my friends have perished, their beauty marred by my grief—are they not merely calamities amidst calamities?
'Because you refuse to make peace, your city will soon perish and the Vānaras will arrive swiftly'—this was the well-spoken advice of Vibhīṣaṇa.
'We, who have been maintained with wealth by the king, shall not merely speak but shall fight'—this was the declaration made by Prahasta.
Shall a mere mortal traveling on foot truly challenge the king of the man-eaters—one who is invincible in battle with his divine weapons and chariot?
Instead, I shall gird myself for battle and not hide like a weakling. Today the carnivores shall be satiated, and the earth shall drink the blood of the enemy.
I shall attract glory and drive away my enemies through my deeds. Today Maithilī shall experience great sorrow due to the destruction of her husband.
Kubera shall be resentful and Yama shall boast to us. The Vānara women in the forest, deprived of their husbands and sons, shall languish in grief.
The Rākṣasas shall sleep soundly and roam without fear. The Rākṣasa women will no longer lament; instead, they will joyfully feast upon the humans.
I shall certainly be happy before dawn. In the coming time, in the very next moment that follows...
...I will go to conquer Indra along with the immortals. Thereafter, I shall return once more to Laṅkā, free from all resentment.
While the deluded Rāvaṇa was speaking thus, Indrajit, the terror of his enemies, approached him, declaring, 'I desire to fight.'
'O Great King, you do not realize! Together we shall conquer the abode of the gods, protected by Indra and crowded with the proud divine hosts.'
'You are unaware of our power. We shall forcibly crush Yama along with Kubera, seize their treasures, and return safely to this city.'
'O Rāvaṇa, I shall face the enemies once more; you shall no longer grieve. You will see a world without Rāma and shall traverse all directions at will.'
'You shall again strike terror in the abode of the gods along with your attendants. Today Indra shall bow to you and offer words of submission.'
'The sages shall tremble because of you, and you shall dominate your enemies. Today in battle, I shall be recognized by all who pride themselves on their heroism.'
Today, I shall come to know the groups of enemies who consider themselves heroes. I will cover the earth today with the severed limbs of the forest-dwellers.

As I set forth, I shall mount my chariot, which emits a deep sound like the collision of clouds at the end of a yuga and shines with the radiance of its raised banner, bow, and sword. Today, in a battle where the enemies are scattered, mangled, fleeing, and slain, you will hear the howling of the satiated flesh-eaters with faces terrifyingly red with blood.
Then the warriors prayed for peace, performed ablutions, kindled the sacred fires, caused the Brāhmaṇas to recite benedictions, and performed auspicious rites.
They honored the family elders, embraced the children, consoled the tearful women, and assigned various duties to be performed.
Then they dressed themselves, anointed their bodies, ate meat with wine, drank honey-wine, and consumed various desired foods.
They took up their preferred weapons, donned their armor, mounted their excellent vehicles, and uttered imprecations against their enemies.
They worshipped the four-faced Brahmā, honored and praised the Brāhmaṇas; then the enemy of Indra (Indrajit) anointed himself and desired his superior vehicle.
He put on armor studded with gems, girded a brilliant sword, mounted a formidable chariot, and then proceeded forward.
They beat loud kettledrums, blew auspicious conchs, struck the mṛdaṅga drums, and filled the shrill-sounding wind instruments.
The bards sang praises, the warriors shouted to one another, roared like lions, and the horses and elephants neighed and trumpeted loudly.
Then they witnessed ill omens: the solar disc burst, clouds showered blood, and unbearable winds blew.
Black deer moved to the left, soldiers forgot their weaponry skills, and horses and elephants spat blood, feeling exhausted and despondent.
Disregarding all those omens, they attacked the foes; they cut the enemies with sharp swords and pierced them with javelins.
They sliced with the edges of discs, struck firmly with spears, pierced with sharp-tipped arrows, and crushed the enemies thoroughly with javelins.
The monkeys hurled trees, struck violently with mountains, hit with their fists in rage, and even bit with their teeth.
They quickly tormented with their knees, struck with palms and elbows, and threw back various weapons discharged by the enemy.
Indrajit crushed the enemies, roamed in all directions, roared terrifically, and there was no one he did not afflict.
The enemies did not perceive him fixing the arrow, nor did they see him holding the bow or notice him discharging arrows. Only when struck did they realize his presence.
They heard a sound from one direction, fled in another, cried out in yet another, and were struck by him from a different side.
They rolled on the ground, were torn asunder, bled all over, became exhausted, remained unsatisfied, and, being wounded by him, they died.
Distressed by the situation, Lakṣmaṇa (Saumitri) desired to invoke the Brahmāstra for the destruction of all Rākṣasas, but Rāma (Raghu-nandana) restrained him.
Then Indrajit, moving through the sky, was seen striking an illusory Sītā with a sword; Hanumān (Marut-suta) spoke these words to him.
Hanumān cries out, "O sinful demon! This Sītā has done no wrong; she was merely separated from her husband's side. Do not harm this sorrowful woman!"
Śakrajit (Indrajit) declared, "That which causes pain to enemies must be done." Having drawn his sword, he then severed her head.
Hanumān (Marut-suta) approached Rāma, saying, "She, for whose sake we fought the enemies and crossed the ocean, has been killed."
Upon hearing this, the two heroic Rāghavas (Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa) fainted. They wept, breathed long hot sighs, and wailed loudly.
Vibhīṣaṇa (Paulastya) spoke to them, "Do not weep. Surely that sinful one has deceived us and gone to Nikumbhilā."
"Do not delay. While he is there, before he has offered oblations to the fire and before he has acquired the fierce Brahma-śiras weapon and the chariot, he must be killed by us."
"Brahmā ordained his death if that ritual remains unfinished." Rāma (Rāghava) then gave the order to Lakṣmaṇa (Saumitri) and the monkey chiefs.
Accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa, they joyfully accepted the command, marched toward Nikumbhilā, and were obstructed by the demons.
A great slaughter took place there between the two armies, aided by the world-guardians. Defeating the demons, Vibhīṣaṇa and Lakṣmaṇa advanced quickly.
There they saw Indrajit, concentrated and seated in his place. He was offering oblations to the fire (Kṛṣṇavartman) while reciting the supreme mantra.
Śakrajit meditated on the sacred spell and did not stir from his trance. Lakṣmaṇa (Saumitri) challenged him and let out a terrifying roar.
Then Indrajit became enraged and spoke to his uncle Vibhīṣaṇa: "You were born here, and your body was nourished here by the sacrificial offerings meant for demons."
"You lived here; how could you then start this cruel act? You did not respect the ritual bond of kinship, nor did you consider the ties of being a relative."
"O sinner! You did not fear unrighteousness, nor were you afraid of public scandal. O defiler of dharma! Surely you neither knew nor heard of this..."
"...that by deserting one's kinsmen, one undoubtedly falls into contempt." Then the uncle replied to Śakrajit (Indrajit).
"Do not transgress with lies, and do not misunderstand my character. It is true that I was born into the lineage of sinful demons."
"But my character did not turn out like that of your father. Though restrained by me, he delighted in vices that bring about destruction."
"For this reason, I abandoned Daśagrīva (Rāvaṇa), not out of hatred. He was seizing others' wealth and violating others' women."
"He constantly sought to harm the gods, neglected the welfare of the virtuous, suspected his friends and kinsmen, and highly esteemed those who were not wise elders."
"Because your father delighted in these vices, I abandoned him." At this, Indrajit grew enraged and roared with his twenty-two eyes and arms.
Rāvaṇi (Indrajit) struck his kinsman, the king Vibhīṣaṇa, with twenty-five arrows. In return, Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa) destroyed the four horses of Indrajit's chariot.
Lakṣmaṇa cut down the charioteer and shattered the chariot with his arrows. Then, Indrajit showered Lakṣmaṇa from all sides with a volley of arrows.
Both warriors increased their energy and repeatedly discharged arrows. Lakṣmaṇa hurled the Vāruṇa missile, while Indrajit launched the Raudra missile.
Those two missiles collided and destroyed each other. Thereupon, the Rākṣasa (Indrajit) released the terrifying Āsura weapon.
From that weapon, a shower of rocks, spears, arrows, and clubs fell. Lakṣmaṇa neutralized that invincible weapon using the Māheśvara missile.
Then, Lakṣmaṇa invoked the Māhendra missile endowed with the power of Rudra. By that terrible weapon, the enemy’s head was severed and brought down.
All the gods rejoiced and the leaders of the monkeys were delighted. Rāghava (Rāma) embraced Lakṣmaṇa and kissed him on the head.
The Rākṣasa army wailed, and the lord of the man-eaters, Rāvaṇa, wept. Overcome with grief, he swore to kill Maithilī (Sītā) and rushed toward her.
Other trusted counselors restrained him, saying, "This is improper." They blocked his path, and their kinship checked his sorrow-driven rage.
Rāvaṇa's heroism flared up and his indignation grew. Consequently, he prepared his entire army for battle.
Fearful of the impending war, the Yātudhānas (demons) worshipped the sacrificial fires, bowed to Śaṅkara, and gratified the Brāhmaṇas for peace.
A pleasant breeze scented with clarified butter blew all around. The sacred chanting of "Auspicious Day" and "Peace" was heard rising high.
The warriors bore consecrated water mixed with grains on their heads for peace. They gave away gems and cows, and sought blessings for victory.
They anointed themselves with white sandalwood paste and dressed in colorful robes. They wore beautiful garlands, while others quickly donned their armor.
They sharpened their weapons and polished their heaps of swords. Mounting elephants and other steeds, they set out in great haste.
The roar arising from the mobilization of the army filled the sky. The quarters of the earth were filled with the tumultuous sounds of trumpets.
There was a massive congestion of chariots, horses, elephants, and Rākṣasas at the gates. Terrifying and great ill-omens occurred simultaneously.
At that sight, the monkeys grew fearful, yet they broke large trees. They quickly uprooted mountains and seized massive boulders.
Then the battle commenced as the monkeys and Rākṣasas struck each other. They overcame one another and endured the fierce crushing conflict.
Dust rose from the earth and spread across the ten directions. It stole away the ability of the monkeys and Rākṣasas to distinguish between friend and foe.
Then, in the pitch darkness, the Rākṣasas hated their own kin and others; likewise, the merciless Vānaras felt enmity even toward fellow Vānaras.
They roared most hideously, and then blood began to flow; by that blood, mire was formed everywhere on the battlefield.
Deep rivers of blood flowed and pools were formed; the rising dust was settled by it, and the enemies became visible to each other.
Then Rāma performed wonders with his multitude of weapons and brandished his great bow; neither his own side nor the enemy could perceive his intended movements.
They saw the mangled and split bodies everywhere pierced by Rāma's arrows and heard the cries of "Alas! Alas!", yet they could not spot Rāma himself.
He split the enemy ranks, crushed horses and elephants, and ground down the chariot divisions, yet he remained unperceived as he moved about.
Ten thousand elephants, fourteen thousand high-souled chariot-warriors, and fourteen thousand horses with their riders were slain.
In just the eighth part of the day, two hundred thousand foot-soldiers were brought to their end by the bow-wielding Rāghava.
With the massive slain Rākṣasas, he made the earth appear like the realm of Yama or the cremation ground of Rudra, piling them up like mountains.
The Devas and Gandharvas praised him, the monkeys were amazed, and joy spread through Sugrīva, while the son of Pulastya (Rāvaṇa) considered it a miracle.
The Rākṣasa women wept loudly and despised Rāvaṇa; the young and the old were bewildered, and the rest of the people wailed together.
They said that Rāvaṇa, who did not desire safety from humans, was now facing this fruit of his wicked speech.
Then Rāvaṇa, mounting a terrifying chariot, rushed forward; the earth trembled, and fearsome vultures began to hover around.
Clouds with lightning showered blood that soaked the clothes; fierce winds blew, and inauspicious jackals howled.
Disregarding these bad omens, he wandered about the battlefield, brandished his bow, and repeatedly covered the enemies with showers of missiles.
Then the mountains hurled by Sugrīva destroyed the enemies; thereafter, the enemy shrieked, grew exhausted, and lay prostrate on the ground.
Blood flowed like water; being extremely distressed and weary, the army of the man-eaters, tormented by Sugrīva, perished.
Then Virūpākṣa sported in battle with a rutting elephant; the lord of monkeys (Sugrīva) shattered his head with a fist.
Immediately after, he crushed Yūpākṣa with a rock; then the enraged Aṅgada struck Mahodara violently with his fist.
Then the infuriated Daśagrīva took the lives of the forest-dwellers, protected the Rākṣasas, and made the enemies flee to different directions.
Rāvaṇa gazed at Rāma, the descendant of Kākutstha, grew bold, and roared terrifyingly. Brandishing his formidable bow, he struck fear into his enemies.
He attacked Lakṣmaṇa with arrows and quickly bypassed him. The victorious Rāvaṇa then rushed toward Rāma and overwhelmed him with a torrential rain of shafts.
The unperturbed Rāma warded off that shower of arrows with his crescent-headed shafts and countered the ten-necked Rāvaṇa with arrows as deadly as venomous serpents.
Moving in wondrous circular orbits and slicing through masses of weapons, the two warriors amazed the world, neither showing any sign of exhaustion.
They filled the sky with arrows and scorched the earth with their swift movements. Wounding each other rapidly, they repeatedly demonstrated their expert martial training.
The demon of cruel prowess discharged the Āsura weapon, which brought forth giant serpents and terrifying tigers and lions.
Rāma neutralized that with the fire weapon. Subsequently, the Rākṣasa employed the exceedingly fierce Raudra weapon, from which maces and other missiles began to fall.
Then the King (Rāma) countered it with the Gāndharva weapon. The man-eater Rāvaṇa then struck the descendant of Kākutstha in all his vital parts with sharp, stone-tipped arrows.
Then Lakṣmaṇa cut down Rāvaṇa's three-headed banner, quickly slew his charioteer, and pierced the demon with numerous arrows.
Vibhīṣaṇa struck the horses and quickly destroyed the chariot. The Rākṣasa did not falter; instead, he pulled out a heavy spear to hurl at his brother.
Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, cut the incoming spear into three pieces with his arrows. While the onlookers cheered, the night-stalker Rāvaṇa became enraged.
Raising a massive spear adorned with eight bells, Rāvaṇa struck Rāma’s younger brother, who then fell to the earth, appearing lifeless.
Rāghava’s arrows grew more intense in their fury. Harassed by them, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa soon fled from the battlefield.
The elder brother (Rāma) pulled the spear from the quivering Lakṣmaṇa and applied the medicinal herbs brought by Hanumān.
The son of Sumitrā returned to life. His brother Rāma embraced him closely, kissed his head, and enquired about his well-being.
Then all regained their courage to fight, and Rāma rushed at the foes. Rāvaṇa, arriving in another chariot, appeared unassailable.
Thinking it an unequal battle between one on the ground and one in a chariot, Mātali, by the command of Maghavān (Indra), brought a formidable, weapon-laden chariot.
Rāma mounted the chariot and discharged the Pāśupata weapon. The King then overcame the Ten-faced one’s weapon using the weapon of Śakra (Indra).
Then Rāma covered the night-stalker with a hundred thousand arrows, killed his lead horses, and quickly distressed his charioteer.
Ill omens appeared and the earth trembled. Rāvaṇa hurled a trident, while Rāma, the Lord of the Earth, hurled the spear of Indra.
Encountering each other, both attained a state of calm determination. The enraged Rākṣasa (Rāvaṇa) then struck the chest of Rāma with a hundred thousand feathered arrows.
Thereafter, Rāma scattered arrows even more profusely and sported with his shafts. Rāvaṇa did not tire, and his charioteer drove the chariot away from immediate danger.
The Rākṣasa rebuked his charioteer and drove the chariot forward again. Both warriors discharged arrows and both pierced the opponent's yoke-horses.
Both sliced through each other’s banners, yet neither felt any pain. These two bold warriors shone brilliantly and displayed great skill in combat.
Both heroes spread forth their illusory powers (māyā), and neither became exhausted. Both swiftly moved through various wonderful circular maneuvers.
Neither warrior was visible to the other, and both struck the opposing charioteers. The chariots of both, drawn by spirited horses, collided with each other.
Then, in the battle, the Rākṣasa manifested numerous illusory heads. Rāma, with his sharp arrows (śilīmukha), cut off a hundred of them.
The oceans became agitated, and the mountains trembled. Śakra (Indra) felt fear, and the disturbed earth swayed violently.
Then, Mātali reminded the King (Rāma) of the fierce weapon that Svayambhū (Brahmā) had fashioned specifically for the destruction of Rāvaṇa.
Wind resided in its feathers, the Sun and Fire in its tip; it possessed weight like Mount Meru, yet its body was subtle and ethereal.
Adorned with wings like those of Garuḍa and serving as the abode of all energies, that terrible weapon, once invoked, pierced Rāvaṇa and laid him low on the ground.

The monkeys' faces beamed with joy, and the gods praised the King who conquered his enemy. The world became free from turmoil, while the descendant of Pulastya (Vibhīṣaṇa), having lost his kinsmen, gave way to grief.
Then, sorrow arising from the ties of brotherhood overcame Vibhīṣaṇa. He wept loudly for the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
The ten-necked one, accustomed to luxurious beds, now lies on the bare ground. He does not even look at me in my distress, nor does he grant me a single word.
O Rāvaṇa! I foresaw this consequence before it arrived. You were advised on what was beneficial, yet why did you not restrain your anger?
Misfortunes quickly strike and prosperity departs from those who, out of pride, do not abide by the counsel of those who speak justly.
Followers, driven by greed, suggest what is harmful in the long run. Prosperity does not come to one who only listens to pleasant words from them.
The wise and brilliant see things clearly and speak the truth. O Great King! When they are disrespected, they become weary and cease to offer counsel.
He who always accepts beneficial advice, even if it is bitter like medicine, and consults trusted well-wishers for that purpose, never perishes.
Pride arises in everyone, leading to negligence toward their own welfare. In times of growth, a person adopts harmful ways, which eventually leads to their destruction.
He who generally hates virtues, lacks affection for anyone, and behaves with hostility toward the great, perishes even if he was once prosperous.
Since my brother, the lord of the three worlds, lies sleeping on the earth, how shall I be consoled? How can I, fallen into such misery, continue to live?
Alas, destiny is awake in times of distress! My kinsmen, who had even conquered Indra, now roll on the ground, suffer, and sleep the sleep of death.
Jackals tear at the flesh and the earth drinks the blood, while birds of prey devour the meat of the kinsmen of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa.
Even on the head of Indrajit, who once stood upon the head of Indra in the great battle, crows now settle due to the turn of fate.
Rāhu spits out the swallowed Sun after finishing his ritual, but no one who is swallowed by Rāma ever attains prosperity again.
O King! Unaware of this fate, you kept praising your own prowess. You did not wish to return Sītā, and now you no longer rule over your territories.
In the council, the ignorant spoke and you agreed with them. How did you not recognize your own benefit in that situation?
O descendant of Pulastya! Your maternal grandfather offered beneficial advice in the council even without being asked. Yet, out of delusion, you told him you would not follow it.
O Great King! You now know the truth of what Vibhīṣaṇa said, whom you angrily insulted and abandoned in the assembly long ago.
Now, Indra eats the sacrificial offerings in rituals without fear. The wind blows at its own will, and the Sun rises freely.
The Yakṣas rule over wealth, Yama subdues the Rākṣasas, Varuṇa spreads his noose, and now the Moon rises unhindered.
The cycle of seasons becomes calm, and the forest-dwellers perform penance. They no longer bow to your kinsmen, and the gods no longer serve you.
Prosperity is departing from Laṅkā, and riches are fading away. There is no one who does not perceive the reversal of fortune that has occurred upon your death.
Śakra (Indra) embraces his power once more, and Hari (Viṣṇu) guards his fortune. The worshipful gods rejoice, and the gathering of clouds appears wondrous.
Full of indignation, the gods bear their weapons and desire battle. They shine against the flesh-eaters and watch for their vulnerabilities.
They roam repeatedly around Laṅkā and surpass even us. They magnify their own strength and diminish our fame.
Arrogant ones pervade all directions and abandon the order established by you. These insignificant ones crush us and laugh at you, who have fallen into misfortune.
O Great King! The winds blow peacefully and purify the world on all sides. Why do you, who are now silent and still, not rise up again?
Grief envelops my mind, and my vital strength seems to fade. Sorrow wipes away my vision, and without you, I lose all my energy.
With whom shall I confer? There is no one more affectionate toward kinsmen than you. I cry out in the void; how shall I cover the outburst of my grief?
Bereft of you, my brother, I weep for my orphaned self. I cannot even fathom the extent of the favors you have bestowed upon me.
O Daśānana! Now Indra and the Lord of Yakṣas (Kubera) are no longer afraid, nor are they deprived. Proudly, they do not abandon their arrogance nor are they distressed anymore.
Even though we are separated from you, we continue our activities and set our minds on living. Fie upon this desire for life that destroys all that has been done!
If you do not grant me a word, I shall destroy my own body. Remembering your virtues indeed lengthens my sorrow.
Who will take off his own garland and laughingly garland me? Who will bring a seat near to me, and who indeed will speak words pleasing to me?
As long as I hold onto life, I shall not enter the city of Laṅkā. If I do not see you, when will I ever find joy?
Distraught by the loss of my brother, I shall surely die after a short while. I used to speak what was beneficial in counsel; I never did anything unpleasant to you.
Hearing that the son of Pulastya (Rāvaṇa) had been killed by Rāma in battle, the women of the inner apartments and the citizens ran toward him, deeply grieved.
They tore their hair and wailed in extreme distress. They repeatedly remembered their lord's favors with great sorrow.
The citizens bowed to Rāvaṇa and wept with tears. Then, Rāma spoke words to the distressed Vibhīṣaṇa (the son of Pulastya).
Why do you grieve for the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), who was a donor, who stood upon the heads of his enemies, who performed sacrifices, who satiated his ancestors, and who died unbowed in battle?
Delusion does not repeatedly overcome those like you in times of calamity. Do you not see that all these people are dependent upon you?

O King of the Rākṣasas, you ought to perform the final rites for your brother and dispel the grief of these people. When the foremost leader has perished, the burden of the kingdom sinks while remaining uncarried, even as you are present.
Then, freed from anger, Vibhīṣaṇa spoke to Rāma: "Does a kinsman, though unworthy of grief, not cause pain when he goes to his destruction?"
May the gods grant us that destiny by which we, like Rāvaṇa, may conquer our enemies and die in battle.
May other man-eaters in our clan, like the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), turn the gods toward heaven and humble the hosts of enemies.
Only he can sustain life in such a disaster involving kinsmen, who has a powerful friend like Rāma as a comforter.
I would die after a moment if you were not my refuge. Now that the ten-headed one is dead, our only hope is that we may live.
How can we find any contemptible pleasure in a land where there is no longer the presence of a brother with twenty hands?
Then Vibhīṣaṇa addressed the bowing ministers: "Go quickly to Laṅkā and enter the royal palace."
"Speedily take up precious garments there; raise excellent banners and bring forth the finest sandalwood."
"Release incense into the air, weave auspicious garlands, and bring plenty of wood, camphor, aloe-wood, and saffron."
"Let the sacrificial vessels be carried, let the fire be brought, let the ghee be borne by the priests, and let the fuel and sacrificial grass be prepared."
"Bathe him quickly with cleansing waters, smear him with beautiful pigments, and adorn the ten-faced one with jewels worthy of Rāvaṇa."
"Dress the lord of the Rākṣasas in two pure, fine garments. Let the priest place him, wearing garlands, upon a deer-skin with his head facing the east."
"Arrange the sacrificial vessels in the specified places according to rite. Offer oblations into the fire, and let the Sāman-singers chant the hymns."
Then they went to the city of Laṅkā, and having performed everything as commanded, tearfully spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa near the time of the final oblation.
"Everything has been done as directed. O Great King, strive now to perform the rites of fire and water along with all your kinsmen."
"You should not behave like an ignorant man; maintain unshakable courage. Stand firm in the duties toward your kinsmen and abandon the darkness born of grief."
"It is not fitting that even you should faint in times of difficulty. A wise person should never be bewildered like an ordinary man."
"Where you stand, no other relative of Rāvaṇa can stand. If you were to sink in despair, it would be condemned by the great."
"It is indeed a wonder that we are advising you; for you are capable of instructing even the priest of Indra, Bṛhaspati, in times of crisis."
"The people desire that you, O Lord of the Niśācaras, abandon neglect. Even enemies might grieve in a calamity; what then to say of kinsmen?"
You should protect all people properly, like a brother. If you do not become deluded, the niśācaras will also find comfort and confidence.
Then he went to perform the fire and water rites for his brother. Thereafter, Rāma spoke these words to the rākṣasa who had fulfilled his duty.
While sprinkling water from a golden pitcher on his head with composure, Rāma said, "O Vibhīṣaṇa, may you, as the king of the rākṣasas, look after Laṅkā."
