O Paulastya, you should properly conciliate the angry, win over the greedy with wealth, honor the proud at the right time, and comfort the terrified.
It is my supreme desire—how might you rejoice like Indra? For every friend naturally wishes for a friend who is established in prosperity.
May you prosper among your own kinsmen and destroy the hosts of enemies. May you be honored by the virtuous and remain firm in their established code of conduct.
May you bestow affection upon your friends and worship the gods. May you drink the soma juice and abandon violent, harmful actions.
O King, you should decide the affairs of the citizens according to dharma. You should always inspire universal affection among the people.
May anger be destroyed by you and may prosperity be attained. May you be seen by the rākṣasas, and may they be looked upon by you with favor.

O King, destroy the grief of the young and old caused by the slaughter of warriors. May wise men learned in the śāstras grace your assembly. Delve into the path of abundant dharma followed by gods and sages. Discern the intentions of enemies through the eyes of sound policy.
Then, the son of the wind (Hanumān), having approached Sītā, said: "O Vaidehī! Congratulations by good fortune! The thorn of the three worlds (Rāvaṇa) has been slain."
"Permit me that these mean-minded ogresses, who were your wardens, be slain by me. Harbor resentment against them."
"I shall crush those whose conduct, appearance, intentions, and actions are terrible. Let your mind be vengeful; treat them harshly."
"O Queen! Let us perform this final service dear to you." Then Sītā, filled with compassion, spoke to the monkey Hanumān.
"Let your mind be appeased toward these low-natured beings who were merely earning their livelihood. He (Rāvaṇa), by whom this wrong was committed, has been slain."
"Indeed, let it not be your intention to commit the terrible slaughter of servants. Be my messenger; go and speak to Rāghava (Rāma)."
"O Rāma! Maithilī (Sītā) desires to see you; let her behold you without delay." Having promised "so be it," Hanumān went and spoke to Rāghava.
"O Joy of the Kakutstha lineage! Let the longing Queen be brought here." Scratching the earth and sighing, Rāma looked at the sky and then at Vibhīṣaṇa.
Rāghava said: "Bring Sītā adorned with ornaments." Having gone and bowed, Vibhīṣaṇa spoke sweet words to Maithilī.
"O Vaidehī! Abandon grief and set your mind on joy. Discard hatred for Rāvaṇa and leave the Pramadavana grove."
"Bathe, apply ointments, perfume yourself, dress, and put on garlands. Wear gems and offer oblations into the blazing fire."
"Consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and dispel the gloom born of confinement. Mount the golden palanquin and defeat the desires of the enemies."
"Let the Lord of Kings (Rāma) destroy the grief arising from separation from you. Henceforth, may you be established in your own home."
"Promptly undergo initiation with Rāma for the Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha). Be beheld by your gratified husband and gaze upon Rāghava with love."
"This is the command of your husband; there should be no hesitation here. If Rāma is your authority, adorn your body and strive to go to him."
"Join the descendant of Kakutstha (Rāma) with joy and personally attain prosperity. O Queen! After a moment, approach the presence of Rāghava."
"O dear one! After a moment of the day, become the mistress of the earth. Rule over the city folk who are established in their duties to the King's consort."
"Arise according to your husband’s wish and strive to adorn yourself. Set out to see the King, who is worthy of being seen."
Having performed the command as directed, the daughter of Janaka (Sītā), with her face veiled by a silken cloth, mounted the vehicle.
Bowed with modesty and overwhelmed by the memory of the sorrow of separation, she, tearful and distressed, approached her husband's presence and wept.
Then the king, having developed a doubt regarding her character, said to her, "O Sītā, I do not accept you. This is my wish; depart from here."
You, who were held in the lap of Rāvaṇa, cause pain to my heart. Fix your mind on Sugrīva or accept the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Enjoy pleasures from Bharata or choose Lakṣmaṇa. Go wherever you wish. Let your hopes tied to Rāma be abandoned.
Where is the renowned lineage of Raghu, and where are you, who have lived in another's house? Give your heart to another; I do not unite with what is undesirable.
O Vaidehī, wander as you please; may your paths be auspicious. Let your desires be fulfilled elsewhere. Abandon any apprehension regarding me.
Then, she of Mithilā extraction spoke these words to the king: "Release the doubt concerning me that has arisen from generalizations about women."
O descendant of Kakutstha, fear fate and be ashamed before the people. Do not be falsely angry at me, who was carried away by the enemy against my will.
The activity of my mind was centered on you, though my body was seized by the Rākṣasa. Let the upright gods bear witness that this statement is true.
O Wind, purifying the three worlds with the thought "purify, purify," and moving within the bodies of living beings, know if there was any deviation in my intellect.
O Waters, most holy, wandering with the command "wander through the sky, the heaven, and the earth," know my auspicious mental state.
O Earth, supporting the worlds with the decree "sustain, sustain," know my character, which remained unwavering day and night.
O Sun, striving to "withdraw fluids, shine, destroy darkness, and roam the sky," endeavor to know my conduct.
O Space, dwelling with the mandate "exist in heaven, stay on earth, be in the abode of serpents," perceive what I have done and what I have not.
O son of Sumitrā, prepare a pyre as the remedy for this calamity. Today, let Rāma be satisfied with me, or let the fire consume me if I am sinful.
Then, seeing the pyre piled by Lakṣmaṇa at the behest of Rāghava, and circumambulating Rāma, she spoke these words.
I have been doubted by you; I shall cast my body into the fire. Let all of you, including the monkeys, know and hear this.

O Fire, with your blazing form, consume me if I am wicked, or protect me like a friend if I am free from blemish. Like a stream of clarified butter in sacrifices, I have reached you whose garland of flames is blazing according to rite.
Lifting Maithilī from the flames, Agni addressed Rāma: "O descendant of Kakutstha! How could you harbor doubts about your virtuous beloved?"
"Had I not protected her, she would not have remained pure. O Rāghava! I have no partiality toward her other than my devotion to Dharma."
"Even the evil-minded enemy would not have dared to desire Sītā. He might have spoken cruelly or boasted of his own opulence, but he could not touch her."
"Pure in heart, she would never have entertained a thought of him. Rāma, your indignation on account of Sītā was truly justified."
"Having lived with her for so long, did you not perceive her character? Could her conduct not have been observed by you over all this time?"
"Had you not abandoned this delusion, you would have grieved for a lifetime. If her virtue had been shaken, even the sun would have fallen to the earth."
"O King of kings! Had there been any feminine fickleness in her, these guardians of the world, who are enemies of sin, would not have descended here."
"It is a wonder that you believed she would remain in such distress. Had she perished out of fear, what possible fruit would you have gained?"
"Had this faultless woman died of terror, it would have provided a false pretext for reproach in a world prone to envy."
"Had your doubts been true, your father, King Daśaratha, would not have appeared here personally in his celestial chariot."
"Had Maithilī been enjoyed by another, the trident-bearing Sthāṇu, who rides the bull, would not have graced this place with his presence."
"O King! If Sītā's character had been stained, how could Brahmā, the creator of the universe seated on the lotus, have come to gladden you?"
Then Brahmā spoke to the lord of kings, who was bowing: "If Maithilī had not performed this trial, she would not have shone so brightly in the world."
"If you had not entertained doubt, we would not have been able to dispel it. What you did was entirely appropriate and not at all surprising."
"If your actions proceeded according to the absolute truth, then in the world governed by you, the people would have lived most righteously."
Then Śaṅkara said to the bowing Rāma: "Would you not have recognized yourself as the unborn Nārāyaṇa?"
"Who else could have severed the lives of the arrogant enemies of the gods? Who else would have exerted himself in deeds for the benefit of all humanity?"
"O Great King! Whatever efforts you exerted for the destruction of the demons, would you not have certainly brought your desired goal to completion?"
Having pacified his father, who had been distressed by Kaikeyī for the sake of Bharata, Rāma, wishing to offer salutations, beheld the thousand-eyed Indra.
Then, by the boon of Śakra, the dead monkeys returned to life, and the trees became full of fruit, bending low and shining with sap.

Mount Suvela displayed the splendor of juicy fruits. It abounded with trees bearing intensely fragrant flowers swarming with bees, while its lofty peaks were tinged tawny by blooming young Madhūka trees. Furthermore, the mountain featured water channels naturally formed amidst the crevices of its rocky summits.

The joy of the Vānaras, born from the anticipation of the enemy’s destruction, was further augmented by breezes blowing with flower pollen, forest regions bowed down under the weight of abundant fruits, and dripping honeycombs.

The fragrant creepers of the trees, bending to the point of breaking under the weight of their own fruits and covered with swarms of bees, could be harvested while standing on the ground. Consequently, they did not cause any pitiless exhaustion to those consuming the fruits.
Then Rāma said to the joyful Hanumān, "O monkey! Tomorrow you shall travel to Ayodhyā, which is protected by Bharata."
You will once again traverse the sky filled with rows of blossoming cloud clusters and witness the cool water-sprays of the lord of the waters, the ocean.
O monkey, you will visit the tablelands of the Mahendra mountain, which possess night-lotuses illuminated by moonlight and where the sun's path is obstructed.
Those auspicious valleys of the Malaya mountains, covered with sandalwood trees and freed from the laxity caused by frost, shall be seen by you.
On the Vindhya mountains, the slender and delicate creepers, adorned with clusters of flowers and swarmed by bees, will not be able to withstand your speed.
Filled with joy and remembering your past sports, you will soon see Kiṣkindhā, frequented by friends, with great partiality and affection.
You will see those regions in the Mālyavat and Daṇḍakā forests where I suffered for a long time, tormented by the pairs of opposites and the pain of separation.
You will reach the beautiful hermitages of Sutīkṣṇa and Śarabhaṅga, which are crowded with deer and filled with holy waters and brāhmaṇas.
You will cross the beautiful penance-grove of Atri with difficulty, and you will stay upon the sacred Citrakūṭa mountain out of curiosity.
After that, the sage Bharadvāja will be seen by you, along with holy people whose sins have been washed away by the waters of the Yamunā.
Then you will plunge into the Gaṅgā, which, flowing from heaven and descending onto Śambhu’s head, has reached the earth like a liquid form of merit.
From the edge of the forest of the Tamasā river, which has the luster of a great sapphire, you will highly admire the trees used by city-dwellers for recreation.
Having seen the beautiful Sarayū, reddish-yellow from the washed-away saffron applied to the breasts of city women, you shall reach the city of Ayodhyā.
Upon seeing you, the mothers will be delighted and will ask about our welfare; Bharata will be greatly pleased along with the news of Maithilī.
You shall quickly report that the enemy is slain, Vibhīṣaṇa is consecrated, Sugrīva is won as an ally, and that everyone is returning home soon.
Upon hearing your words, the citizens will attain great joy. Having known this, Bharata will certainly come forward to meet us.
Once you have gone by this path, we too shall set out. When you appear before me again, I shall obtain peace of mind.
When Hanumān had departed after grasping the message, Rāma said to Sugrīva and the Rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa, "Tomorrow, you both shall go to the city with me."
There you will see my three mothers, who will be pleased in their hearts, and you will attain an everlasting friendship and refuge with Bharata.
Thus we shall not be struck by the sorrow of separation, and the exhaustion born of parting from you both will not be experienced.
"O Monkey and Rākṣasa! If you both endeavor to travel with me tomorrow morning, you will have prepared yourselves for my satisfaction," said Rāma.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa and the Monkey Sugrīva spoke to Rāma: "O Kakutstha! It is a great favor that we shall go along with you."
"We do not consent to be separated from you. Even if we attained the status of the king of gods, what use would that position be if granted by you but without your presence?"
Then, having spent the night in conversation, they boarded the Puṣpaka chariot with their armies and set forth, agitating the deep waters of the ocean with their great speed.
Rāma journeyed on, pointing out the Bridge, Mount Mahendra, Malaya, the Vindhyas, Mount Mālyavān, Mount Ṛṣyamūka, the regions of the Daṇḍaka forest, and the Pampā lake to his beloved Sītā.

"O slender-waisted one! Here are those regions adorned by sages; this is that Mount Citrakūṭa with its swaying forests; and this is the Gaṅgā, beautiful with her wide banks." Pointing these out to Maithilī, the descendant of Raghu rejoiced.
"O fair-limbed one! Look at these delightful forest outskirts, fit for the enjoyment of city-dwellers, where bees buzz around flowers and cool waters overflow, pleasing the eyes."

"This is the seat of our ancestors; from afar is seen the most beloved city Ayodhyā, where all gods are pleased by various oblations. O Sītā! This is the place from which we, along with the resolute Lakṣmaṇa, departed for the forest at dawn, leaving the citizens weeping."

Then Bharata arrived, accompanied by Hanumān, filling the world with the sound of trumpets and shaking the earth with the stride of mountain-like elephants. With eyes full of tears of joy, he approached humbly alongside his mothers, the royal ladies, and the ministers.
Then the delight of the Raghus entered the city, surrounded by the excited citizens, while Bharata held the bright fly-whisk for him. He was greeted and praised by his elders, brahmins, and bards.

Having established great contentment among the people and having anointed Bharata as the crown prince, the lord of subjects, having made all preparations, endeavored to perform the Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha).

This work, which illustrates the path to liberation through its excellent composition, brings victory to those who debate and speak, just as the well-aimed weapon of Śiva (Aiśvara-astra) brings victory in battle.
This composition is like a lamp to those who possess the eye of grammar. Without grammar, it would be like a mere touch of the hand to the blind.
This poem is understandable only through commentary; it is a great festival for the wise. In this work, because of my love for scholars, I have frustrated the dull-witted.
I composed this poem in Valabhī, protected by King Śrīdharasena. May the fame of that king flourish, for he is a ruler who brings affection to his subjects.
